title: (Digitaler) Omnibus: „Größter Rückschritt für Grundrechte in der Geschichte der EU“ und beginnender Widerstand
content:
Dossier


„

Die Europäische Kommission arbeitet an Plänen für einen Kahlschlag bei ihren Regeln für die digitale Welt. Das belegen unter anderem Dokumente, die wir veröffentlicht haben. Im Europäischen Parlament und in der Zivilgesellschaft formiert sich dagegen massiver Widerstand.

Das erklärte Ziel von Ursula von der Leyen ist es, die Europäische Union in ihrer zweiten Amtszeit als Präsidentin der EU-Kommission wirtschaftlich und geopolitisch zu stärken. Erreichen will sie das offenbar auch durch einen weitgehenden Rückbau des Regelwerkes für die digitale Welt, welches die EU in den vergangenen zehn Jahren gestrickt hat. Davon zeugen

Entwürfe für ein geplantes Gesetzespaket


, die wir am vergangenen Freitag veröffentlicht haben.  

Vier Regulierungsbereiche stehen im Fokus des sogenannten „digitalen Omnibus“: der Datenschutz, Regeln für die Datennutzung, Cyber-Sicherheit und die KI-Verordnung

…“

Beitrag von Ingo Dachwitz vom 13.11.2025 in Netzpolitik


 – siehe mehr Informationen und einen Offenen Brief dagegen:


[Offener Brief] Letzte Chance, den europäischen Datenschutz zu retten: Der „Digitale Omnibus“ der EU ist der größte Angriff auf unsere Daten seit Jahren


„

Digitalcourage kämpft mit breitem europäischem Bündnis dagegen an.


Der „Digitale Omnibus“ ist ein Gesetzespaket der EU, das uns als „Vereinfachung“ verkauft wird. Tatsächlich aber höhlt es die Datenschutz-Rechte aus, die wir über Jahrzehnte erkämpft haben. Der Rat der Europäischen Union hat seine Position zum Digitalen Omnibus nun beschlossen. Sein Vorschlag liest sich als das faktische Ende der europäischen Datenschutz-Grundverordnung (DSGVO). Aktuell stimmt das Europäische Parlament seine Position ab – die Verhandlungen im Hintergrund laufen auf Hochtouren. In den kommenden Wochen ist die letzte Möglichkeit, die massiven Einschnitte in die Grundrechte europäischer Bürgerinnen und Bürger zu verhindern.


Gemeinsam mit einem breiten europäischen Bündnis aus Zivilgesellschaft, Wirtschaft und Wissenschaft fordert Digitalcourage deshalb das Europäische Parlament und die Mitgliedsstaaten in einem Offenen Brief dazu auf, die vorgesehenen Gesetzesänderungen abzulehnen. Mit dem geplanten Digitalen Omnibus droht die EU, die Grundrechte aller europäischen Bürgerinnen und Bürgern auszuhöhlen und ihre Privatleben an KI-Unternehmen zu verkaufen. (…)


Das EU-Parlament soll Anfang 2027 über das Gesetzespaket abstimmen. Danach verhandeln EU-Parlament und Ministerrat den endgültigen Text. Dabei ist klar: Eine deutliche Mehrheit der Bürger.innen ist für den Schutz unserer Rechte und für eine strenge Regulierung von KI. Jetzt gilt es, die Stimme der europäischen Zivilgesellschaft hörbar zu machen

…“

Meldung von Digitalcourage vom 26.11.2026


 zum

Offenen Brief

 


 (engl.)


EU-Länder einig beim Daten-Omnibus: Mehr KI-Training, weniger Datenschutz, Geschäftsgeheimnisse schützen


„… Künftig soll es in der EU weniger Cookie-Banner geben – aber nicht zu wenige, geht es nach den EU-Mitgliedstaaten. Zudem sollen personenbezogene Daten einfacher verwendet dürfen, um damit Künstliche Intelligenz zu trainieren. Das sind zwei der Punkte, auf die sich die EU-Länder in den Verhandlungen zum Daten-Omnibus geeinigt haben, wie gestern die irische Ratspräsidentschaft verkündete. Mit dieser Position wird der EU-Rat in die Trilog-Verhandlungen ziehen, sobald sich das EU-Parlament ebenfalls auf eine gemeinsame Position verständigt hat. Dies soll im Februar der Fall sein. Mit dem Gesetzespaket will die EU-Kommission die Nutzung von Daten vereinfachen, Regeln entschlacken und überlappende Gesetze harmonisieren. Während die Deregulierungsagenda der Kommission bei der Wirtschaft auf offene Ohren gestoßen ist, kritisierten Gewerkschaften, Verbraucherschutzorganisationen und zahlreiche zivilgesellschaftliche Gruppen sie als „größten Rückschritt für digitale Grundrechte“. (…) Nur ein Punkt wurde in der Zivilgesellschaft positiv aufgenommen: So hatte die EU-Kommission vorgeschlagen, die Cookie-Flut spürbar einzuschränken. (…) Keine Zustimmung wäre etwa dann nötig, wenn ein Cookie für die Erbringung einer Dienstleistung, für die Reichweitenmessung oder zur Gewährleistung der Sicherheit des Endgeräts der Nutzer:innen erforderlich ist, führt der Rat aus. Damit würden wohl einige Cookie-Banner verschwinden, allerdings zum Preis einer teils einfacheren Verfolgung von Nutzer:innen im Netz. Gegen den Vorschlag der Kommission hatten sich Länder wie Deutschland und Frankreich gestellt …

author: TGEU
title: Joint LGBTI+ NGO letter to the Turkish Embassy in Berlin, Germany
content:
On 25 November, TGEU – Trans Europe and Central Asia,

OII Europe

 and

OII Germany

 have sent a joint letter to the German foreign ministries to express serious concerns about the situation in Türkiye and the recent targeting of the LGBTI+ organisations and human rights defenders.


Since 12 September, several police raids have been conducted in Türkiye, targeting LGBTI+ human rights defenders and organisations, as part of the so-called “My Family is Safe” operations. During these raids, police seized digital equipment of the activists and organisations. Websites and social media accounts of LGBTI+ activists and organisations were blocked. 78 people have been in detention for 2 months. On 23 October, in a new wave of arrests, 45 people across 7 provinces were taken into custody and more than 20 of them, including 10 trans women, were imprisoned. Again, on 3 November, 22 people were detained and questioned, several of whom are trans women, in relation to “forming an organisation for the purpose of committing a crime”. Relying on obscenity clauses and provisions on prostitution, Turkish authorities have targeted trans people and sex workers in all waves of the arrests. 


Already, in January 2026, Ankara Public Prosecutor’s Office filed a lawsuit against head of the

17 Mayıs Association

 Defne Güzel with alleged charges of violating public morality by publishing the Turkish translation of

OII Europe’s publication #MyIntersexStory

, a collection of testimonies of intersex people, and an exhibition catalogue. The lawsuit followed an expert report from 2025 which concluded that the activities of the 17 Mayıs Association are entirely consistent with the objectives set out in its statutes and that there are no irregularities whatsoever. Güzel was later acquitted of all charges in the first hearing in May.  


Human rights at stake


These operations mark a significant escalation in the criminalisation of LGBTI+ human rights activism in Türkiye, and a direct attack on freedom of expression, association, and the defence of human rights. The October operations criminalise non-normative identities and bodies, including trans and intersex people and organisations, based only on social media posts declared by the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office as “contrary to public morality, targeting families, children and young people, detrimental to their development, encouraging gender neutrality and disruptive to public order”.


LGBTI+ organisations in Türkiye are targeted for their legitimate activities. The domestic and international funding they receive is lawful, and they operate as registered associations under Turkish law. With these actions, the Turkish government continues to undermine the right of legally registered organisations to participate in democratic processes.


The ongoing imprisonment of 78 individuals since September, the inhumane prison conditions and the torture perpetrated against them breach international human rights law, as well as the Constitution of Türkiye and the Turkish Penal Code. The European Court of Human Rights and the UN Human Rights Committee have made clear that public morality cannot justify infringing fundamental rights. These operations also institutionalise discrimination and arbitrary detention, fuel a climate of hatred, threaten the right to life of LGBTI+ people, and increase state-sanctioned hate speech.


Germany’s role


It is clear that the rights of LGBTI+ people in Türkiye and civic freedoms enjoyed by all Turkish citizens are at stake. As a longstanding strategic partner of Türkiye and a vocal critic of Türkiye’s backsliding on rule of law, it is imperative that Germany speaks up and reminds Türkiye of its obligations as a member of the Council of Europe and a candidate country of the EU, to respect fundamental human rights standards that apply to all, no matter a person’s sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics.


As the home to the largest Turkish diaspora, Germany hosts several LGBTI+ human rights defenders, whose work and ability to return to Turkey safely also depends on the end to the targeting of LGBTI+ human rights defenders. As one of the strongest supporters of Türkiye’s accession, Germany should actively support the freedom of association and LGBTI+ human rights in Türkiye.


Our demands


Therefore, the undersigned organisations operating in Germany urge the German foreign ministries to:


Call for the immediate release …

author: Main alba channel
title: Entretien avec Garcia Oliver
content:
Un entretien avec Juan García Oliver


120 min – espagnol sous-titré en français


■ «  La rencontre avec Juan García Oliver eut lieu à Paris, en juin de l’année 1977. De passage dans la capitale pour superviser les épreuves de ses mémoires, il me fut présenté par son éditeur, José Martínez. Le premier contact eut pour cadre un restaurant de la rue de Bièvre. Là, García Oliver m’apparut comme une sorte de fantôme nimbé d’histoire. C’est que l’homme, d’abord assez froid, semblait tout droit sorti d’un arrêt sur image. Comme si, au quarantième anniversaire d’une révolution presque oubliée, un de ses principaux protagonistes avait résisté au passage du temps et à ses effets sournoisement correctifs. Étrangement, le García Oliver de ce printemps 1977 était, physique mis à part, le même que celui qui, dans les années 1930, avait fait trembler, avec un semblable aplomb, la société espagnole et – pourquoi le taire ? – quelques anarchistes et syndicalistes de renom, que son « catastrophisme » inquiétait. Pour qui a travaillé sur le témoignage, une telle rencontre est rare, non tant parce qu’elle met en présence d’un authentique personnage – ce qui est somme toute banal quand il s’agit de la révolution espagnole –, mais parce que le bonhomme que vous avez en face de vous n’a pas changé d’un poil, qu’il argumente comme si l’événement durait encore, qu’il est toujours ce qu’il était, et non ce qu’il est devenu. Cette invariance – qui, à l’évidence, peut apparaître comme un défaut dans la vie courante – représente, dans le travail de mémoire, une appréciable qualité parce qu’elle restitue la vérité d’époque, dimension psychologique comprise, à un récit qui, sans elle, n’est souvent qu’une version corrigée et embellie d’un temps définitivement révolu. García Oliver, probablement encouragé en sous-main par son éditeur et ami, accepta sans réticence de se prêter au jeu – difficile et risqué – de l’entretien. Celui-ci eut lieu le 29 juin 1977 dans un appartement du douzième arrondissement de Paris. Pour l’occasion, García Oliver apparut batailleur, précis, sûr de lui, tranchant et quelque peu dominateur. Comme à la grande époque, disais-je. À l’évidence, le lecteur pourra être irrité par certaines affirmations péremptoires de l’interviewé, mais, tous comptes faits, il appréciera sûrement la valeur de cette personnelle part de vérité, d’autant qu’à ce jour, cette transcription – inédite en français – constitue l’unique témoignage de García Oliver dans notre langue.– Freddy Gomez  »


Pour en savoir plus : À contretemps, n° 17, juillet 2004

author: Joshua Carroll
title: Pollution From US Data Centres Caused 650 Early Deaths in 2023 Alone
content:
Increased pollution driven by data centres caused hundreds of premature deaths across the US in 2023, research by MIT scientists has found.


The modelling study,

published in Environmental Research Letters

, identified spikes in particulate matter from coal and gas power plants as they ramped up energy production to meet demand from the power-hungry infrastructure. 


An estimated 513 people died prematurely because of increased exposure to PM2.5, microscopic particles that are able to reach

deep areas of the lung

 and are linked to heart attacks, strokes and lung disease.


Another 137 deaths were attributed to higher concentrations of ozone, which can cause heart disease, the study said. 


The amount of toxic pollution from data centres has likely increased substantially since 2023 due to the rapid expansion of the facilities across the US, according to the authors of the study.


Because of the way the power grid is structured, the pollution is often emitted far from the sites of the data centres using the power. 


“Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data centre near you, think again,” said Noelle Selin, a co-author of the study and head of the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy at MIT. 


“When people think about the negative impacts of data centres, they usually focus on the neighbours. But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centres are very widespread across a large region.”


The impact of such pollution was most pronounced in the Midwest, a group of 12 states including Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota and Iowa. 


Residents of Iowa and elsewhere have been gripped by separate concerns about toxic pollution this week because of the US military’s

decision to detonate

 several tonnes of lead azide, a bomb-making chemical.

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: "I'm Not Going to Give Up": Leonard Peltier on Indigenous Rights, His Half-Century in Prison & Coming Home
content:
In September 2025,

Democracy Now!

 host Amy Goodman sat down with longtime political prisoner and Indigenous activist Leonard Peltier for his first extended television and radio broadcast interview since his release to home confinement in February 2025. Before his commutation by former President Joe Biden, the 82-year-old Peltier spent nearly 50 years behind bars. Peltier has always maintained his innocence for the 1975 killing of two

FBI

 officers. He is expected to serve the remainder of his life sentences under house arrest at the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Nation in Belcourt, North Dakota. In a wide-ranging conversation, we spoke to Peltier about his case, his time in prison, his childhood spent at an American Indian boarding school and his later involvement in the American Indian Movement (

AIM

) and more.


“We still have to live under that, that fear of losing our identity, losing our culture, our religion,” Peltier says about his continued commitment to Indigenous rights. “The struggle still goes on for me. I’m not going to give up.”

author: CNT Santander
title: No hay Revolución Social sin Revolución Feminista
content:
25N, DÍA INTERNACIONAL DE LA ELIMINACIÓN DE LA VIOLENCIA EJERCIDA SOBRE LA MUJER


 


Este 25 N, volvemos a salir a las calles

 para denunciar todas las formas de violencia que el patriarcado ejerce sobre nuestros cuerpos, nuestras vidas y nuestras libertades. Una violencia que no puede entenderse como un problema individual, porque es una violencia estructural. Está profundamente arraigada en un sistema que pretende controlar nuestros cuerpos, condicionar nuestras decisiones, limitar nuestra autonomía y mantenernos en una posición de subordinación.


El patriarcado nunca ha actuado solo. Lo sostiene el sistema capitalista en el que vivimos, y se reproduce a través del capacitismo, el edadismo, el racismo, la explotación laboral, el colonialismo, la homofobia, la transfobia, y todas aquellas estructuras de poder que no aceptan las disidencias y las diversidades, esas estructuras que generan desigualdades y convierten nuestras vidas en territorios de dominación.


La violencia machista tiene muchas caras, las mujeres lo sabemos bien; feminicidios, agresiones sexuales, acoso, maltrato psicológico, violencia sexual digital, abuso infantil, amenazas, control económico, humillación…


Y no debemos olvidar que se alimenta de la precariedad a la que nos condena, la explotación de las trabajadoras del hogar y quienes se encargan de los cuidados, la discriminación laboral, el racismo institucional, la violencia obstétrica, la negación de derechos y la falta de recursos y protección para quienes necesitan escapar de situaciones de violencia.


No todas las mujeres vivimos la violencia de la misma manera, pero somos capaces de entender el sufrimiento de nuestras iguales. Y queremos dejar claro que cuando hablamos de nuestras iguales, cuando utilizamos este femenino, no lo hacemos de una manera neutra. Nuestro plural femenino es, y será siempre, inclusivo con todas las disidencias, interseccional, transfeminista,

 

antirracista y sin jerarquías. Porque ha de ser una herramienta de emancipación colectiva.


Estamos con las mujeres migrantes y las racializadas, porque nos queremos sin fronteras. Estamos con las mujeres discas y las neurodivergentes, porque no nos queremos por nuestra capacidad de producir más y más. Estamos con las mayores, ancianas o viejas*, porque hay mucha vida y mucha lucha en la que nos necesitamos de todas las edades. Estamos con las mujeres encarceladas y las niñas que pasan su infancia y adolescencia en centros de menores, porque nos queremos libres. Estamos con las infancias abusadas. Estamos con las bolleras, las bi, las personas trans y no binarias, y todas las disidencias, porque nadie nos tiene que decir quiénes somos.


Sabemos que quienes viven en situaciones de exclusión social, por una parte de la sociedad enferma de odio, encuentran obstáculos añadidos para defenderse, denunciar y acceder a una vida digna y libre. Sus hermanas y hermanes no lo olvidamos.


Nuestros cuerpos no tienen dueño y nuestros corazones no necesitan pedir permiso para ser. Cada una tenemos derecho a vivir nuestra identidad, nuestra sexualidad y nuestra vida con dignidad, autonomía y total libertad.


La solución a esta violencia machista que nos mata y nos ahoga, es y siempre será la respuesta colectiva. Desde

CNT Santander

, denunciamos la indiferencia institucional, la falta de recursos públicos, la precarización de los servicios de atención y una justicia que muchas veces ni escucha ni protege a nuestras hermanas y hermanes, la precariedad laboral que impide a muchas mujeres tener su independencia económica y autonomía.


Por ello, la respuesta debe ser colectiva, sin fisuras, todas a una, hasta destruir todas las relaciones de poder que permiten que unas personas sometan a otras.


¡Frente a sus violencias, organización y autodefensa!


Como anarcosindicalistas, apostamos por el apoyo mutuo, la solidaridad combativa, la organización desde abajo y la construcción de redes comunitarias capaces de acompañar, escuchar, proteger y sostener a todas las mujeres. Reivindicamos la autodefensa feminista como una herramienta colectiva para recuperar nuestra autonomía, acabar con las agresiones machistas y romper el aislamiento que tantas veces impone esa maldita violencia.


Queremos espacios de trabajo libres de acoso y explotación, sindicatos comprometidos con la igualdad real y efectiva, barrios seguros para todas las personas y relaciones construidas desde el respeto, el consentimiento y la libertad.

author: Faiz Naeem
title: Supporting a progressive digital reform agenda for Bangladesh
content:
To: 

Mr. Tarique Rahman

Honourable Prime Minister

Government of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh


Subject: supporting a progressive digital reform agenda for Bangladesh


Bangladesh’s digital reforms are at a turning point. We, the undersigned organisations, urge your government to protect what has been achieved, restore the safeguards that have been stripped away, and build a legal and institutional framework that centres people’s rights, democratic accountability, and a free, open and secure internet.


Digital reform is an essential part of delivering on your

stated commitment

 to strengthen accountability and prevent authoritarianism. Laws and institutions governing online expression,  privacy, cybersecurity, surveillance and artificial intelligence shape how people participate in public life, access services, organise, communicate and hold power to account.


Prior to the interim government assuming office, the

Digital Security Act, 2018 (DSA) and Cyber Security Act, 2023 (CSA)

 were

repeatedly used to target journalists, activists and others for online expression

, internet

shutdowns were imposed

 during periods of political mobilisation; and

surveillance and interception capabilities expanded

 without sufficient transparency or independent oversight. Some reforms were initiated during the interim administration, which included somewhat

narrowing the criminalisation of some forms of online expression

 through the repeal of the CSA and enactment of the Cyber Security Ordinance, 2025, introducing requirements for explicit consent to process personal data with exemptions to such protection in limited circumstances under the

Personal Data Protection Ordinance, 2025

, and establishing a

prohibition on internet shutdowns

, now retained in

section


63 of the Bangladesh Telecommunication (Amendment) Act, 2026

, which amends

section 97 of the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulation Act, 2001

.


The subsequent legislative process has exposed how easily rights safeguards can be weakened while broader state powers remain intact. The Bangladesh

Telecommunication (Amendment) Act, 2026

 kept the Ordinance’s

wide interception powers

 but removed or diluted several safeguards. The Ordinance had

abolished the National Telecommunication Monitoring Centre (NTMC)

 and replaced it with the Centre for Information Support, prohibited interception for political or ideological purposes, and required every interception to be approved by a court or review council under detailed conditions. But the 2026 Act reversed all three. According to section 64 of the 2026 Act, which amends section 97(A) of the 2001 Act, interception may now be approved

by a court or simply by “an authority constituted by the government”,

 and the government alone decides which agency carries it out. The NTMC,

whose operations were extended for another year by the Ministry of Home Affairs

, continues to function without a clear, public-facing statutory mandate, independent oversight framework or meaningful transparency requirements. The

Personal Data Protection Act, 2026

, likewise,

exempts state authorities on broad and undefined grounds such as national security, public order and public interes

t

, without judicial supervision or any duty of transparency when the exemption on consent requirements for the processing of personal information is invoked.


These concerns are not abstract. The

UN fact-finding investigation

 into the events of July and August 2024 described how surveillance-derived intelligence was used in connection with repression of civil and political rights. A

government committee subsequently reviewed

 the procurement and use of surveillance technologies, but its report has still not been made public.


At the same time, proposals to criminalise “rumours”, “disinformation”, and “defamatory information” through

amendments to the


Cyber Security Act 2026

 would reverse the progress made by repealing earlier speech offences. Our objection is not to how these terms are drafted but to treating them as crimes at all. Under international human rights law, the dissemination of false or unverified information is not in itself a legitimate ground for criminal sanction; the UN Human Rights Committee has made clear that imprisonment is never an appropriate penalty for defamation.  The vaguely defined proposed offences fail this test: for instance, “rumours” could cover any unverified information that creates …

author: webadmin
title: Researched And ‘Observated’ To Death In The Barle Valley
content:
Stag chased to exhaustion and killed as the hunt invoked bogus exemptions when caught on camera.


WATCH THE VIDEO (VIEWER DISCRETION ADVISED)


The stag was pursued for hours. Credit North Dorset Hunt Sabs


On 17 October 2026, a North Dorset Hunt Saboteur witnessed the final moments of a stag pursued for hours through the Barle Valley before being shot in Marsh Wood. The stag was barely able to walk, his mouth wide open and tongue hanging out, with hounds and a gunman following behind.


Gunman James Wyatt following the stag, who by now was barely able to walk. Credit North Dorset Hunt Sabs


After they shot him, the excuses began.


Predictably, the focus turned to why the sab was there, rather than what they had just done to the animal. Perhaps the stress of having a sab witness their cruelty, made the hunters forget their well-rehearsed lines.


Wyatt was upset that his cruelty was being filmed. Credit: North Dorset Hunt Sabs.


This hunt hides behind the ‘Research and Observation’ smokescreen, but it is clearly a ruse, and the hunt even made up its own word to justify its cruelty.


Apparently, they had

‘observated’

 the stag. It’s not even a real word.


But those were the words of gunman James Wyatt. Mangled English aside, this exemption is nothing but a smokescreen for barbarism and bloodlust.


There is no research on these animals, there has never been – there are no known peer-reviewed research papers produced by hunts, from the hundreds or thousands of days spent hunting these magnificent animals.


In March 2019,

Defra told Parliament

 that it held no information about ‘research’ published under the exemption. That has not changed since. Shouting ‘Research and Observated’ over a tortured animal does not make it legal or acceptable.


James Wyatt alleged the stag was ‘researched and observated’ before being shot for his breeding behaviour. Credit: North Dorset Hunt Sabs.


After claiming that the stag was killed under the exemption, the hunter went on to immediately contradict himself – claiming that it was killed because of the stag’s breeding behaviour.


The animal – according to the hunters – had apparently been ‘servicing hinds’ for four or five years so that is why they took him out.


At first they claimed to kill this due to the ‘research and ‘observated’ exemption – then it was because of his breeding behaviour. Credit: North Dorset Hunt Sabs.


To hunt and kill an animal because of his breeding behaviour is not an exemption under the Hunting Act.


The mature stag was doing exactly what nature intended during the autumn rut. Where is the evidence to suggest this stag had been assessed and posed a problem to the wider deer population?


More importantly, how would any such concern justify pursuing him to exhaustion with dogs?


The Hunting Act sets out specific circumstances in which dogs may be used. Vague concerns around breeding are not one of them.


Other hunters warned the gunman that the hunt sab was below him on the hillside, but he fired the shot regardless, and this was followed by loud cheers.


Hunters attempted to prevent the sab from filming. Credit: North Dorset Hunt Sabs.


Hunters then attempted to shield the dead stag from the sab’s camera, before dragging his body down the hillside, the slit in his neck visible from where he had been bled.


The hunters drag the body away to be cut up into trophies. Credit: North Dorset Hunt Sabs.


The stag spent his final hours being hunted through the Barle Valley, he was exhausted, cornered and shot. He had done nothing wrong, and he was shot purely for living as a wild animal, breeding during the rut and attempting to evade those who wanted to kill him.


No words – real or made-up – should be allowed to obscure what happened to this animal and the cruelty inflicted upon him.


The government must confront the continuing barbaric cruelty and criminality that lie behind these exemptions.


Labour promised us a ban, a manifesto pledge to end this. Where is it?


A Hunt Saboteurs Association spokesperson said:


“It is not just foxes that are tormented and brutalised in our countryside by these bloodsports enthusiasts. Stag hunting is a particularly sickening form of cruelty, where terrified animals are pursued for hours, driving to complete exhaustion and then shot.


The idea that this barbarism can be passed off as ‘research and observation’ is an insult to anyone with an ounce of intelligence. These are not scientists conducting …

author: Justin Umali
title: Lakbayan nati’y hindi papipigil: detention and the Southern Tagalog Lakbayan
content:
Detention is neither romantic nor heroic. Writing about it even less so.

To be detained is to be denied your rights, whether for a few hours or for years. For activists, detention is the state’s reward for standing up to fight. For me and the rest of Southern Tagalog Lakbayanis, detention was a method of last resort.

November 15 was the fourth day of the Lakbayan. What was supposed to be a protest march from Los Baños, Laguna to Liwasang Bonifacio became a daily struggle against police checkpoints and blockades. On the second day, our jeep’s brake lines were cut, and we were held for four hours in Biñan, Laguna. On the third day, we were blocked from crossing from San Pedro to Muntinlupa.

So we found ways to skirt around and continue our Lakbayan. On the fourth day, the police had cordoned off all routes going outside of Brgy. Sucat, Muntinlupa. Regardless, we were determined to find a way to continue.

Thus, the arrests. It took the police roughly two hours to brutalize and transport us to Camp Bagong Diwa. At least eight officers manhandled me while I tried to rescue Southern Tagalog Exposure journalist Marky Casaquite. I felt the back of my head kiss the concrete pole before the two of us went down on the ground.

The rest of us received similar treatments. Some of us were sucker punched. Others were kicked around. The worst had his knee dislocated. The entire time we asserted that there were no charges against us.

There is nothing romantic about police brutality. The state, with its monopoly on violence, can choose to impose it on the people at will. We were activists, unionists, media workers, paralegals, peasants, and indigenous youth from all over Southern Tagalog. Our weapons were our words and our principles. What could we have done against truncheons and riot shields?

But despite the brutality, I saw firsthand how determination beats physical strength. The police had barely begun their arrests when we started sending our alerts, communication, and other means. In the police trucks, we consoled each other that things would be fine while medics tended to our injuries. Those of us who were familiar with the legal system explained to the others what our rights were and what was to be expected.

When our trucks finally began to move, we started chanting: “Ang tao, ang bayan, ngayon ay lumalaban!” “Timog Katagalugan, tuloy-tuloy ang laban!” and “Reject, oppose, junk Pax Silica!” The neighborhood responded by cheering, raising their fists, and thanking us for fighting the good fight.

Even before the arrests, they were already showing their support by giving what they can. Some residents climbed a gate to give us packs of water bottles. One resident gave out hats that we could wear.

Another woman went back and forth to a nearby grocery store to buy snacks and water. She was a sari-sari store owner who asked me where we came from. When she found out that we started the Lakbayan in Los Baños, she said that she couldn’t imagine why anybody would march from Laguna to Muntinlupa. But she understood what we were marching for, and for me, that was enough.

A few days after the ASEAN Summit, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. went on record to say that he was “perplexed” why people were protesting against Pax Silica. He couldn’t imagine the ordinary Filipino being able to dissect the issue and see the initiative for what it really was: a sell-out of Philippine sovereignty for US interests.

In Sucat, coastal communities are threatened by the construction of the Laguna Lakeshore Road Network, a stretch of highway meant to expedite the transportation of raw materials and finished products from Laguna’s industrial enclaves to Manila, and ultimately, to the economic security zone in Capas, Tarlac. The reasons why the people of Sucat oppose Pax Silica are blatantly obvious.

Because we were organized and determined, we already knew going to Camp Bagong Diwa that we were only being detained to ensure that the US-Marcos II regime wouldn’t be embarrassed by popular dissent. Any charges were trumped-up and superficial. The police must have calculated that this would scare us into silence. Police officers aren’t known for being good at math.

The detention “facility” in Camp Bagong Diwa was a run-down multi-purpose hall. The tiles were broken and there were shards of ceramic on the ground. There was no ventilation to speak of. Only three out of eight air conditioners worked. Water in the bathrooms was intermittent, especially in …

title: 25 novembre: giornata di lotta contro la violenza patriarcale
content:
Ieri 25 novembre è stata un’importante giornata di mobilitazione contro la violenza patriarcale chiamata dalla rete Non Una di Meno al suo decimo anno di attività.


Oltre 40 città in Italia sono scese in piazza per ribadire quanto la violenza di genere si intersechi con il peggioramento delle condizioni di vita, produttiva e riproduttiva, in tempi di guerra e di crisi. Non è stata questa una giornata di ricorrenza slegata dalle mobilitazioni delle ultime settimane contro riarmo e carovita, infatti “il patriarcato ci costa la vita” è stato lo slogan che ha unito le diverse piazze. Il presente di guerre, genocidio e riarmo segnano infatti un approfondirsi della violenza e le iniziative nelle varie città hanno tematizzato questo nesso.


Di seguito alcuni contributi raccolti da

Radio Onda d’Urto

 dalle piazze:


Non Una di Meno

 torna in piazza e, come ogni anno da dieci anni a questa parte, chiama alla 

mobilitazione nazionale

 in occasione del 

25 novembre, Giornata internazionale contro la violenza maschile sulle donne e di genere

. Una ricorrenza che affonda le proprie radici nell’

omicidio delle tre sorelle Mirabal

 – militanti politiche della Repubblica Dominicana, note con il nome di “Las Mariposas”, uccise il 25 novembre 1960 – e che, proprio sulla spinta della rete femminista e transfemminista, si è trasformata nel tempo in una 

giornata di lotta e rivendicazione contro la violenza patriarcale

.


In occasione di questo 25 novembre, Non Una di Meno ha indetto gli

 

Stati Generali dell’Autodeterminazione,

 una 

settimana di agitazione

 che ha preso il via il 20 novembre in concomitanza del 

TDOR – Trangender Day Of Remembrance

 e della grande mobilitazione di studenti e studentesse nel quadro dello sciopero generale, e che si chiuderà il 

28 novembre con il corteo nazionale a Roma

 (ore 14.30, piazza Repubblica). Appuntamento centrale di questa settimana di lotta, la 

mobilitazione diffusa sui territori

 prevista per oggi, mercoledì 25 novembre, che vedrà presidi, cortei e iniziative in oltre 70 città.


“A 10 anni dalla prima marea contro la violenza patriarcale – scrive Non Una di Meno sul comunicato di indizione della mobilitazione – ci prepariamo a occupare le strade con l’urgenza e il desiderio di cambiare tutto e rivendicare futuro. Lo facciamo con ancora più determinazione oggi, nel

 salto di scala della violenza patriarcale segnato da guerra, riarmo e fascismo che avanza

“.


Ai microfoni di Radio Onda d’Urto, Miriam, di Non Una di Meno Milano, con cui abbiamo approfondito la cornice politica e le istanze della mobilitazione, oltre a rilanciare l’appuntamento milanese, in programma alle ore 18,00 in piazzale Loreto

title: Jusqu'au permis de tuer... / mayday / podcast
content:
Une émission qui revient en plusieurs séquences documentaires sur la violence de la police dans trois pays européens au moment où le permis de tuer vient d'être voté en France.


Le mouvement lycéen qui a gagné la France en Octobre 2026 et le mouvement social qui lui a emboîté le pas, subissent dans la rue un niveau de répression rare.


Dans le même temps l'arsenal législatif mis à disposition des policiers, le permis de tuer voté vendredi dernier au sénat, sonne comme un nouveau crachat à figure des morts de la police et de leurs familles. Et plus largement comme une volonté de mise au pas de tout ce qui se soulève encore contre l'ordre.


Ailleurs, en Belgique et en Suisse par exemple, la police mutile et tue aussi.


Jusqu'au permis de tuer, c'est une émission d'1 heure sur ce que fait la police dans quelques pays européens.

author: Anarchista
title: Wyrok ETPCz ws. Usnarza Górnego nie znaczy dla nas nic [KOMENTARZ]
content:
To o czym mówi dziś Europejski Trybunał Praw Człowieka wiemy od pierwszych dni kryzysu humanitarnego na granicy polsko-białoruskiej


Ponad 5 lat – tyle zajęło ETPCz stwierdzenie tego, co w Usnarzu wiedzieliśmy od jego pierwszych dni. Polska naruszyła Konwencję Praw Człowieka, bo instrumentalizacja migracji nie zwalnia państwa z obowiązku przestrzegania praw człowieka, lub mówiąc naszym językiem – żaden człowiek nie jest nielegalny. Co z tego dla nas wynika? Możemy oprawić sobie wyrok ETPCz w social-mediowe ramki z dopiskiem „a nie mówiłem/mówiłam” i karmić przybywającymi kciukami i serduszkami nasze ego – lub możemy wyciągnąć wnioski.


Poczucie słuszności własnych przekonań owszem może być cenne choćby w walce z wypaleniem tak powszechnym, gdy krzyczymy o sprawę, której zwycięstwa możemy nie dożyć. Ale dla nas wyrok ETPCz nie powinien znaczyć wiele. W zasadzie to powinien znaczyć dla nas tyle co nic.

 


Wyrok daje władzy prezent


Zaraz obok stwierdzenia naruszenia konwencji, ETPCz uznaje, że państwo ma prawo chronić granice, nie musi więc sprawdzać, czy zawracany cudzoziemiec będzie miał na Białorusi dostęp do procedury azylowej. Co więcej, ETPCz orzeka, że konwencja została naruszona w stosunku do jednej osoby, jeśli chodzi o pozostałych nie – bo nie przedstawiono bowiem, zdaniem trybunału, dostatecznych dowodów na to, że znajdowali się w Polsce. Warto też zaznaczyć, że z grona skarżących do końca dotrwały dwie osoby – reszta się wycofała. Czy z braku wiary w sprawiedliwość, czy z braku poczucia bezpieczeństwa? Możemy się tylko domyślać.


Wyrok ETPCz zapada w czasie, gdy granica Polski z Białorusią jest maksymalnie uszczelniona, a przekroczeń w zasadzie nie ma. Nielicznych, którym udaje się tę granicę przekroczyć czeka push-back – tym razem, w przeciwieństwie do czasów PiS – w pełnym majestacie prawa, bo przecież za Tuska o azyl na granicy ubiegać się nie wolno. Dziś rząd dostaje do ręki dodatkowy argument, bo czyta wyrok wybiórczo, skupiając się na prawie do ochrony granicy. A sam wyrok skonstruowano tak, że daje asumpt do jeszcze radykalniejszych ograniczeń prawa do ochrony.


Próżno mieć więc nadzieję, że Polska uzna wyrok ETPCz w całości, czy wyciągnie jakiekolwiek wnioski na korzyść osób migrujących. Władza ponad prawem międzynarodowym stawia doraźne korzyści polityczne, a otwartość na migrację nie leży w interesie partii rządzącej. Skoro większość społeczeństwa uległa wbijanej do głów od grubo ponad dekady ciężkiej antymigracyjnej propagandzie i obcych w Polsce nie chce – to żaden polityk czy polityczka nie zdecyduje się iść pod prąd oczekiwaniom wyborców i wyborczyń i ryzykować śmierci nad urną w imię tak abstrakcyjnych idei jak prawa człowieka.

 


W interesie władzy leży zachowanie władzy. A rozchwiane nastroje społeczne i inkorporowanie idei oraz języka skrajnej prawicy to dla Tuska i jego popleczników i tak żadna cena. Wszak zastraszonymi ludźmi rządzi się łatwiej.


Próżno też mieć nadzieję, że jakakolwiek deklaratywnie progresywna siła polityczna w Polsce byłaby w stanie zmienić politykę graniczną. Reformistycznemu ruchowi aktywistycznemu wypada przypomnieć, że granica Polski z Białorusią jest zewnętrzną granicą Unii Europejskiej i państwo ma obowiązek jej uszczelniania. W przeciwnym razie zostaną zastosowane retorsje z zawieszeniem Schengen włącznie, co odbije się negatywnie na transgranicznym handlu i interesach wielkiego biznesu, który dyktuje polityce co robić.

 


Entuzjaści partii Razem muszą zrozumieć, że nawet Adrian Zandberg granic nie otworzy – jedyne na co mogą liczyć, to może na mniej bicia ludzi i mniej wyrzucania ich w ręce siepaczy Łukaszenki.


O co tak naprawdę walczymy?


Tylko, że nas – anarchistów i anarchistki – nie interesuje otwieranie bram zwieńczonych drutem żyletkowym dla co dziesiątej osoby, tak jak miało to miejsce przez całe lata na przejściu granicznym Brześć-Terespol wobec osób z Czeczenii. Nas interesuje świat otwarty na oścież, w którym każdy człowiek ma prawo do swobodnego poszukiwania bezpieczeństwa, dostatku i godnego życia dla siebie i swoich bliskich.

 


O to samo walczyli i walczyły mieszkańcy i mieszkanki Podlasia, które i którzy jako pierwsze niosły pomoc dla ludzi w drodze, jeszcze przed Usnarzem.


Ruch pomocowy działający na Podlasiu nie wybierał osób, którym pomoc się należała – tak jak robi to państwo i instytucje międzynarodowe, dzieląc ludzi na uchodźców i migrantów oraz na grupy wrażliwe i mniej wrażliwe.

 


Ruch nie pytał o płeć, wiek i kraj …

Nous Vivrons instrumentalise les luttes féministes pour légitimer le sionisme, tout en niant les violences systématiques subies par les Palestinien-nes sous l'occupation.


Le sionisme est une idéologie raciste, qui s'est traduit par le Nakba (expulsion massive des Palestinien-nes de leurs terres lors de la partition coloniale de la Palestine historique en 1948) ou encore par le génocide en cours à Gaza.

être juif

être sioniste

 

» et «

 

être antisioniste

 

» = «

».


Nous réfutons cette essentialisation raciste des personnes juives et réaffirmons que les sionistes, les colons et les racistes ne sont pas les bienvenus dans nos manifs

 

!


Némésis : racistes, fascistes, transphobes, hors de nos manifs


Némésis est un groupe raciste, islamophobe et transphobe. Ce collectif fémonationaliste est soutenu par Éric Zemmour, Sarah Knafo et Bruno Retailleau, dont elles servent activement l'agenda politique.


En s'affichant avec des organisations comme le

GUD

, l'

UNI

Pour «

 

protéger les femmes

 

» et la «

 

civilisation européenne

 

», le collectif appelle à la «

 

remigration

 Continuons la lutte et construisons ensemble la victoire


Depuis le mois de septembre, la jeunesse se mobilise contre l'injustice, la vie chère, les conditions d'éducation, le racisme d'État, les violences policières et pour des vies dignes.


Continuons à nous mobiliser et barrons la route aux fascistes et aux sionistes.


Pour la justice et pour la libération de la Palestine de la mer au Jourdain

author: Shame Mugova
title: Africa educates its people. But where are the economic returns?
content:
What does an African country get back when it spends US$30,000 training a nurse, only for that professional to build a career elsewhere?


This is not a hypothetical training cost. Zimbabwe’s official Health Labour Market Analysis, prepared with technical assistance from the World Health Organisation,

estimated the cost of training a registered general nurse at US$30,000

. The estimate includes educational and training expenses, allowances and associated institutional costs. This is important because many Zimbabwean nurses do not migrate out of the desire to live abroad but local economic and workplace conditions make it difficult to sustain a livelihood at home.


 


Now imagine that nurse graduating and leaving for the United Kingdom. The British health system gains a trained professional, while Zimbabwe may lose years of patient care, potential tax revenue over the nurse’s working life and the experience that nurse could have passed on to younger colleagues.


The financial calculation is not straightforward. The nurse may send money home, support relatives or eventually return. But it raises a question that I believe African governments should be asking more systematically: how much of the economic return on educating our people do our economies actually capture?


We celebrate the construction of schools, the expansion of universities and the number of graduates produced each year. Governments regularly report these achievements alongside GDP growth, investment inflows and improvements in fiscal stability. Yet we rarely connect these indicators to what happens to people after they have acquired their qualifications.


Do they find productive employment? Can they develop rewarding careers? Are their skills used effectively? And, when they leave, what economic value returns to the country that helped develop them?


Zimbabwe’s health workforce provides a revealing example

. A study by Abel Chikanda of Zimbabwean nurse migration

 recorded an increase in Zimbabwean trained nurses on the United Kingdom’s professional register from 2,633 in 2020 to 4,596 in 2023.


These figures do not mean that every nurse registered abroad would otherwise have worked in Zimbabwe. Nor does registration necessarily establish where someone is employed at a particular moment. Nevertheless, the figures demonstrate the international demand for skills developed in a country facing substantial health workforce pressures.


According to the

WHO’s 2026 assessment

, Zimbabwe had approximately 23 doctors, nurses and midwives per 10,000 people in 2022, less than half the WHO threshold referenced for universal health coverage.


Here lies the economic contradiction. A country needs more health professionals, invests scarce resources in training them, yet may struggle to create the conditions necessary to retain their services.


Consider the US$30,000 nurse again.


If that nurse works in Zimbabwe, the public receives healthcare services. Patients may recover sooner and return to work. Experienced nurses train younger colleagues. The nurse spends earnings locally and contributes to economic activity and potentially tax revenue.


These benefits are not all captured in the government’s accounts.


Economists distinguish between fiscal returns, such as taxes flowing to the state, and wider social returns, such as healthier workers, stronger institutions and improved productivity.


When the nurse migrates, some benefits shift abroad. But others may return through remittances, investment, knowledge transfers and support for family members.


In Zimbabwe,

World Bank figures

 show personal remittances received at approximately 8.5% of GDP in 2024. Those flows are economically significant and improve the lives of many households.


Yet money sent home does not automatically replace the services of a nurse in a rural clinic. Financial transfers and locally available professional expertise are different forms of economic value.


The objective should not be to prevent nurses from migrating. Individuals have every reason to pursue better earnings, security and professional development. The question is why their home economies so often struggle to offer sufficiently attractive alternatives.


South Africa demonstrates that the challenge extends beyond migration.


Its

2026 national budget

 allocates R527.2 billion to learning and culture, including substantial funding for basic education, universities and student financial aid.

author: A. K. Kaiza
title: Healing the Elephant: Life and History on the Mental Edge of Uganda
content:
Colonial governors live in the half shadows of history, and in Uganda the ghost of Sir John Hathorn Hall, in power from 1944 to 1952, repeatedly returns to mind – to think of the psychological wreck of the man under whose tenure Britain lost Uganda.


What did Hall think on that afternoon of 17 January 1952 when his plane flew him out for the last time? Would it have been far from what was going through President Milton Obote’s mind that dusky 27 July 1985 when he crossed the Kenyan border, or President Idi Amin’s during his helicopter escape from Kampala on 11 April 1979? Much graver would have been the minds of Kabaka Mwanga and Omukama Kabalega when the two monarchs were sent into exile in 1899. We can only imagine with horror the state of Kabaka Muteesa’s mind during that most fraught and dramatic exit in the country’s post-colonial history in May 1966.


The one constant of Ugandan politics is the brutality with which it dispatches its rulers.


The question rarely asked is what goes through the minds of the masses these men ruled over. For the crowd that thronged the capital on 10 May 1899 as Mwanga and Kabalega were marched into Fort Lugard on Kampala Hill, the disturbance dug deep. The Acting Commissioner, Lieutenant Colonel Trevor Ternant, may have expected a triumphant entry; after all, he was marching into the capital two men he had labelled as rebels. The scenes of despair and wailing forced him to quickly send the two away to Entebbe and organize a rapid evacuation to Seychelles. Here was tumult their world had not prepared them for, the caving in of the cosmos their heritage knew nothing else of life without, now facing a future no prior narrative had prepared them for. 


When it was over, and this future came, and they had lost their lands and freedom, the closure that came, first for Buganda in 1910 when at last Mwanga was buried, provided some solace; he had been dead seven years. For Bunyoro-Kitara, there was only heartbreak. The kingdom was buoyed first by the announcement that the old lion was on his way back. At the very banks of the River Nile, a place Kabalega named Mpumudde, I have rested; he died. Barely a kilometre from crossing the river. The final caving in of their universe was not helped by the salty funeral speech sitting governor Sir Geoffrey Archer gave at the Rukurato on his burial that April 1923. Bunyoro-Kitara’s world ended. The age would not extend to them the hand of kindness for generations to come. For the next twenty years, more than a quarter million died of sleeping sickness; the plague took thousands; forced labour, punitive taxation, and decades of enduring racial abuse followed.


What we now know as “psychology” came to our consciousness four decades after the burial of Omukama Kabalega. When psychiatrist Dr Benjamin Kagwa made a study in 1963-64, some revelation of what the common folk were going through showed. 


Glimpses of this disturbance we can catch when TikTok, Facebook, X, and Instagram revelations leave us stumped. They return in quotidian form what in bygone eras Ugandans framed in mythological terms. I recall with my child’s mind the air around 1979, at the fall of Idi Amin, rumours of a wooden-legged monster stalking the land; it was whispered that homes without a cross dug into the front yard would be visited by this creature. In Kampala, news spread by “Radio Katwe” – literally “head radio”. I do not recall anyone in Aboke digging crosses into their front yards. As it was with these whispered fears, what the calamity would be was never concretely stated. This was code-speak foretelling the fall of big men. 


Just before the fall of the Tito Okello regime, cassava and sorghum slurry brewing in vats, one for liquor, the other for beer, bubbled prophecies of end times. The man driving the Okellos to their fall, Mr Museveni, was called a changeling, able to turn himself into any creature or object when his pursuers came too close.


Such stirrings are beginning to disturb Uganda once again. Under trauma’s blind impress, the concrete and the quotidian recede into the realm of fantasy while myth congeals into fact.


Towards the end of 2025, the word “

gumite

” – loosely translatable as “toughen” – began to puncture speech. “Chwezi dynasty”, the second oldest of Ugandan myth tales, sprung a second-coming, and in the byways of town edges, where mechanics and fabricators, hawkers and layabouts hold court, the words “basement” and “fridge” are tossed about …

author: Memuna Konteh
title: The mountains we miss
content:
Ahmed Koroma’s

Freetown Echoes: Tales from Along the Odokoko

 traces a city in the process of transformation through the eyes of a boy becoming. The novel is a collection of stories, sitting somewhere between fiction, folklore and memoir, in which a young Ahmed and his friends are shaped by their community, like rocks in the stream that flows through it. The cadence and colorful cast of characters in the stories are distinctly Sierra Leonean, while the tension, optimism and anticipation dripping through the pages will be familiar to anyone, African or otherwise, who knows the necessary unease of surrendering to an environment with energy greater than the sum of its inhabitants.

The novel paints a portrait of Freetown in its prime: lush green hills towering over a bubbling metropolis, where market-women, morimen and ministers mingle under the hot sun, everyone hustling for their daily bread. Along the Odokoko, a decade on from independence, things progress and pause to the pulse of a youthful, overzealous nation, where the prospect of perpetually “developing” has not yet been corrupted into the geopolitical hallmark of damnation that it is today. As someone born toward the tail of Sierra Leone’s civil war, Ahmed’s Freetown is not a Freetown that I recognize. It is, however, a Freetown I can embrace with open arms, and respect immensely, like one would the grandparent of a close friend.

The Freetown I know is rebellious and resigned in equal measure. Its hills still loom majestically over a bright and busy coastline, but much of the greenery has been replaced, razed in favor of concrete compounds. The city is in a constant state of construction, never quite finished. The hustlers, in the many forms they take, grow in number by the day, always hungry, too consumed by the never-ending grind to stop and acknowledge each other properly. By night, my Freetown becomes a playground much like the riverbank where Ahmed and his friends would run riot. It’s a place where I can party, free of all inhibition, from dusk until daybreak.

The resulting atmosphere is a chaos that enchants me on my frequent visits from the UK. From a perspective hued by privilege, I see Freetown as a boot camp for my patience, one I enter willingly. I can look upon the frequent blackouts, traffic bottlenecks, broken-down buildings on beach road, overpriced entertainment complexes and overcrowded malls, cramped club dancefloors and palm-body slums with affection or righteous indignation. I’ve no use for the armor of apathy worn by full-time Freetonians with no alternative home.

In Ahmed’s Freetown — one he looks back on from comforts hard-won in California — the Cotton Tree still stands tall; Victoria Park is lush with greenery and the Sierra Leone Library is a free and accessible sanctuary for bookworms across the city. More than just fuel for nostalgia, memorializing Freetown’s history in this way allows us to imagine (and thus enact) better for Freetown’s future. But this book is not a call to arms. It makes no judgments about the country’s politics and presents no arguments as to where things went wrong. It is reflective, retrospective and seductive in its simplicity, leaning on age-old traditions of Sierra Leonean storytelling. Because it’s written from a personal place, concerned more with capturing emotional truths of the protagonist’s childhood than anything else, it avoids the traps of preachiness and didacticism that African historical fiction sometimes falls victim to.

Silky prose and dynamic dialogue usher the reader through a series of tragedies and triumphs, weaving in wives’ tales and local legends for cultural grounding. The country’s layered spiritual tapestry comes to the fore in stories like Aladura, Eku Mason and The Girl Who Has Eyes; in When Death Came, and A Child is Born, we see both grief and glory held collectively as sacrament; and in The Days of Elephant, Baby Moon, and Bad Kahina we see how the rhythms of a community can be shifted by a handful of imposing individuals. Each story provides its own window into different aspects of the Sierra Leonean psyche. We meet dancers, chiefs, teachers, thieves, nurses, herbalists, pastors, psychics, among many others, all through the equalizing lens of boyhood.

I think much of the novel’s charm can be attributed to that spirit of youth which Ahmed captures so well. It’s a spirit that leads with curiosity, unafraid to call things into question and test its theories, and not yet too …

author: ROAPE
title: When ‘the people’ become a problem
content:
The return of political economy to the centre of debates on minerals, sovereignty, and wealth also politicises a more concealed but fundamental category of politics: the people. The people as the foundational logic of politics is obscured either by reducing agency to voting and institutionally mediated participation or through the introduction of ‘meta’ categories for understanding people and their behaviour, such as those found in modern economics. While both tendencies draw legitimacy from the people, neither represents the ultimate contour of popular participation.


In fact, the liberal framework itself often produces a greater degree of depoliticisation of popular will, contradicting its claims to popular legitimacy. Within the neoliberal ‘free trade’ world, this depoliticisation is further amplified by reducing state capacity in favour of private enterprise and ownership.


As I argued in my

earlier piece

, the recent political trajectory of Burkina Faso is significant precisely because questions of ownership, extraction, production, and economic sovereignty have returned to the sphere of popular political contestation. Reduced state capacity does not simply diminish sovereign power; it transforms the role of the state into an arbitrator of bourgeois interests over popular representation, privileging profit over people while representing the category of the people through differentiated and graded notions of ‘development’.


The question of state agency in Africa against neoliberal and neo-imperial interventions has long been a subject of scholarly and theoretical debate. Reduced state capacity facilitates neoliberal extraction of resources, the INGO raj, environmental destruction, and the undermining of mechanisms of popular representation. When popular will is asserted, a subtler yet visible distinction between the liberal and the illiberal is often mobilised to critique the economics and politics of such movements.


In popular discourse, this binary is largely treated as a neutral descriptive category, almost self-evident in its meaning. Yet an inquiry into its history reveals it as a political technology: a method of political discourse through which popular movements – particularly in the Third World – have been classified, disciplined, and, when necessary, delegitimised by pitching one side against the other.


The liberal/illiberal binary has, of course, acquired considerable complexity, and recent scholarly interventions have captured its variability, particularly in Africa and Latin America. But its political uses remain consequential.


From the hypocrisy of the West to the selective deployment of human rights, justice, and other ‘moral’ equivalents – while ongoing crises in Gaza, Sudan, and elsewhere in the Global South are largely ignored by the mainstream – to the concealment of economic dependency and the relationship of the ‘First’ World to the ‘Third’, depoliticisation has become a norm rather than an exception.


As Eyob Balcha Gebremariam has

recently argued

 writing for roape.net, Eurocentrism and the selective application of the so-called ‘rules-based world order’ continue to shape international narratives in ways that privilege Western interests while presenting them as universal norms. Liberal-democratic states, whether the United States, France, or India, have themselves mobilised brutal armed power to crush popular agitations by farmers, students, and workers.


The fissures in the liberal/illiberal binary, therefore, reveal not only its poverty as an account of political life, but also the hollowness of ‘by the people, for the people’ sloganeering when confronted with people acting beyond the institutional boundaries prescribed for them. The question, then, is what can some of the political-economic changes in today’s Africa teach us about the people and their political agency?


One of the first and most important lessons from Burkina Faso and the political transitions there comes from de-concealing the concealed: the people. The Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland (VDPs) have been

a particular focus of discussion

 on Burkina Faso. Established in 2020, the VDPs are

locally and voluntarily recruited civilian auxiliaries

, provided with arms and military training, who support the national armed forces in defending communities against jihadist insurgent groups. Their

mobilisation was substantially expanded

 under Ibrahim Traoré after 2022.

author: WoMin
title: Practising solidarity economy: Women’s collective action and community finance in Memirlosho
content:
Conversations about economic development often portray rural women as people who need support, training, or assistance. Far less attention is paid to how women organise themselves to solve problems, manage resources, and build livelihoods together. During a recent visit to the

Memirlosho Women Cultural Village

 in Isiolo County, northern Kenya, we saw how Samburu women offer a powerful example of a community and solidarity economy in practice. The cultural village brings together four women’s groups (Narasha, Muruguti, Narupa, and Rapunye) that work as a collective to create opportunities, strengthen resilience, and improve livelihoods. Their lived experience demonstrates that solidarity economies are not solely theoretical concepts or future possibilities. They are already being built every day through cooperation, mutual support, and shared responsibility.


Collective organising as a condition for economic agency


The first foundation of Memirlosho’s economic model is collective organising. The women registered a Community Based Organisation (CBO) through which they transformed dispersed individual survival strategies into a legally recognised collective entity. This shift carries important economic and political implications as they gained greater visibility, legitimacy, and bargaining power. The umbrella structure allows the four groups to support one another while maintaining their own identities. Together, they can access external support, coordinate activities, and speak with a stronger collective voice.


More importantly, the organisation creates a sense of shared purpose. Members are no longer facing challenges alone, they have built a community that pools resources, shares risks, and works toward common goals.


Productive activities: turning livelihoods into collective assets


Memirlosho’s economic activities are rooted in skills and resources that already exist within the community. Hence, two productive activities form the backbone of the village. The first is beadwork. Women use their cultural knowledge and craftsmanship to produce traditional beadwork that can be sold for income. Working collectively allows them to purchase materials more efficiently, share information, and explore markets together.


Another important activity is goat rearing and trading. Through support from the

Samburu Women Trust

, the groups received forty goats, with ten goats allocated to each group. Rather than viewing these animals as a one-time gift, the women transformed them into a revolving community asset.


The goats are raised and later sold, with the proceeds used to purchase new livestock. In this way, the original investment continues to generate benefits over time. Instead of being consumed, the asset grows and supports future opportunities. This approach reflects one of the central principles of solidarity economies: resources are managed not only for individual gain but for the long-term benefit of the collective.


Financial solidarity: A savings system built around people’s needs


While productive activities constitute the foundation of

Memirlosho’s

 solidarity economy, the Village Savings and Loan Association (VSLA) serves as its circulatory system. The VSLA operates as a community-owned financial institution managed according to principles of mutual support rather than external profit extraction. The system has three main characteristics:


a

) Socially oriented lending:

  Women can access loans for socially important needs especially school fees, respond to emergencies, or meet household needs. Interest collected on loans is not extracted by an outside institution. Instead, it returns to the group’s common fund, benefiting all members. This way, capital serves the community’s wellbeing and social reproduction rather than simply financial accumulation.


b) Inclusive flexibility:

 The savings model is also flexible. Members contribute according to their means and circumstances, recognising that income can fluctuate throughout the year, as a pastoral community. This allows participation even during difficult periods and helps ensure that nobody is excluded because they cannot meet rigid contribution requirements. It’s a system that prioritises participation and inclusion.


c) Community control over finance:

 The VSLA enables members to maintain ownership and control over their financial resources. By keeping financial decision-making within the community, the group reduces dependence on …

author: Mzi Velapi
title: Two men sentenced for Khayelitsha church sexual assault
content:
On Easter Sunday in 2023, two young men stormed the Showers of Blessings Christian Church in Zion, in Site C carrying a gun and a knife and robbed the women congregants before sexually assaulting and raping them. Yamkela Jobo and Okuhle Beya were found guilty on all 21 charges and were sentenced to 25 years in prison by the regional court in Khayelitsha today.


Thembinkosi Fati, the secretary of South African Zionist Churches, said they welcome the sentencing of the two. “The guilty verdict was a victory on its own, given how cases like this one just disappear into thin air. It might not be exactly what we wanted, but it shows that the investigating officers and the state did a good job,” he said.


According to Fati, Jobo and Beya took advantage of loadshedding, and the fact that the women and children were alone in the church hall where they were sleeping.


Nolukholo Jezile, one of the church leaders, said that they would sleep at the church during Easter. “It’s clear that they planned the attacks on us, because they waited until all the men were gone and they stormed the church,” she said.


She commended the courage of the women of the church for overcoming their trauma. “It was not easy at all; we could have easily given up,” but they are still not able to go to church alone.


Community-based organisations supported the church during the trial, including

Amadoda Aqotho

 and Sidima Sam Gentlemen’s Organisation.


Amadoda Aqotho supported the church members during the trial.


The prosecutors told the court that the pair ordered the congregants to strip naked, robbed 19 women of their cellphones, and sexually assaulted two of them before fleeing.


One of the mitigating circumstances offered by the defence lawyer was that the two young men were abandoned by their parents.


“Not having a parent does not give an excuse to be a thief and a rapist. Instead, it should teach you to be independent. I was not aware that they were this young. The women that the accused assaulted are old enough to be their mothers and grandparents,” said Sabelo Zekevu, the chairperson of Amadoda Aqotho. He called on men to stop abuse and report cases of gender-based violence when they witness them.
