author: Abahlali_3
title: South Africa, Palestine and the Urgency of Solidarity
content:
South Africa, Palestine and the Urgency of Solidarity

Address at a public meeting hosted by Palestine Solidarity Network Aotearoa at the Ellen Melville Centre in Auckland on Sunday, 8 November 2026.

Comrades, thank you for inviting me to return to Aotearoa. I bring you greetings of solidarity from Abahlali baseMjondolo, the shack dwellers’ movement of South Africa, which was formed in Durban in 2005 and now has more than 200 000 members across South Africa.

It is fifteen years since I was last here, in 2011, when we commemorated the thirtieth anniversary of the great protests against the Springbok rugby tour of 1981. I want to begin by remembering that history, and by thanking all the people of this country who stood with us against apartheid. People marched, confronted the police, and sometimes faced arrest and violence. You refused to allow the apartheid state to present itself as a normal member of the international community.

This was an outstanding example of international solidarity, and an example that we should seek to emulate in our solidarity with the people of Palestine.

In our movement we speak of living solidarity. This means solidarity that exists in action, not just in words. It means solidarity between people who recognise one another as equals.

Settler colonialism in South Africa and Israel

South Africa and Palestine are both countries that have been oppressed by settler colonialism. This is part of the reason for the long solidarity with Palestine among South Africans.

But there are important differences between these two forms of settler colonialism. In South Africa, the colonial system was organised around the dispossession of Africans from their land, the theft of their cattle and the exploitation of their labour. The economy depended on African workers in the mines, on the farms, in the factories and in the homes of white people. The settlers wanted the land, but they also wanted the labour of the people they had dispossessed.

Huge numbers of people were forced from their homes and land as African people were pushed into ‘reserves’, based on the system used to oppress Native Americans, and later into the ‘Bantustans’, the so-called ‘homelands’. The Bantustans were not just used to confine the African people on tiny bits of land. They were also central to the migrant labour system that ensured cheap labour for white capital and for white families in their homes.

African workers were forced by economic necessity to leave their families and communities to find work in the mines and cities. Many were compelled to live in single-sex hostels, separated from their families. Africans were wanted as workers but rejected as citizens with equal rights. They were systematically dehumanised. This system was maintained through the police, the army, prisons, torture and killing. Those who resisted were treated as criminals and terrorists.

When we look at Palestine today, we recognise many of these methods of oppression. We see a fundamentally racist settler colonial system in which there is ongoing dispossession of people from their land by the Israeli state and settlers. We see homes being demolished. We see communities separated from one another by walls, checkpoints and military restrictions. We see people who stand up against oppression being called ‘terrorists’ and subject to mass imprisonment, torture and murder.

The struggles against racism and for land are central to the struggle for freedom, both in South Africa and in Palestine. But there are also differences between apartheid in South Africa and oppression in Palestine.

While Palestinians have been exploited as workers, the fundamental drive of settler colonialism in Israel is to remove or destroy the Palestinian people rather than to exploit them for their labour.

In South Africa, the apartheid system required the continued presence of a large and hyper-exploited African workforce, while seeking to control, segregate and impoverish it. In Palestine, the settler-colonial project has involved the destruction of Palestinian communities, the removal of Palestinians from their land and the attempt to establish and maintain territorial and political control through their displacement.

The Nakba of 1948 forced hundreds of thousands of Palestinians from their homes. Many became refugees in other countries, and they and their descendants remain unable to return. The occupation of the West Bank and East Jerusalem since 1967 has brought …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Thirty Years On, Intersex Africans Set Their Own Agenda for Rights and Belonging
content:
It was a rare energy, fueled by our shared trials nd triumphs, and by stories that stretched beyond these walls. We, intersex activists from across Africa, came together, gathering on the shoulders of those who paved the way, held together by a promise that our voices would carry us far. Seeing the adoption of the Nairobi Declaration reminded me that our voices are now influencing regional conversations, policies and demands for justice.


We have come a long way. Years ago, people would laugh at you for raising intersex issues in Ghana; today, journalists call us to make documentaries.


On 26 October, we marked thirty years of Intersex Awareness Day. The day commemorates a

1996 protest

 by intersex activists against unnecessary, irreversible surgeries on intersex children and their demand that we decide what happens to our own bodies. Thirty years on, that is still our demand: that we decide. Many gains since then have been won on this continent. South Africa’s equality law has recognised intersex status since 2005. Kenya became the first African country to

count intersex people in a census

 in 2019, and its

Children Act 2022

 recognised intersex children in law. In 2023, the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights adopted

Resolution 552

, calling on states to end non-consensual surgeries, infanticide and abandonment. This year, Zimbabwe’s Minister of Justice

convened a high-level meeting

 on legal recognition, and South Africa’s Human Rights Commission now

guides parents towards alternatives to invasive procedures

.


We are also building  and expanding our spaces.


From 30 September to 2 October, intersex Africans gathered in Nairobi for the first-ever Africa Intersex Movement conference. Activists came from East, Southern, North and West Afric

a.

For the first time, intersex activists, community members, scholars, cultural workers, and allies from across Africa came together.

We told our stories in our own words and s

et our own agenda and demands. It was a community in communion and a platform to press for rights, protection and dignity.


We left with the Nairobi Declaration, whose ten demands range from legal recognition and an end to infanticide and non-consensual surgeries to equal access to healthcare, education and work, and a real say in decisions that affect us, alongside a call for an African intersex rights framework. Meeting openly, as gatherings like ours are criminalised across the continent, was itself a statement.


It mattered that we met in Kenya, whose census showed why being counted matters. Who a state refuses to count, it can pretend does not exist. Yet this win must be built on, because Kenya’s

Intersex Persons Bill, 2024

 has yet to

become law

.


Who decides who we are, and which children are protected?


During the conference, one question kept coming up. Who gets to decide who is intersex? There are dozens of intersex variations, and many people never know until they are tested. Yet the first response is often, “What shows you are intersex?” Demanding medical proof leaves the power to define us with medical and state systems, not with intersex people ourselves.


I hear the question, “What are you?” most often in hospitals, from family members and communities, where people feel entitled to question bodies they do not understand. Often, these probing questions determine whether you receive medical care or can use services freely accessible to others. It creates shame, fear and self-doubt, turning spaces meant to offer care and belonging into places of rejection.


The cost of not fitting is real.

Policy guidance

 from the Africa Intersex Movement and the UN Development Programme documents these harms across the continent. In Ghana, we have witnessed the same infanticide and abandonment of babies seen as a curse, children operated on to make them fit, and adults hiding their identities from their own families.


In that room, we listened and held space for one another. Every variation is unique, yet people hold fixed expectations of what an intersex person looks like. Intersex people must define who we are.


In Ghana, an opening and its limits


In Ghana, intersex people lack legal recognition and protection. Last year, with support from traditional leaders (queen mothers) and lawyers, we urged

the Constitution Review Committee

 to ban non-consensual surgeries and infanticide and recognise intersex people. The president’s white paper supported …

author: Francesco Rota
title: Moyale and the Limits of Kenya’s Silence on Ethiopia
content:
At the end of October, staff from UNHCR and the Kenya Red Cross began

issuing coded wristbands

 to Ethiopian families sheltering in schools and churches in Moyale, a town in Kenya’s Marsabit County that shares its name, and in practice its streets, with the Ethiopian town across the border. By 29 October around

50,000 people

 had crossed in little more than a week, most of them women and children, and the Kenyan government and its humanitarian partners are now

planning for as many as 80,000

.


These people are not fleeing the war in northern Ethiopia, where fighting resumed in Tigray in late September and federal troops

retook Mekelle on 3 October

. That conflict has also brought Ethiopia and Eritrea to the edge of open war, as the two governments have

broken off diplomatic relations

 and accused each other at the United Nations of

starting a war

. They are fleeing a separate conflict more than a thousand kilometres further south, between two of Ethiopia’s own regional governments. Nevertheless, the two crises are connected, and the connection matters for Kenya, because a war between Ethiopia and Eritrea would make the present numbers at Moyale look small.


A dispute inside Ethiopia, on Kenya’s border


Ethiopian Moyale is shared between the Oromia and Somali regions, which run the town jointly and have argued for decades over the land around it. In the middle of October, Somali regional officials

opened a new office in a district that Oromia claims and raised their regional flag over it

, and a girl of thirteen was

killed in the violence that followed

. Within a few days the security forces of the two regions were fighting each other with heavy weapons inside the town, and the violence

spread to the districts of Gumi Eldallo, Wachile and Arero

.


Clashes along this same boundary in 2017

displaced hundreds of thousands of people

, which suggests that the problem lies in the way Ethiopia’s federal system works rather than in a single provocation. The system gives territory to regions defined by ethnic identity and leaves mixed towns such as Moyale to argue over where they belong. What has changed since 2017 is that the federal army is now heavily committed in the north, and the regional forces in the south have been left to settle the question among themselves. In this sense the two crises meet, since every unit that Addis Ababa sends towards Tigray and the Eritrean border is a unit no longer available to keep rival regional forces apart elsewhere in the country.


Because the border at Moyale runs through the middle of a single town and through communities that live on both sides of it, the fighting has not stayed in Ethiopia. Kenyan police reported

stray bullets

 landing on the Kenyan side within the first week, Kenya Defence Forces teams have since

found and destroyed several grenades

, and a woman in Kenyan Moyale has been

killed by what appears to have been a stray bullet

. Kenya’s acting Commissioner for Refugee Affairs, Mercy Mwasaru, now describes the situation as

a matter of national security

.


Kenya’s selective role in the region


Kenya is sometimes described as a passive observer of conflict in the Horn of Africa, but its record suggests a country that intervenes where it judges its interests to be at stake and stays quiet elsewhere. It sent troops into Somalia in 2011 and still has soldiers there, it hosted the talks that led to the

2005 agreement

 ending the war between northern and southern Sudan, and in November 2022 it hosted the meeting of Tigrayan and federal commanders that produced the

Nairobi Declaration

. Under President William Ruto, Kenya went further on Sudan than any other neighbour by hosting the Rapid Support Forces as they launched a charter for a rival government, a decision that led the military authorities in Sudan to

ban Kenyan imports

.


On Ethiopia, by contrast, Kenya has chosen to say very little, and the reasons for that choice are practical. Ethiopia is Kenya’s largest neighbour and a central economic and security partner. The two governments

revived their 2012 Special Status Agreement

 in 2024, signed a defence cooperation agreement the following year, and in March this year

agreed to carry out joint military operations

 along the road corridor that links Moyale, Marsabit and Turkana. Nairobi has generally treated disorder inside Ethiopia as Ethiopia’s own affair and has handled its effects on Kenyan soil as a humanitarian question …

author: Dauti Kahura
title: How Ruto Lost Gikuyus and What Happens Next?
content:
We recently buried our aunt, Wahito. She hailed from Ndumberi in Kiambu County and was my mother’s elder sister. A staunch Catholic, she was practically buried by the Catholic Women Association. Resplendent in their headscarves and their blue and white uniforms, the CWA practically took charge during the long funeral mass. The officiating priest eulogized my aunt, who died at 87, as a beacon of steadfastness in her Catholicism and reminded us that dead men and women tell no tales. She was gone, and we the living had the duty to reclaim our stories. As he wound up his sermon, the priest asked the congregation whether it was steadfast in its resolve to do the right thing come 10 August 2027. The congregation responded in unison, and the

Wantam

 slogan rent the air. A flash of satisfaction crossed the priest’s face; his smile was unmistakable. At the burial site, the priest was unrelenting: “Once again I implore you, we must do the right thing, and we mustn’t forget.”


The Wantam gospel


The Catholic Church of Kenya, through the powerful voice of Archbishop Anthony Muheria, the Opus Dei cleric overseeing the Nyeri diocese, recently warned its clergy against allowing politics at pulpits across the country. The priest presiding over my aunt’s funeral must have heard Archbishop Muheria loud and clear, but in the Mt Kenya region, the mainstream churches have taken it upon themselves to preach the

Wantam

 gospel, the clarion call that sums up the opposition to President William Ruto, nine months to the general election. The Church was at the forefront of canvassing for votes for Ruto in the Mt Kenya region in the run-up to the 2022 elections, but less than two years later, after the region had overwhelmingly voted for the president, cracks began to appear, and things were falling apart. 


Christian president


Whatever happened? Why has a community that had overwhelmingly voted for Ruto despite all the iniquities that it accused him of having perpetrated against it now with the same vigour, turned its back on him? In a region that is supremely religious, the mainstream churches – the Anglican Church of Kenya (ACK), the Catholic Church, the Methodist Church, and the Presbyterian Church of East Africa (PCEA) – play a central role in shepherding their congregations in the direction in which it is going to vote. In the lead-up to the August 2022 elections, the churches threw their support behind Ruto and asked their faithful to follow suit. They cast Ruto as a born-again, bible-reading Christian, as opposed to Raila Odinga, whose Christianity was considered dodgy as far as the Mt Kenya region’s religious leaders were concerned. The clerics looked forward to enhanced social engagements with the forthcoming “Christian president”. But woe unto them, because as they would soon find out, President Ruto’s only interest was to capture state power, after which he would discard their “anointed and holy” support.


Betrayal


That betrayal – the feeling of having been used and abused despite the supposedly gentleman’s agreement on an anticipated state – church revival – is what led the Mt Kenya region’s ACK leadership, barely two years into President Ruto’s rule, to ask their congregations for forgiveness for having campaigned for him and for asking them to do the same and vote for him. As an ACK Mt Kenya diocese elder told me, the Church was truly remorseful for having misled its worshippers and regretted its liaison with a president who had deliberately lied to the Church leadership. Always circumspect in its dealings with the state, the leadership of the powerful Catholic Church of Kenya, through the Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops (KCCB), finds President Ruto insincere in his politics – a euphemism for liar. “He lies like a sieve,” one Catholic priest told me. “He believes that the Catholic Church leadership in Mt Kenya is ‘biased’ against him because he’s not a Catholic. The region’s Catholic clergy didn’t fight Mwai Kibaki; why? Because he was a Catholic. The same clergy didn’t fight Uhuru Kenyatta; why? For the same reason; he is Catholic.” Ruto is caught up in his lies and deceptions, and he has come to believe in those lies, said the priest.   


“Ruto lied to us”


If the Church in the Mt Kenya region has experienced betrayal from Ruto, it is the voter who has verbalized that betrayal. As early as 2024, the Mt Kenya region voter complained about the “punitive taxes” that were introduced, especially on the Hass …

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Public hearing set for Canadian North flight attendants’ potential strike
content:
There will be

a public hearing in Iqaluit next week to determine which Canadian North services must continue if the airline’s flight attendants go on strike.


The Canada Industrial Relations Board is holding the hearing next week at the Iqaluit Cadet Hall. It starts at 10 a.m. Nov. 30 and runs until Dec. 2,

Jean-Daniel Tardif, the board’s senior director of alternative dispute resolution services, said in an email.


The public can attend in person or remotely through Zoom

.


About 200 flight attendants, who are represented by the Canadian Union of Public Employees Local 8111,

could strike

 as early as Dec. 19 if they do not reach a new collective agreement with the airline.


The hearings will determine which of the airline’s services are essential, and therefore can’t cease, in the event of a strike or lockout.


The board previously invited the public to submit information about how a potential work stoppage could affect health and safety. The deadline for submissions was Nov. 20.

author: Justin Hardy
title: Child welfare dispute in Peguis First Nation in Manitoba sparks lockdown
content:
A dispute over the leadership and operations of Peguis First Nation’s Child and Family Services escalated Thursday with community members, the chief and a councillor gathering outside the agency’s main office and chaining its doors shut.


The protest started Nov. 19 amid calls for changes to the agency’s leadership on the reserve located 200 km north of Winnipeg on the Interlake Region of Manitoba.


“Despite my attempts in the past to speak up for membership, there has been complete disregard for me as the chief of our nation, complete disregard for the concerns identified by members, and complete disregard for the safety and wellbeing of our children and our families,” Chief Stan Bird said in a video posted to social media in the days leading up to the protest.


RCMP officers arrived and spoke with the group. Bird has previously said he wants the band to take control of the CFS agency and reassert its inherent jurisdiction over child welfare.


He has also raised concerns about child safety and the agency’s operations.


Bird has not responded to further requests for comment.


Peguis CFS responded by announcing that its main office was in lockdown following Thursday’s incident.


“The agency is an essential service provider to Peguis members and wants to ensure to members that programs and services will continue as normal,” the announcement on their website read.


The dispute has also exposed disagreements within the community over how the agency should be governed and who should have authority over its operations.


Four of the community’s six councillors issued a notice to the community dated Nov. 21, condemning the protest, they said, was led by Bird and that that a quorum of council is needed to make any changes to the agency.


As of Nov. 25, the situation remains unresolved, with questions surrounding the agency’s leadership, its financial accountability and the future of child and family services in Peguis.


A band meeting was held in Peguis on Nov. 24. Media were not allowed in. Bird has called a news conference in Winnipeg on Thursday.


We will have more on that in the coming days.

Child welfare dispute in Peguis First Nation in Manitoba sparks lockdown

APTN News

author: Chris Walker
title: Nearly 3 in 10 Americans Are Changing Thanksgiving Plans Due to Higher Costs
content:
The year-over-year cost of a Thanksgiving turkey has increased by 10 percent, according to the Farm Bureau.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

New polling demonstrates that millions of Americans are likely to change their Thanksgiving plans due to concerns about costs, as prices for many staple items have shot up over the past year.

An Economist/YouGov poll published earlier this week asked respondents whether they would be altering their “turkey day” plans due to price increases. According to the survey, nearly 3 in 10 Americans (28 percent) said they would be making changes to their ordinary traditions.

While 49 percent of respondents said they weren’t changing anything about Thanksgiving, a significant number said they were, yet another indicator that the economy under the Trump administration isn’t working for everybody.

Travel expenses and concerns could be one reason many are making changes to their plans. Gasoline prices have dropped somewhat since reaching over $4.50/gallon on average across the U.S. this past spring, due to restrictions on oil exports that occurred after President Donald Trump’s decision to launch a war on Iran. But even with some respite in those expenses, the average cost of gasoline for this year’s Thanksgiving is almost 20 percent higher than it was a year ago. Soaring ticket prices for air travel — in conjunction with concerns about air safety in general — could also be affecting people’s plans.

Travel isn’t the only matter on people’s minds. With those higher gas prices — and higher prices for diesel fuel — costs for food and other consumer goods have increased, too.

Indeed, the cost of the Thanksgiving meal itself has gone up. According to figures compiled by the Farm Bureau, this year’s meal will likely cost 6 percent more than last year’s — with a 10 percent increase for the turkey alone. Other staple items that are seeing increases in costs include milk, dinner rolls, potatoes, and cranberries, products that are transported across the country on vehicles that use diesel fuel.

Beyond Thanksgiving, higher consumer costs could lead families to change their holiday plans, too. One survey found, for example, that 45 percent of families are going to buy fewer gifts this year as a result of high prices.

Unfortunately, there are signs that the economy isn’t going to get better anytime soon. Indeed, on Wednesday, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index — the preferred measure for inflation that is used by the Fed — showed a seasonally adjusted 3.8 percent annual inflation rate, the highest annual rate seen in that measure since August 2025.

The Trump administration also announced this week that it is preparing to impose a new round of high tariffs on China, the European Union, and other countries. Such tariffs, many economists point out, are essentially a tax on consumers, raising prices on products they purchase from outside the U.S.

author: William Gillis
title: Il Vuoto della “Sinistra”
content:
Di

William Gillis

. Originale pubblicato il 21 febbraio 2017 con il titolo

The Emptiness of “The Left”

. Tradotto da

Enrico Sanna

.


Non credo che la “sinistra” rappresenti qualcosa di coerente; mi sembra piuttosto una coalizione storicamente contingente di posizioni ideologiche diverse. Nell’assemblea nazionale francese, Bastiat e altri liberomercatisti sedevano a sinistra; se da un lato si trattava di una coerente tradizione di libero mercato di sinistra, dobbiamo anche ammettere però che questo non significava molto in quei particolari frangenti rivoluzionari, e ancora meno in frangenti rivoluzionari in generale. Ci sono sempre rivoluzionari che ambiscono a sistemi molto peggiori del nostro, e molti rivoluzionari riconosciuti come “di sinistra” avevano propositi che erano un veleno per la libertà.


Sinistra e destra oggi sono generalmente considerate egalitarie e gerarchiche. Si tratta non solo di una lettura imposta di una realtà storica e sociologica molto più complessa, ma anche filosoficamente priva di contenuto. Nessuno sa dire chiaramente cos’è l’egalitarismo, o anche il potere gerarchico, molte teorie non solo si escludono reciprocamente, ma evidenziano come pretese presumibilmente identiche siano in realtà profondamente antagonistiche. Egalitarismo significa la stessa esatta ricchezza (comunque la si misuri) per tutti? Significa, nell’ambito astratto delle relazioni, uguaglianza giuridica o sociale davanti al Popolo o alle leggi dello Stato? Significa la stessa opportunità di impegno economico o la stessa possibilità di accedere ai granai? L’uguaglianza sostituisce altre virtù come la libertà? È meglio che tutti siano ugualmente oppressi o che qualcuno sia più libero? Non faccio dello spirito. Noi insabbiamo queste questioni serie dicendo che vanno lasciate al “buonsenso”, o sperando che i compagni affronteranno i dettagli così come faremmo noi, valutando i pro e i contro, mentre sappiamo per esperienza che non è così. Siamo in disaccordo costante.


Si parla di “democrazia diretta collettiva” come se qualcosa che rappresenta il volere pressoché unanime di un qualche organismo costituisse una condizione egalitaria. Certo, per certi versi è così. Ma se un qualche organismo collettivo decide della mia vita, io non voglio “partecipare”, gli lancio una bomba. C’è gente di sinistra che usa slogan come “potere al popolo” o “aboliamo il potere”, e questo dovrebbe essere un forte segnale d’allarme per tutti: parliamo di sistemi concettuali e valori completamente diversi. È una grossa illusione pensare che se ci si siede a discutere alla fine ci si ritrova tutti dalla stessa parte. Il presupposto di un obiettivo comune o di una solidarietà che abbraccia tutta la sinistra è una rassicurante bugia.


La sinistra non è una serie di assiomi etici su cui accordarsi per poi dibattere sulle conseguenti pratica e strategia. La sinistra è una coalizione storica assemblata per caso. Come nelle rivoluzioni, noi tendiamo ad identificarci con i vinti, formiamo le nostre coalizioni con le classi che reputiamo perdenti in opposizione alle classi che reputiamo di governo, ma così facendo confondiamo le cose. Siamo per l’aborto perché vediamo nelle donne il lato perdente del patriarcato. Ma stiamo anche dalla parte dei vegani perché gli animali sono (a volte letteralmente) i perdenti del dominio dell’uomo. Ma attribuiamo lo stesso valore a tutte le forme di vita? E cos’è una forma di vita? Valutiamo tutte le forme di vita allo stesso modo o secondo il loro grado di coscienza? O secondo il rapporto che hanno con noi? Il nostro giudizio cambia secondo che i perdenti siano nostri famigliari o altri.


Non sto dicendo che non c’è un filo conduttore che unisce queste dinamiche diverse, o una guida etica di fondo, una pratica attenta e sfumata; anzi, credo nella sua esistenza (anche se quando dico che esiste un ampio spettro di coscienza tra zigoti o nematodi e chiunque abbia una coscienza anche lontanamente umana molti a sinistra pensano che non sono egalitario). Voglio dire che il nostro atteggiamento nei confronti dei vinti è spesso una risposta istintiva a ciò che ci appare più che il risultato di un’analisi etica. La sinistra è raramente una filosofia, più spesso è una coalizione tenuta assieme da una dottrina. Possiamo immaginare un mondo diverso in cui, in seguito a un percorso storico diverso,

l’illegalità

 dell’aborto è una delle basi della sinistra, in linea con la lotta contro l’omofobia, il patriarcato, l’abilismo …

author: Amy Romer, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: The word ‘kokum’ has entered the dictionary — but it’s deeper than a simple definition
content:
Cree Knowledge Keeper Elsie Paul sits surrounded by artwork and belongings in a video she shared on Youtube and TikTok.

Screenshot courtesy Elsie Paul/

YouTube


Kôhkom (grandmother) Elsie Paul was nervous about posting her first TikTok. 


The young people Paul worked with at the Kohkum Kisewatisowin Society encouraged her to share her teachings online. Paul had established the society to pass on Cree language and teachings after being punished for speaking Cree at a day school in Saddle Lake.


“You could probably reach 500 people in one day,” her oskâpêw (helper), Kathy Hamelin, told her. 


“Oh my,” Paul, who was 77 at the time, replied. 


It was December 2021, and the COVID-19 pandemic was still keeping people apart. Hoping to reach more young people in the amiskwaciwâskahikan (Edmonton) community, Paul decided to try something new.


From her kitchen, the Cree-Métis knowledge keeper from Treaty 6 territory could share her culture with people beyond her immediate circle. 


Ping! Her phone chimed. 


Ping! 


“I don’t know why this one keeps pinging,” said Paul.


“I bet it’s your TikTok,” Hamelin replied. 


Within an hour, Paul’s first video, a 21-second clip of her dancing the Red River jig in her kitchen, had racked up 2,000 views. By the end of the day, that number had climbed to 12,000.


Paul couldn’t believe so many people had watched it. 


“That many people around the world,” Hamelin laughed.


Paul soon became known as the

#technokokum

, with some of her videos reaching 350,000 views. 


Her time on TikTok was relatively brief, ending when she retired in late 2022. But the response to her videos showed how far a Cree kinship term could travel, reaching people far beyond the communities where it originated — with comments like “thank you for being everyone’s kokum” and “I can smell the smudge and tea through the screen.”


In June 2026,

kokum


— an anglicized spelling of the Cree word kôhkom —

entered the Oxford English Dictionary

 (OED).


According to the OED, it’s the first kinship term from an Indigenous language in “Canada” to be added to the dictionary. 


READ MORE:


May we all have a kôhkom, or a kokum


For Danica Salazar, a lexicographer and the executive editor for “World Englishes” at Oxford Languages, the addition reflects a shift in how Indigenous Languages are represented in English. 


“There’s something quite anthropological about most of our early evidence for these words,” she said in an interview with IndigiNews. 


Words like

muskimoot

 (bag or sack),

shaganappi

 (rawhide strip, from pîsâkanâpiy) and

pemmican

 (dried meat and berries, from pimîhkân) are all anglicized Cree words already recorded in the OED.


Those earlier entries often reflected the objects and cultural practices that outsiders encountered and documented.


“Kokum,” on the other hand, is the first example of a word rooted in the familiar relationships and everyday lives among Indigenous communities in “Canada.” 


Salazar believes the addition reflects a growing influence of Indigenous communities on the English language, as their words circulate beyond the accounts of anthropologists and other outside observers.


“So that’s really interesting because you can really see the more direct influence of Indigenous languages on English,” she said, “without the third party involvement.” 


But for Hamelin, the word’s inclusion raised another question: what happens to a word’s meaning once it’s recorded in English?


How a word enters the dictionary


To be considered for inclusion in the OED, a word must have an established presence in the English language


Oxford Languages

, part of Oxford University Press, uses a vast digital collection of texts, known as a corpus, containing billions of words gathered from across the internet. Software helps lexicographers follow the ebb and flow of language, tracking which words are gaining momentum, how often they’re used, and by whom — whether in particular regions, communities or fields of study.

When lexicographers noticed “kokum” appearing more frequently in “Canadian” English, they flagged it for further research. They found evidence of its use dating back to 1973, when Métis writer Maria Campbell

published her memoir

Halfbreed

, about growing up in Saskatchewan.


Hamelin remembers the

impact


Halfbreed

 had when it was first published.


“Everybody read that book,” she said. “It’s where a lot of people were introduced to that word.”


For Salazar …

author: Arezu Fayyazi
title: Denied Education, Denied Choice: The Rise of Child Marriage in Afghanistan
content:
Five years after the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan, reports of child marriage are increasing. Globally, more than 12 million girls are married before the age of 18 every year. UN Women identifies education, legal protections, and social support as critical measures for preventing child marriage. Yet in Afghanistan, the Taliban have systematically dismantled these very protections. By banning girls from education beyond the sixth grade, restricting women’s participation in public life, and eliminating pathways to independence, the Taliban are leaving Afghan girls increasingly vulnerable to early and forced marriage.

The Taliban have created an environment in which women and girls are cut off from opportunities, resources, and support systems that would allow them to shape their own futures. With secondary schools and universities closed to girls, millions have lost access to higher education, professional opportunities, and the possibility of financial independence. Restrictions on women’s employment further compound this vulnerability, limiting their ability to support themselves and exercise control over decisions affecting their lives. In addition to these restrictions, the Taliban have issued over 160 decrees and directives affecting all aspects of Afghan girls’ and women’s lives.

The consequences of child marriage extend far beyond economic hardship. Marriage at an early age often forces girls into adulthood before they are physically, emotionally, or socially prepared. It can end their education, increase their exposure to domestic violence, and put them at greater risk of early pregnancy and serious maternal health complications. These risks are especially severe in Afghanistan, where women’s access to healthcare is increasingly threatened and limited by restrictions on female healthcare workers, women’s freedom of movement, and international aid organizations.

The loss of education is particularly consequential because schools provided far more than academic instruction. They offered girls a sense of community, a degree of protection, and access to trusted adults who could recognize abuse and intervene when necessary. Without these spaces, girls have fewer opportunities to seek help, build support networks, or challenge decisions made about their futures. The Taliban’s dismantling of legal protections, including the Ministry of Women’s Affairs and the removal of women from judicial positions, has further weakened the systems through which women and girls could seek protection and justice.

For Afghan girls, the fundamental right to decide when and whom to marry is increasingly constrained by circumstances beyond their control. The closure of schools, restrictions on employment, and dismantling of legal and social protections have steadily narrowed their choices. What should be decisions about their own lives and futures are increasingly shaped by a system designed to deny them agency and independence.

Preventing child marriage requires more than addressing individual cases. It means restoring the conditions that allow girls to remain in school, women to achieve financial independence, and all women and girls to exercise their rights and make decisions about their own lives. Until Afghan girls regain access to education, opportunity, and meaningful protection, the Taliban’s policies will continue to leave them increasingly vulnerable to early marriage and rob them of the freedom to grow and to determine their own futures.

Sources: Kabul Tribune, UNICEF, Afghanistan International, OHCHR

author: Valerie Anne
title: Liv Hewson Opens Up to Drew Barrymore About the Early Parts of Their Career
content:
feature image photo by The Drew Barrymore Show/Ash Bean via Getty Images

Yellowjackets star Liv Hewson reunited with their former Santa Clarita Diet co-star Drew Barrymore on Drew’s talk show this week.

In the interview, they discuss all sorts of topics, including but not limited to Yellowjackets, of course. Drew presents Liv with gifts for what she thought was their engagement, but Liv reveals that actually they got married already. (There are actually really cute pics that pop up behind them of the couple as well in the clip, so you should check it out.) Drew’s now-wedding gifts are two beautiful candlesticks Drew said represents the two of them living together in harmony.

Liv talks about meeting their now-spouse on the set of Yellowjackets when they were AD, and recounts seeing them for the first time and having a “who IS that” moment immediately.

Drew shows Liv a clip of another of their Santa Clarita Diet co-stars, Skyler Gisondo, asking Liv to share dating advice, and their advice boils down to the fact that people want to feel safe and that should be a priority in any relationship, not just romantic. (This is not really here nor there but I could listen to Liv talk for hours. They have such a calming presence and such a thoughtful way of speaking and you can tell, even just from little clips and interviews, that they are a deeply intelligent person, both intellectually and emotionally, and I just really love hearing them talk about pretty much anything.)

The pair also talks about Molly Ringwald coming on Yellowjackets to play Van’s mother, and Liv says they really hit the jackpot when it came to fictional moms, having now had two legends (Molly and Drew herself) play their mom on television.

Liv also talks about how they felt like they were living in a “defensive crouch” for a long time; they came to the US to work when they were 20 and felt like they had to go back in the closet as nonbinary when they started working in Hollywood, but that Drew and the cast of Santa Clarita Diet became a soft place for them to land and they are really grateful to her for that.

It’s a very sweet interview and as sad as I am to see Yellowjackets come to an end, I’m really excited to see what Liv will get up to next, mostly because they are extremely talented and should be cast in whatever the hell they want, but also because, selfishly, I want to watch them on more press tours.

+ Hunter Schafer is kicking ass and taking names in her new series, Bladerunner 2099

+ Speaking of Hunter Schafer, she said she tried polyamory but is more into monogamy; she supports it of course but says there’s too much scheduling for her

+ Jennifer Love Hewitt is going to reunite with I Know What You Did Last Summer costar Ryan Phillippe in an upcoming 911/911: Nashville crossover (I know this is a stretch to include here but both shows do have queer women on them and also J.Love was one of my roots so LET ME HAVE THIS)

author: Jonathan Pinckney
title: Rebuilding American democracy with resistance and relationships
content:
This article

Rebuilding American democracy with resistance and relationships

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


What comes next for American democracy? Our research into authoritarian regimes reveals a striking pattern in how autocracies begin to fall apart — and democracy starts to regain ground.


The 2026 U.S. midterms revealed deep and growing frustration with the Trump administration, including among communities that

have traditionally

 supported Republicans. The secretary of the army, a Trump appointee,

resigned

 after disputes over military readiness and the Iran war. Small businesses

sued

 the administration over tariffs, while companies denounced ICE raids for gutting profits. The CEO of the South Texas Builders Association, a three-time Trump voter,

attacked the administration

 over ICE raids, saying that “South Texas will never be red again.” On Nov. 3, his prediction came true as Texas border counties

saw historic swings

 toward the Democratic party. These signs reveal widening cracks in alliances that have kept Trump in power.


This expanding circle of dissent evokes a common global pattern: When compliance with an authoritarian leader begins to break down, it can trigger a cascade of opposition that ultimately leads to regime collapse. Brazilian businesses that backed Jair Bolsonaro eventually denounced his anti-democratic behaviors, contributing to his electoral defeat. When parts of the Catholic Church removed support from the far-right Law and Justice Party in Poland, its governing coalition fragmented. And in Hungary, the electoral coalition that brought down Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was led by defectors from Orbán’s own party.  


When and why do people stop complying with dictators? We studied the behavior of thousands of key social groups whose compliance is critical for dictatorships to remain in power. These include businesses, unions, security forces and faith groups, key pillars whose political, economic and moral resources keep regimes standing. Looking at dictatorships and backsliding democracies in the post-Cold War era, one clear pattern stands out: Broad civic mobilization

and

 dense social ties between those complying with the regime and members of a pro-democracy opposition encourages non-compliance. Mass noncompliance is how autocracies fall. Indeed, the

chances of stopping democratic backsliding

 while relying only on institutional channels like litigation, legislation and voting is about 7.5 percent. The presence of a broad-based civil resistance increases the probability of success to around 53 percent.  


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


Both broad mobilization and social connection are crucial because of the nature of compliance. While some people comply because of true ideological alignment, most do so for more ordinary reasons: to advance careers, protect business interests, show deference to authority, or out of simple psychological inertia. Others may for their safety. When people fear political retaliation, public support can mask private indifference or even opposition. For example, while farm bureaus across the U.S. may avoid publicly denouncing the administration, plenty of farmers and ranchers are

seething

. While big business has largely refrained from publicly criticizing the administration,

behind closed doors

 many CEOs are exasperated. A pro-democracy front should make room for people withdrawing their support for all of these reasons.  


Broad-based civic mobilization — where diverse groups use

protests

, marches,

boycotts

 and walkouts to push back — changes this picture. If people both see and believe that dissent is widespread, they are more likely to shift their behavior. Courage becomes contagious. 


Strong social ties between a regime’s pillars of support and its opponents can facilitate a cascade of dissent. If people only see those who are different from them protesting, their dissent is easy to dismiss as the actions of a radical few. Yet if those they know and trust begin to speak out, such actions are more difficult to discount. This helps explain why the

spread of protests

 into rural and traditionally conservative parts of the U.S. is noteworthy. In Tunisia’s “Jasmine Revolution,” the national labor union — initially a co-opted part of the Ben Ali dictatorship — shifted to supporting the revolution when local offices that had been regularly …

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: 6- Cuttings will regrow – Sitting-in for Grandmother Cottonwood
content:
On July 27th, 2026 the U.S. government and Fisher industries cut down three ancient cottonwood trees in a small town called Lochiel, Arizona in order to build not just one but two border walls. This area is the habitat of the endangered Mexican Wolf as well as jaguars, bears, foxes and many other bizarre, beautiful bugs and animals. It is also the home of the Tohono O’odham people, important to many indigenous tribes on both sides of the border. When the three grandmother cottonwoods were cut, one brave comrade stood in front of construction equipment, preventing the destruction of the last ancient tree and the construction of the border wall. In that last tree, we began our tree sit. With the support of hundreds of activists, the land owners, nearby towns and tribes, and even the local sheriff department, we halted construction of the walls for 75 days.

For 75 days, activists sat in the remaining cottonwood as ground support grew into a sprawling camp. It was the first tree sit to stop border wall construction and was briefly the first binational tree sit in history, with a sit erecting on the Mexican side for three days in August. During these 75 days, O:shad camp, jaguar in O’odham, held morning ceremony in the easement, the road which enforced the border. Ceremony frequently extended to effectively halt all construction vehicles for the day, or days at a time. People fell in love, they danced in the mud, cooked communal meals, all while defending the land. Utopia felt nearby.

Then, on October 5th, hundreds of border patrol officers, accompanied by turning point usa, invaded O:shad camp. They cut down the grandmother cottonwood and forcibly removed the tree sitter without a proper extraction team, risking her life. Activists on the ground circled the trunk to protect the tree and continue their resistance against the wall. More than 10 activists were arrested and many more brutalized. Though on private property and with no warrant, they ransacked the camp and destroyed our belongings.

Indigenous and non-white activists were singled out and beaten much worse than white comrades. Border Patrol violently pushed, pulled and dragged, but also kneeled on throats, punched eyes, pushed skin into barbed wire. They specifically targeted our medic (who is Indigenous) to be violently dragged, beaten, and arrested. They prevented our media team from capturing what happened, while escorting Turning Point USA to film the day in order to spread their right wing propaganda.

The next day, as Border Patrol expanded their boundaries further into private property to make way for the wall, five more of us were taken, and lawyers were unable to find them in the system while border patrol ignored calls from their lawyers, friends and family.

A day later, my comrade locked herself to a cement truck and stayed in a stress position without food or water for 7 hours while Border Patrol covered her with an emergency blanket despite the hot climate. One officer told her and the other officers that they should drive her to the middle of nowhere where no one would be able to hear her scream. They began to move the vehicle with her still above the tire; we all thought she would be killed. Two comrades who ran towards her, worried for her life, were tackled, brutalized, and arrested – one was sexually assaulted during her arrest. Finally they brought in an expert extractor who took her out of lockdown and she was taken to detention and then federal prison. She is now facing federal assault charges.

The rest of us were shot with pepper balls, tear gassed, leaving us vomiting, injured, bruised and emotionally exhausted. After the tree sitter was removed from the grandmother tree in Lochiel, a comrade reinstated the sit on the mexico side. Cut off from ground support by border patrol, she went over two days without food or water. When mexican firefighters and Fisher construction workers went to pull her out, she free climbed further up the tree. They destroyed her platform and life sustaining materials, leaving her to perch in the cottonwood branches without a platform or supplies. She suffered dehydration and starvation in high heat but still managed to keep a backpack on her, which she filled with clippings of the Abuela tree so that no matter what happened, the trees offspring could be replanted.

The following day the wall continued.

In total 30+ of us have been arrested, and many more brutalized, injured, and traumatized. We are the …

title: Announcing Black Rose/Rosa Negra Locals in Austin, New York City, and Chicago
content:
We’re thrilled to announce the formation of three new Locals of Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN)! From the Texas Hill Country, to the Great Lakes, to the Northeast, our organization is growing deeper roots and expanding our capacity to organize, struggle, and build popular power in communities across the country.


As you will read below, each new local grows out of its members’ deep involvement in the popular struggles of their neighborhoods, workplaces, and broader communities. What follows are brief introductions in their members’ own words — including their contact info and social media handles.


Austin, TX


The Austin Local has officially re-formed! Our members are primarily focused on labor and tenant organizing, as well as rapid response to ICE. We are also making preparations for an open reading group to discuss

BRRN’s Program

.


We welcome those with interest to contact us.


Email:

 austin@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_atx


Chicago, IL


The Chicago local is back! Our logo honors the Haymarket Martyrs Memorial — a symbol of the organizers who made anarchism a powerful current in immigrant and women workers’ struggles of their time, as well as the place we gathered for our first event all together as a local. 


We carry their memory with us alongside others as we work in the social movements where we are rooted. These include tenant struggles on the South and Northwest sides, as well as labor organizing in the Chicago Teachers Union. We look forward to deepening our connections with comrades in our movements and others through collective study and struggle.


Email:

 chicago@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_chicago

 


New York City, NY


Members of the New York City Local organize with tenants, neighbors, youth, coworkers, and parents to build Black, Brown, and working-class popular power throughout the city. Sites of social insertion include the Astoria Tenant Union in Queens, anticarceral youth and parent programs in Manhattan, immigrant defense coalitions in Brooklyn, the American Association of University Professors, and more. True to BRRN’s internationalist character, we also organize within the Palestinian and Sudanese solidarity movements.


From the Young Lords to Occupy Wall Street, we recognize the integral role that revolutionaries in NYC have played in past freedom struggles and look forward to reviving organized anarchism in the especifista tradition across the five boroughs.

BRRN’s Program

 serves as a blueprint for renewed efforts to confront imperial and capitalist violence as anarchist militants living at the nexus of US empire and global capital .


Email:

 nyc@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:

 @blackrose_nyc


Are you organizing at your workplace, on your campus, or in your neighborhood? Looking for a political home in which you can strategize with others about how to build power, force concessions, and push our mass movements in a revolutionary direction?


Black Rose/Rosa Negra could be right for you.

Join

 page and send us a membership inquiry!

author: Joshua Davis, Whitney K. Taylor
title: Federal Government Is Targeting Officials Who Are Trying to Hold ICE Accountable
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


In the months leading up to the 2026 midterm elections, congressional Republicans and federal prosecutors have targeted dozens of local officials in cities and counties across the country that have adopted some sanctuary policies. The investigations have increasingly focused on prosecutors and law enforcement officers, many of whom have publicly announced plans to go after Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents who commit crimes in their jurisdictions or refuse demands to cooperate with federal immigration policing.


In total, 65 officials in 16 states have been targeted since January, according to a review of documents released by the

House Judiciary


Committee

 and the

Department of Justice

 (DOJ), as well as interviews with senior officials who have direct knowledge of individual investigations. The House Judiciary Committee has issued subpoenas and other demands for testimony, documents, and records to more than 40 officials, 15 of them local prosecutors. Alongside that, the DOJ has initiated investigations into 50 local or state officials since 2025, including five involving local prosecutors. In all, 17 local prosecutors have been swept up in House Judiciary or DOJ investigations and lawsuits related to immigration policies.


House Judiciary Committee Chair Rep. Jim Jordan said in a recent

report

 that “Democrats’ open-borders policies at the federal level and sanctuary policies at the state and local level allow millions of illegal aliens to pour into the country and ensure that criminal aliens, after encountered by local law enforcement, are released back into American communities,” echoing language the committee has commonly used in its investigations.


Many experts describe these investigations as unprecedented, and view the move as retaliation against local officials who refuse to cooperate with federal immigration agents or threaten legal action against ICE officers.


“These [prosecutors] are being intentionally intimidated by congressional and federal authorities,” said Mona Sahaf, the director of the Reshaping Prosecution initiative at the Vera Institute of Justice. “The use of [the] DOJ to target perceived political opponents is new. It’s busting norms, and it’s highly dangerous.”


The targeting of local prosecutors appears to be a matter of policy in the second Trump administration. “

Sanctuary Jurisdictions Directives

” issued by the attorney general’s office on February 5, 2025, held that the DOJ Civil Rights Division should “identify state and local laws, policies, and practices that facilitate violations of federal immigration laws or impede lawful federal immigration operations,” and “where appropriate, take legal action to challenge such laws, policies, or practices.”


The Appeal in Your Inbox


Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.


          Sign Up


The DOJ, in a June 18

press release

 announcing an investigation into local officials in Philadelphia — including District Attorney Larry Krasner — concerning a policy prohibiting federal agents from wearing masks, said that its “series of lawsuits brought by the Civil Division” targeted “illegal policies designed to thwart federal law enforcement across the country.”


Rebecca Roiphe, the Joseph Solomon Distinguished Professor of Law at New York Law School, said the investigations into local prosecutors represented “a wholesale abandonment” of the principle of separation between the DOJ and the political branches of government. “This administration has pretty openly suggested that it is normal and appropriate and even laudable for the political branches to have some degree of control over the Department of Justice,” she said.


Referring to the DOJ investigations, Roiphe said, “The bottom line is that these federal prosecutions can end up threatening local prosecutors to fall in line with federal priorities, and that’s illegitimate in our system.”


These overlapping investigations, reports, and the DOJ directives follow the Heritage Foundation’s

Project 2025 threat to “initiate legal action against” prosecutors

 who refuse to adhere to the priorities of the Trump administration. For many of the targeted prosecutors, the political influence has become impossible to ignore.


Among the targeted is Parisa Dehghani-Tafti, the top prosecutor in Arlington, Virginia, who drew the ire of Representative Jordan’s …

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: ‘No other option’: former RCMP leader stands by tactics that led to Rankin Inlet man’s death
content:
The RCMP detachment commander who approved the plan that led to police fatally shooting a 21-year-old Rankin Inlet man says that police couldn’t have done any better.


On Wednesday, the third day of the coroner’s inquest into Trey Angootealuk’s death, coroner’s counsel Jessi Casebeer asked Robert Gallant, now retired from the RCMP, if he could have done anything differently


“There was no other option,” he said. “If I had to redo the scenario, I would do the same thing.”


On Nov. 6, 2021, Angootealuk hijacked a truck, drove it to the outskirts of town, shot at police officers, and began a standoff with police that lasted several hours, inquest jury members have heard. Two officers fatally shot him early the next morning, after a canister of tear gas was launched through the rear window of his truck, forcing him to exit the truck.


Gallant, who was working from a command post in Iqaluit to direct officers on the ground, said he approved the plan to launch the gas canister and to shoot if necessary.


Supt. Stephen Bergerman, the critical incident commander before Gallant took over on the morning of Nov. 7, also testified Wednesday.


The Angootealuk family’s lawyer Nikolai Sittman asked him if mental health professionals were contacted at any point in the lead up to Angootealuk’s death.


Bergerman said he didn’t recall getting any mental health staff involved, though RCMP would have had access to hospital staff.


On Nov. 6, a

negotiator

 managed to speak on the phone with Angootealuk, who told him he wanted to end his life before hanging up.


Throughout his testimony, Bergerman reiterated that it was not safe enough to allow anyone other than police to approach Angootealuk because he had rifle.


The inquest by Nunavut Chief Coroner Marianna Cervantes, which is taking place at the Siniktarvik Hotel, began Monday and is scheduled to end Friday. It will determine the circumstances surrounding Angootealuk’s death. The coroner’s office gave Nunatsiaq News a video link to cover the inquest remotely.


Coroner’s inquests are mandatory under Nunavut law for all deaths involving an on-duty police officer. They do not determine the guilt or innocence of anyone involved. The jury will be expected to make recommendations aimed at avoiding future deaths in similar situations.


On Tuesday, attendees heard from Clark Plaetinck and Const. Jordan Booth of the emergency response team, who testified to firing the fatal gunshots. Both described fearing for their lives when they pulled the trigger.


The inquest will resume Thursday at 9:30 a.m. CT, with testimony from an expert on use of force.

author: anred
title: Encuesta Inquilina 2026: seis de cada 10 hogares del AMBA se endeudan para pagar el alquiler y solo uno de cada 10 puede ahorrar
content:
La ACIJ, el CELS, el CEUR-CONICET, el IEALC-UBA y la EIDAES-UNSAM, presentaron la Encuesta Inquilina 2026, un relevamiento sobre las condiciones de vida de las familias que alquilan en el Área Metropolitana de Buenos Aires. Los resultados arrojan que el 59% pidió dinero prestado durante el último año, el 72% de quienes se endeudaron usó esos recursos para pagar el alquiler y apenas el 10% logró ahorrar. El informe también revela que el 53% destina más de la mitad de sus ingresos al alquiler, el 70% recortó consumos y el 49% gastó sus ahorros. A tres años de la derogación de la Ley de Alquileres, aumentaron los contratos más cortos, las actualizaciones trimestrales y la informalidad: el 30% alquila sin contrato escrito y el 46% paga en efectivo. Tras el conocido caso de la jubilada Maricarmen Abascal, que desató movilizaciones y acampes en diversas ciudades españolas: ¿cuándo podrá convertirse este malestar extendido en una movilización colectiva por el derecho a la vivienda? ¿Habrá que esperar a que una historia individual se convierta en emblema para que la crisis habitacional ocupe las calles?

Por ANRed.


La

Asociación Civil por la Igualdad y la Justicia (ACIJ)

, el

Centro de Estudios Legales y Sociales (CELS)

, el

Centro de Estudios Urbanos y Regionales del CONICET (CEUR)

, la

Escuela Interdisciplinaria de Altos Estudios Sociales de la Universidad Nacional de San Martín (EIDAES-UNSAM)

 y el

Instituto de Estudios de América Latina y el Caribe de la UBA (IEALC)

 presentaron la

Encuesta Inquilina 2026

, un relevamiento sobre las

condiciones de vida de los hogares que alquilan en el Área Metropolitana de Buenos Aires (AMBA)

. Los resultados muestran un escenario de creciente precarización habitacional:

el 59% pidió dinero prestado

 durante el último año, frente al 37% en 2025; entre quienes se endeudaron,

el 72% utilizó esos recursos para pagar el alquiler

. Además, el

70% recortó consumos

, el

49% gastó sus ahorros

 y apenas el

10% pudo ahorrar

.


El endeudamiento aparece como una estrategia para sostener el pago de la vivienda aun cuando eso implique postergar otras necesidades

. El 31% de los hogares se atrasó en el pago de gastos corrientes o deudas, casi el doble que en 2025, cuando ese porcentaje había sido del 16%. Entre quienes recurrieron a préstamos,

el 35% pidió dinero a familiares o amistades, el 32% acudió a billeteras virtuales, el 22% tomó préstamos personales o pidió adelantos de haberes y el 13% recurrió a financieras o prestamistas

. Aunque el 91% se encuentra al día con el alquiler, los datos muestran el costo que implica cumplir con esa obligación:

endeudarse, consumir menos y agotar los ahorros

.


Foto: Federico Imas.


La presión sobre los ingresos también es cada vez mayor:

el 53% de los hogares destina más de la mitad de sus ingresos al alquiler, frente al 38% registrado en 2024

.

La situación es todavía más grave entre quienes dependen principalmente de jubilaciones o pensiones: allí la proporción alcanza el 74%

. Apenas el 6% de los hogares destina un cuarto o menos de sus ingresos a pagar la vivienda. A esto se suma el deterioro de la situación laboral:

la desocupación entre los hogares inquilinos llegó al 10,1%

, frente al 7,4% de 2025, mientras que quienes tienen trabajo pero quisieran trabajar más horas pasaron del 17,3% al 24,8%.


El informe señala que,

desde la derogación de la Ley Nacional de Alquileres en diciembre de 2023, se consolidó una tendencia hacia contratos más cortos y actualizaciones más frecuentes

. Los contratos de tres años cayeron del 30% al 7% entre 2024 y 2026, mientras que el 52% de los acuerdos vigentes tiene una duración de dos años. En cuanto a los aumentos,

las actualizaciones trimestrales pasaron del 23% al 46%

, mientras que los incrementos anuales descendieron del 17% al 2%. El 19% de los contratos, además, no tiene un índice de actualización definido de antemano.


La informalidad también forma parte de este escenario:

el 30% de los hogares inquilinos no cuenta con un contrato escrito, frente al 22% registrado en 2025, y el 46% paga el alquiler en efectivo

. El relevamiento también expone los abusos vinculados a la intermediación inmobiliaria:

el 83% de quienes alquilaron mediante una inmobiliaria pagó una comisión

. En la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, donde está prohibido cobrarla a la parte inquilina, el porcentaje llegó al 76%. Además, los contratos gestionados por inmobiliarias son, en promedio, un 15% más caros …

author: Comunizar
title: Crítica Anticapitalista no. 7 – Convocatoria
content:
¿Qué está pasando?


            En las últimas semanas hemos visto una serie de eventos que parecen abrir la esperanza de un cambio en la dirección de las luchas sociales. Estamos pensando en primer lugar en las protestas en las calles de Francia, Italia, Portugal, Alemania, Albania, India y muchos otros países. También hemos visto la derrota de la derecha en una serie de elecciones: Hungría, Serbia, Brasil, Estados Unidos. Pero al mismo tiempo y, sobre todo, sigue el genocidio en Gaza. ¿Qué está pasando?


            ¿Cómo entender la serie de protestas de las últimas semanas en Francia, Italia, Portugal, Alemania, Albania, India y muchos otros países? ¿Hasta qué punto se está abriendo, sobre todo entre lxs jóvenes, una perspectiva o una forma de organización que va contra-y-más-allá del capitalismo? ¿Es la rabia -volcánica- la conexión entre todas esas luchas actuales y pasadas?


            ¿Cómo entender la derrota de la derecha en las elecciones? ¿Pensamos que hay una diferencia significativa entre un gobierno de extrema derecha y uno de centro-izquierda? ¿Pensamos que el descontento expresado en esas elecciones podría desbordar la forma-Estado?


            ¿Cómo entender las luchas actuales en el marco del genocidio en Gaza? ¿En la virulencia de las recientes protestas en varios países de Europa, no estará escondido también un grito de impotencia/desahogo por el genocidio impune de Gaza? ¿Hay una rabia que esté tratando de salir del encierro que este sistema genocida nos impone? ¿Es posible sostener la esperanza crítica de un mundo otro no capitalista en un mundo que no ha logrado impedir ni detener el genocidio en Gaza?


Call for Papers


What’s Going On?


           

 In recent weeks we’ve seen a series of events that seem to open hope for a change in the direction of social struggle. We are thinking in the first place of the protests in the streets of France, Italy, Portugal, Germany, Albania, India and many other countries. And we have also seen the defeat of the right in a series of elections: Hungary, Serbia, Brazil, the Unites States. But at the same time, and above all, the genocide continues in Gaza. What’s going on?


            How do we understand the protests in all these countries? To what extent can we see, especially amongst the young, a perspective that goes against-and-beyond capitalism? To what extent are these protests breaking with the state-form and creating communising or other forms of organisation? Is volcanic rage the connection between all these struggles of the present and the past?


            How do we understand the defeat of the right in the various elections? Do we think that there is a significant difference between a government of the extreme right and one of the centre-left? Do we think that the discontent expressed in these elections could overflow from the state-form?


            How do we understand these struggles in the context of the genocide in Gaza? Does the virulence of these protests reflect a scream of hopelessness or fury in the face of the unpunished genocide in Gaza? In the violence of these protests is there a rage that is trying to break the enclosure that this genocidal system imposes on us? Is it still possible to maintain the hope of a world beyond capitalism in a world that has not succeeded in stopping the genocide in Gaza? In this context, of what significance are the elections in the USA or the visit of the Pope to Argentina and other countries of South America?


The post

Crítica Anticapitalista no. 7 – Convocatoria

 first appeared on

Comunizar

.

author: Darío Aranda
title: Denuncia penal contra autoridades del INTA: contaminación,  censura y venenos en la sangre
content:
Por Anabel Pomar


Tras la

exoneración de la investigadora del INTA

 Virginia Aparicio, las repercusiones en torno al

censurado Proyecto Sprint

 suman un nuevo capítulo, esta vez en sede judicial. En carácter de ciudadano habitante del sudeste bonaerense, el abogado Mario Bolla (representante también de Aparicio), ingresó una denuncia ante tribunales federales. Solicitó se investigue a las autoridades jerárquicas del INTA por incumplimiento de los deberes de funcionario público y posible puesta en peligro de la salud de la población.


En la presentación ante el Ministerio Público Fiscal de Mar del Plata, el denunciante —que es acompañado en el escrito por 19 voluntarios del Proyecto Sprint en calidad de testigos— pide se investigue la posible comisión del delito contemplado en el artículo 249 del Código Penal Argentino.


Los funcionarios denunciados por el período 2023 (cuando se suspendió la participación del INTA en la investigación) son: Mariano Garmendia (presidente), Nacira Muñoz (vicepresidenta), Carlos Parera (director nacional) y Horacio Berger (director regional, que sigue en su cargo en la actualidad). Y los actuales: Presidente: Nicolás Bronzovich (presidente), Carlos Vera (vicepresidente) y Ariel Pereda (directo nacional).


La denuncia también pide que se evalué la participación del resto de los

integrantes del Consejo Directivo

, que ocupan cargos como vocales (con derecho a voto en las decisiones institucionales) tanto del sector público (son funcionarios nacionales) como del sector privado. Allí se encuentran representantes del INTA, de la Secretaría de Agricultura, Facultades de Agronomía, Facultades de Ciencias Veterinarias (Universidades Nacionales), la Asociación Argentina de Consorcios Regionales de Experimentación Agrícola (Aacrea), Confederación Intercooperativa Confederaciones Agropecuaria (Coninagro), Confederaciones Rurales Argentinas (CRA), Federación Agraria Argentina (FAA) y de la Sociedad Rural Argentina (SRA), entre otros.


Foto: Naranja Ciencia y Técnica


Ciudadanos contaminados y “huérfanos” de asistencia


El escrito de la denuncia penal señala que, desde junio de 2023, fecha en que las autoridades del INTA

decidieron suspender intempestivamente las actividades

 del Proyecto Sprint, hasta finalmente retirarse completamente en diciembre de ese año, y hasta la actualidad, los voluntarios participantes quedaron “huérfanos” de toda asistencia, contención, guía y asesoramiento oficial por parte del organismo que los convocó a participar.


El

Proyecto Sprint

, representado por el INTA en Argentina (socio número 16 identificado como CSS11-Buenos Aires dentro del proyecto), convocó la participación de personas en carácter de voluntarios. Son habitantes de zonas rurales o ciudades bonaerenses, comprendiendo las localidades de Balcarce, Necochea, Tres Arroyos, Lobería, San Cayetano y Mar del Plata. Fueron un total de 73 personas de Argentina que se prestaron como voluntarios donantes para que se les analizara en sus cuerpos la presencia de agrotóxicos.


Como informó Tierra Viva

, todas las personas testeadas tenían glifosato en su cuerpo con rango de 6 a 13 plaguicidas en orina, de 2 a 10 plaguicidas en sangre y hasta 18 plaguicidas en materia fecal. En el momento de conocerse internamente los resultados, las autoridades del INTA aceleraron la salida del organismo de ese proyecto, y jamás dieron a conocer públicamente esos resultados. Tampoco los que señalaban presencia alarmante en alimento, aire, agua y suelo, que documentan la presencia de una mezcla de agrotóxicos de 20, 30 o hasta más de 80 plaguicidas según la matriz estudiada.


La presentación judicial señala que era obligación de un organismo estatal, una vez que tuvieron en su poder los resultados alarmantes del estudio, dar intervención a las áreas de Salud de la Nación, de las provincias (en el caso, autoridades sanitarias de Buenos Aires) y de cada comuna en la cual se llevaron a cabo los muestreos. Por el contrario, institucionalmente se decidió "guardar silencio" sobre el tema, ocultar a la opinión pública y, en particular, no informar a la mayoría de los "voluntarios" los resultados obtenidos respecto a su salud.


“Ante el hallazgo de contaminantes químicos, con efectos lesivos sanitarios y ambientales diversos, tanto en el agua de consumo, el aire, como en organismos humanos y animales, los funcionarios responsables de realizar acciones tendientes a revertir un problema de salud pública, decidieron censurar …

title: CONCEPCIÓN: REALIZAN CONCENTRACIÓN EN APOYO A LOS PPM DE CASO GROLLMUS EN HUELGA DE HAMBRE
content:
Durante la mañana de este miércoles 25 de noviembre, se realizó una concentración a las afueras del Cp Biobío en apoyo a los ppm condenados por el Caso Grollmus, quienes se encuentran en su tercer día de huelga de hambre, exigiendo la anulación del juicio racista y parcial que los condenó, sin pruebas materiales y en base a los relatos de testigos protegidos.

En el lugar se realizó un ayekan y se ingresó a la visita de los huelguistas, en la cual se pudo corroborar la inestable condición de salud de estos, considerando que varios de ellos tienen enfermedades base que agudizan el peligro de su movilización por la falta de alimentos. Así mismo, se pudo corroborar que su peso ha variado, disminuyendo casi en un kilo por día de huelga.

Los presos políticos mapuche en huelga de hambre son: Nelson Alonso Llempi, Rodrigo Valenzuela Canullan, Felipe Paineo Antiman, José Melgarejo Calbullanca, David Mariñan Millahual y Javier Mariñan Millahual, y dentro de los próximos días otros ppm se sumarán a la movilización.

A la salida de la visita el werken Auka Castro declaró:

Para los próximos días se esperan más movilizaciones por la anulación del juicio.-

title: Comunicado familia de Julia Chuñil ante desestimación de osamentas humanas en su vivienda
content:
COMUNICADO FAMILIA JULIA CHUÑIL


En la reciente audiencia de revisión de medidas cautelares el Juzgado de Garantía de los Lagos resolvió mantener la prisión preventiva de Javier Troncoso, quien cumple 10 meses privado de libertad.


En dicha instancia se presentó formalmente el informe técnico emitido por el Servicio Médico Legal (SML). En razón de la rigurosidad técnica y científica con que el organismo forense realizó sus análisis antropométricos y de laboratorio, el informe concluye de manera objetiva la desestimación de osamentas humanas en el predio habitacional de la familia, confirmando el origen animal de los restos analizados.


Dada la validez técnica acreditada por el SML, la familia ha resuelto solicitar formalmente que peritos especializados del propio Servicio Médico Legal lleven a cabo un conjunto de nuevas diligencias investigativas. El objetivo prioritario es avanzar en la búsqueda de nuestra madre y abuela Julia del Carmen Chiuñil Catricura con estándares científicos rigurosos.


Entre estas diligencias se incluye la realización de levantamientos de muestras y peritajes en puntos específicos previamente indicados por la familia, los cuales no fueron abordados en las etapas iniciales de la investigación o se llevaron a cabo sin la rigurosidad requerida. Confiamos en que la intervención de los profesionales del SML permitirá subsanar dichas omisiones. Dicha solicitud significa que la investigación deba nuevamente ampliar su plazo, costo que como familia asumimos con la finalidad de encontrar la verdad, el día de hoy el J.G. de Los Lagos amplió la investigación por 90 días más.


Junto a las conclusiones del informe del SML, consta en el proceso la apertura de una causa penal que investiga las circunstancias en que se obtuvo la declaración inicial del coimputado el día de la formalización, la cual se ejecutó sin la asistencia de un abogado defensor.


Frente al descarte científico de restos humanos en el inmueble y el cuestionamiento a la validez de la única declaración incriminatoria, la representación legal insistirá en las instancias correspondientes para obtener la modificación de la cautelar de Javier Troncoso, la que será apelada dentro del plazo de ésta semana.


24 de Noviembre 2026

Familia Julia Chuñil

author: Kay Pacha / Equipo Pueblos Originarios del SERPAJ
title: Denuncia de Indios Amazónicos frente al Papa León XIV
content:
Del 9 al 11 de noviembre tuvimos en nuestro país la visita del Papa León XIV y su presencia provocó una importante movilización popular. Mucha gente lo esperó con ansiedad, con devoción y hubo una gran organización para que se presente, ya sea saludando, dando misa o escuchando a representantes de distintos sectores de la sociedad.


https://argentina.indymedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/KAY-PACHA-LEON-XIV.mp3


https://argentina.indymedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/KAY-PACHA-LEON-XIV.mp3


Descargar audio


En sus presentaciones en nuestro país, si bien hubo momentos donde estuvieron presentes indígenas Mapuche, Huarpe, Guaraní y Nivačlé, no tuvo posibilidad de escuchar sus justos reclamos en público, a pesar de lo cual, en uno de sus discursos, hablando de la conformación de la sociedad, se refirió a los pueblos indígenas en la frase «Otros pertenecen a pueblos originarios cuya presencia precede al nacimiento de la nación». Es decir, reconoce la preexistencia indígena.


Pero en donde realmente pudo escuchar  importantes reclamos y situaciones en la que se encuentran estos pueblos, fue en su permanencia en Perú, en Pucallpa, donde representantes de pueblos amazónicos pudieron hablar frente a él y hacerle partícipe de sus distintos conflictos. No olvidemos que en la Amazonía de varios países, los pueblos indígenas son amenazados, corridos y asesinados por la ambición de los vastos recursos que la zona presenta.


Por eso nos pareció muy interesante presentar los testimonios de quienes hablaron en esa oportunidad. Está por un lado, la dirigente indígena Susy Díaz que le dice al Papa León XIV que desde la visita del Papa Francisco hasta la fecha han sido asesinados 37 líderes indígenas y defensores ambientales.


Por otro lado, el dirigente y comunicador indígena Cecilio Soria le dice entre otras cosas, al Papa León XIV que los derechos de los Pueblos Indígenas en Aislamiento Voluntario y Contacto Inicial deben ser respetados por el Estado peruano.


También oiremos  fragmentos del discurso del Papa, luego de que escuchara los de estos hermanos indígenas.


El Micro Kay Pacha se realiza con el apoyo de la organización Otto per Mille-Chiessa Valdense.
