author: Kodao Productions
title: Dismissal of petitions challenging Duterte’s arrest major step towards justice – Bayan Muna
content:
Bayan Muna (BM) welcomed the Supreme Court dismissal of the habeas corpus petitions challenging the arrest of former President Rodrigo Duterte and his turnover to the International Criminal Court (ICC).


Bayan Muna chairperson Neri Colmenares said on Wednesday said the decision is “another nail in the coffin of impunity” during the Duterte administration and is a major step in the victims’ search for justice and accountability.


“We support the decision of the Court because the warrant of arrest and surrender of Duterte has legal basis under Republic Act 9851 (the Philippine Act on Crimes Against International Humanitarian Law, Genocide, and Other Crimes Against Humanity of 2009) and our obligations in the Rome Statute of the ICC,” Colmenares said.


In a November 11 decision released on Tuesday, the high tribunal voted 9-4 with one dissenting vote to deny the petitions filed by Duterte’s children, Sebastian, Veronica and Paolo.


The Court said the petitions are “moot” and that Philippine courts “cannot enforce the writ since he is already in the custody of the ICC in The Hague, the Netherlands.”


Duterte was on March 11, 2025 and flown to The Hague, awaiting the formal start of crimes against humanity trial at the ICC on Monday, November 30.


Duterte’s children filed the habeas corpus petitions the day after his arrest, arguing that the ICC arrest warrant could not be enforced in the Philippines because the country had already withdrawn from the Rome Statute.


The SC decision, however, said a writ of habeas corpus is a domestic remedy enforceable only within the country. “Significantly, [Duterte] is not just beyond the Court’s coercive powers, but also stands accused before an international tribunal that has assumed jurisdiction over his person,” the SC said.


The Court likewise noted that Duterte is already participating in ICC proceedings and has pursued remedies available under the international tribunal rules, even challenging – albeit unsuccessfully – the basis of his detention.


Colmenares said all that remains now is for Duterte to defend himself during the trial, likewise urging the Ferdinand Marcos Jr. government to arrest Senator Ronald dela Rosa, Duterte’s co-accused in the alleged killings of thousands of suspected drug dependents as well as political critics.


“His (dela Rosa) arrest is not merely an issue of law but also an issue of justice for thousands of victims who were killed in the drug war conducted when Dela Rosa was Chief of the Philippine National Police,” the human rights lawyer said.


“He should be tried together with Duterte for the atrocious crimes committed when they were in power,” Colmenares added. #

(Raymund B. Villanueva)

author: rti_admin
title: Class Interests in Casteless Disguise: Can Caste Be Disowned Without Surrendering Property and Lineage?
content:
‘I don’t believe in caste. I have no caste. Let’s build a casteless society.’ One hears this all the time now, from people who call themselves progressive, rationalist, liberal. On the face of it, there’s nothing to argue with. Who could object to that?

But look at the Indian socio-economic structure honestly, and the slogan starts to look less like idealism and more like a sleight of hand. Because you can’t abandon caste in your speech while quietly holding on to the wealth and advantages caste handed you. That isn’t annihilation of caste. It’s a way of protecting the hierarchy while pretending to be above it.

Louis Althusser, in Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses (1970), made a point worth taking seriously here: ideology always exists in an apparatus, in practices—its existence is material. Caste is no different. It isn’t just a mental delusion people can shrug off. It has a material life, and in India that life runs through what we might call PPP: Property, Parents, Privileges.

Property means land, urban real estate, commercial capital—concentrated over generations in dominant-caste hands. Parents means lineage: hereditary prestige, ancestral standing, social capital kept carefully inside kin groups through endogamous marriage. Privileges means the leverage that comes from all of it—the networks that open doors in elite schools, boardrooms, professions, and commerce.

So when someone says they’ve “given up caste” because they dropped their surname, while still inheriting the family estate, the legacy networks, and the generational cultural capital—what exactly have they given up? You cannot disown caste while safeguarding the material lineage and property that caste produced. The two don’t come apart that easily.

Ambedkar: Annihilating Caste Means Annihilating Class

Ambedkar saw this clearly in Annihilation of Caste (1936). The caste order, he insisted, is not some innocent functional division of labour: “The Caste System is not merely division of labour. It is also a division of labourers.”

To the socialists of his day who thought economic reorganization alone would dismantle caste, he put the question squarely: can you have economic reform without first reforming the social order? If that order is graded by caste, what guarantee is there that Indian proletarians—divided into watertight caste compartments—will ever combine against their exploiters?

And on the myth of individual merit, he was blunt: those who benefit from birth, education, family name, business connections, and inherited wealth will win the race. But that isn’t a selection of the able. It’s a selection of the privileged. For Ambedkar, annihilation of caste was never about nominal changes in personal conduct. It demanded structural equality across economic, educational, political, and material life. Keeping the assets inside dominant groups while claiming caste is abolished runs directly against everything he argued.

The Biography of the “General Category”

Sociologist Satish Deshpande, in “Caste and Castelessness: Towards a Biography of the ‘General Category'” (2013), gave this rhetoric its proper name. Upper castes, he showed, have systematically laundered historical caste capital into the secular language of “merit” and individual competence. They shed the overt markers of caste, settle comfortably into the constitutionally unmarked “General Category,” and reinvent themselves as casteless modern citizens.

The burden of caste then gets shifted entirely onto SC, ST, and OBC communities—who are caricatured as “casteist” or backward for invoking affirmative action. Constitutional certificates become a badge of sectarian identity, while upper-caste generational capital passes as unmarked merit. That’s the strategy of the General Category, and Deshpande names it for what it is.

Lately there have been petitions before high courts—Telangana, Madras—asking for a “No Caste / Casteless” column in census forms, school transfer certificates, state applications. These deserve a closer look, because they tend to come in two flavours.

One is misguided cluelessness: well-meaning but politically naive people, from oppressed or liberal backgrounds, who imagine that leaving a box blank on a form dissolves structural violence. It doesn’t.

The other is more deliberate: an upper-caste design to escape structural accountability. If caste disappears from the census and public records, surveys can no longer measure how land, corporate wealth, and …

author: Dae-Oup Chang
title: International Labour Solidarity from Below: Reflections on Inter-Asian Solidarity Building of Asia Monitor Resource Centre
content:
Since its establishment in 1976, the Asia Monitor Resource Centre (AMRC) has served as a regional hub for labour solidarity in Asia. This article reflects on the AMRC’s half-century journey towards building inter-Asian labour solidarity. It discusses not only what AMRC has achieved, but also what it has failed to achieve, why it has failed, and what these experiences might tell us about the future of inter-Asian labour solidarity. This is a personal reflection, drawing on my 23 years of involvement with the AMRC in various capacities: as a full-time activist, a member of the Board of Directors, a member of the Regional Council, and Chair of the Board of Directors.


International labour solidarity has long occupied a prominent place in the political imagination of labour movements. Almost every major trade union has declared its commitment to internationalism. However, there is a considerable distance between internationalism as a declared principle and internationalism as an actual process of movement building. Affiliation to international trade unions, participation in international conferences, and occasional solidarity campaigns do not necessarily generate lasting solidarity among workers across national borders.


This distinction between international solidarity as a dead principle and as a living practice was central to an experiment in building bottom-up inter-Asian labour solidarity in which I participated during the 2000s as an AMRC activist coordinating the Asian Transnational Corporation Monitoring Network (ATNC Network). As  one of the regional labour networks AMRC initiated, the ATNC network sought to connect grassroots workers’ organisations across Asia. Its broader ambition was to build an alternative foundation for international labour solidarity in Asia. 


Building a Network from Below


When I joined AMRC in 2003, the ATNC Network already existed as a pilot initiative, with a substantial emphasis on

corporate codes of conduct

. Such an approach was becoming increasingly popular in international labour advocacy, particularly following the emergence of consumer campaigns targeting major international brands during the late 1990s and early 2000s.

1


We were sceptical of the political consequences of this prevailing model of north–south labour solidarity. Our scepticism concerned the underlying structure of solidarity that this approach

reproduced

. Northern organisations possessed the resources, connections, and influence required to pressure major brands, while workers and their organisations in Asian production sites were primarily positioned as

recipients of assistance

. The political focus often shifted from workers’ collective struggles to consumer organisations’strategies and their relationships with corporations.


Such campaigns sometimes achieved meaningful results. They can generate international attention, provide protection to workers, and force employers to negotiate. We did not deny their practical value. However, they had little to do with building the larger collective power of workers. For us, workers’ power was something to be built collectively by workers in and beyond workplaces rather than granted by individual employers’ moral behaviour. 


Therefore, we sought to reverse the direction of the network’s activities. Instead of beginning with corporations and their codes of conduct, we wanted to begin with workers’ struggles, their own organisations emerging from such struggles, and solidarity-based relationships built  between such organisations. 


These relationships developed through practical engagement. A group of workers or worker organisations might initiate a strike or an organising campaign. AMRC and its local partners could support the struggles on the ground. Over time, this process allowed us to include more organisations, whether unions or NGOs. Through such activities, new relationships emerged between organisations participating in the same struggles. 


Our criteria for partnership were therefore not primarily based on size, institutional recognition, or formal representativeness. We were interested in organisations with real connections to workers’ struggles. This frequently meant working with small but independent unions and grassroots NGOs rather than established national trade union centres.


While building a network of such organisations, the network operated through collaborative research, education, organising, and advocacy. Activities involved …

author: John David Parol
title: Trump Out, dumagundong sa Maynila sa kulminasyon ng protesta
content:
Sinalubong ng military honors ni Ferdinand Marcos Jr. si US President Donald Trump sa Malacañang kaninang umaga, Nobyemre 18, para sa kanilang bilateral meeting.

​Sa kabilang banda, kilometro lang ang layo mula sa palasyo, dumagundong ang panawagan ng sambayanan sa kulminasyon ng apat na araw na protesta kontra sa Pax Silica at sa imperyalistang Estados Unidos.

​Taliwas sa mainit na pagtanggap sa loob ng Malacañang, dahas at harang ang sumalubong sa mga nagpoprotesta sa lansangan.

Sa kahabaan pa lang ng Recto Avenue, hinarang na ang hanay ng mga raliyista at hindi pinayagang makapagmartsa patungong Mendiola. Hinarang din ng mga pulis ang mga delegasyon ng Gitnang Luson at Timong Katagalugan na nagmantini sa kampuhan sa Liwasang Bonifacio.

Hindi na napigilan ng galit na bulto ang magbulalas ng “Pax you, Trump” kasabay ng panawagang itigil ang Pax Silica at Trump Out.

Noong Nobyembre 17, pinuri ni Trump si Marcos Jr. sa pagsasabing mayroon itong “very good genetics” sa kanyang talumpati sa hapunan para sa mga lider ng ASEAN at Estados Unidos sa Maynila. Inalala rin ni Trump ang matagal na niyang pagkakakilala sa mga magulang ni Marcos Jr. bago pa siya naging pangulo ng Estados Unidos.

Para sa mga progresibong grupo, tumatagos sa katotohanan ang papuring ito, ngunit hindi bilang karangalan, kundi bilang patunay na manang-mana si Marcos Jr. sa kanyang ama at ina bilang masugid na papet ng Estados Unidos.

Hindi lingid sa kaalaman ng nakararami ang pagpapatayo ni Imelda Marcos ng mga pader upang itago ang kahirapan ng mga maralita noong idinaos ang Miss Universe sa bansa noong 1974. Sa kasalukuyan, gumastos ng humigit-kumulang ₱22.9 bilyon ang administrasyong Marcos Jr. kaugnay sa 49th ASEAN Summit. Ayon sa Defend Jobs Philippines, libo-libong maliliit na manininda at manggagawa ang pinatigil sa paghahanapbuhay sa tabing ng paglilinis sa daraanan ng mga dayuhang lider.

Sa isinagawang program sa Recto Ave., binatikos ni Bayan Secretary-General Raymond Palatino ang pag-host ni Marcos Jr. ng kauna-unahang leader-level QUAD meeting sa Pilipinas kahit hindi naman miyembro ng nasabing alyansang militar ang bansa.

Aniya, manang-mana rin si Marcos Jr. sa diktadurya ng kanyang ama sa paggamit ng makinarya ng estado at kapulisan upang supilin ang lehitimong pagkilos ng taumbayan.

Bago pa man buksan ang ASEAN summit, tatlong kabataang estudyante na ang inaresto sa University of Makati na lumahok sa ikinasang kilos-proteta laban sa Pax Silica noong Nobyembre 13. Habang may higit 200 indibidwal ang marahas na dinampot sa malawakang pag-aresto sa Muntinlupa at Kamaynilaan noong Nobyemre 15. Dagdag pa rito ang sa marahas na pagharang, panggigipit, paniniktik at iba pang porma ng brutalidad na ipinatupad ng Philippine National Police.

Inihalintulad naman ng National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (NUPL) sa kalagayan noong Martial Law at pagkakaroon ng concentration camps noong World War II ang pagtrato sa mahigit 200 indibidwal na inaresto sa kasagsagan ng mga protesta kaugnay ng 49th ASEAN Summit.

“Ang pagtrato sa kanila bilang mga detinido ay hindi nalalayo sa pagtrato ni Marcos Sr. sa mga protesters noong Martial Law at pagtrato ni Hitler sa mga Hudyo noong World War II,” ani Atty. Arman Hernando ng Pro-Labor Legal Assistance Center (PLACE), isa sa mga abogadong tumayong legal counsel ng mga inaresto sa Muntinlupa.

Nanawagan ang NUPL sa agarang pagpapalaya sa lahat ng inaresto at pagpapanagot sa Philippine National Police (PNP), Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), at administrasyong Marcos Jr. sa paghahasik ng dahas at brutalidad laban sa mga aktibista.

​Wala mang 24 oras ang itinagal ng pagbisita ni Trump sa bansa, babala ng mga grupo na habambuhay namang pasanin ng sambayanang Pilipino ang epekto ng anumang hindi pantay na kasunduan o lihim na napag-usapan sa bilateral meeting nina Marcos Jr. at Trump.

Sa kabila ng maagang pahayag nina Marcos Jr. at Trump sa harap ng media na hindi muna pipirmahan ang Pax Silica sa biyaheng ito, bigla namang ibinida ni Trump sa state luncheon sa Malacañang na nakapagkasundo na sila sa tinawag niyang “very big trade deal—the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made by far.”

Nagsara naman ang programa sa Mendiola sa pamamagitan ng simbolikong pagsunog sa watawat ng Estados Unidos habang dumadagundong sa mga sound system ang kantang “Trump Out” ng Switchbitch na sinabayan ng sigaw at indak ng bulto.

author: Dulce Amor Rodriguez
title: Filipino migrant healthcare workers denounce ICE detention, deportation threats
content:
Image of packaged sent to Balllesteros (photo from CLSU USSC)

Filipino migrant healthcare workers condemned the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown while raising concerns over medical neglect inside US detention facilities.

Speaking at a press conference organized by Tanggol Migrante Movement USA on November 13, two Filipino healthcare workers called for humane treatment and due process for migrants, regardless of their immigration status or profession.

Mariae “LC” Nacu was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Phoenix, Arizona, on August 22.

The 22-year-old registered nurse had been working at St. Joseph’s Hospital in Phoenix and has a valid employment authorization.

She was held at the Eloy Detention Center for three weeks before her release on bond, according to Tanggol Migrante Movement USA.

The organization said that her bond was set at $17,000 (P1.08 million) on November 13.

Nacu also estimated that she spent around $300 weekly (P19,068) on commissary items and phone calls while detained.

More than two months after her detention, ICE continued to hold her identification documents, including her driver’s license, according to the organization.

“The difficult part was that I wasn’t there [in the detention center] as a nurse. I was another person in detention, locked in a cell, trying to get someone to listen,” Nacu said.

She recalled witnessing a medical emergency involving another detainee and struggling to get someone to listen to her concerns.

Nacu described the separation from loved ones, handcuffing, and transfers between detention facilities without knowing where she was going as “traumatizing and dehumanizing.”

Dr. Veronica Velasquez, a Filipino physical therapist and recipient of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA), faces the threat of being deported.

Co-chair of the Los Angeles Kalusugan Collective, Velasquez regularly visits detainees at the Adelanto Detention Center where she witnessed brutality and medical neglect.

Velasquez said that she has organized with Tanggol Migrante Movement USA for two years and continues to support detained migrants despite facing immigration-related uncertainty herself. “I am a healthcare worker who has seen firsthand the brutality inside detention centers. I, myself, am threatened with deportation and have experienced over 23 years of this immigrant injustice system. Even so, I’m here still fighting for my community while the community fights for me.”

She said that nearly 100 community members attended her first court hearing.

Both healthcare workers raised concerns about the treatment of migrants inside US detention facilities, particularly their access to medical attention.

Velasquez said that her experience in visiting detainees exposed her to cases of alleged brutality and medical neglect. “As healthcare workers, we are in a special position to shed light on these issues of migrants in detention […] You cannot deny us from saying that there is medical violence happening in these detention centers.”

Nacu’s account of witnessing another detainee’s medical emergency also underscored the difficulties people in detention face when seeking help.

Her testimony, however, does not independently establish the circumstances or outcome of the medical emergency.

Bulatlat previously reported the case of a Filipino detainee, Kuya G, who underwent a toe amputation after months of alleged medical neglect at the Northwest Detention Center in Tacoma, Washington.

Migrant rights advocates said that detention facility personnel failed to properly diagnose and address his condition.

The case adds to concerns raised by migrant organizations about the treatment and medical care available to people held in immigration detention.

Read: Filipino migrants face inhumane treatment at ICE detention centers

Velasquez raised concerns over the slow response and lack of accountability of Philippine consulates who are supposed to be assisting detained migrants. She cited one case where a consulate called the police on mothers of detainees who were seeking assistance.

Her remarks echo concerns raised by Filipino migrant organizations about the Philippine government’s response to the detention of Filipino nationals in the United States.

author: Jordan Humphreys
title: German Left Party expels pro-Palestine politician
content:
German pro-Palestine politician Vanessa Emde has been expelled from 

Die Linke’s 

(the Left Party’s) parliamentary group in Berlin.

On Tuesday 24 November, 33 out of 44 representatives of the party’s Berlin parliamentary group voted to oust Emde, overcoming the two-thirds requirement.

Emde, a theatre director associated with the Left Party’s Trotskyist Marx21 wing and co-founder of Neukölln’s Palestine solidarity working group, won her Neukölln constituency directly with 46.2 percent of the first preference vote in September’s Berlin state election. Like many supporters of Palestinian freedom, she has been falsely slandered as an antisemite.

For months, a hysterical campaign has been waged against Emde. Major German news outlets—from conservative Axel Springer publications (

Bild

, 

Welt

) to centrist and centre-left papers (

Der Spiegel

, 

Die Zeit

, 

Tagesspiegel

)—have united in denouncing her. They have repeatedly decried her statement that “nations don’t have a right to exist, people have a right to exist” and her criticism of Israel’s genocide in Gaza as antisemitic.

This campaign intensified with the prospect of a Berlin coalition government led by the Left Party, which won the most votes in September’s election. The Greens and the Social Democrats (SPD) made Emde’s expulsion a prerequisite for any coalition with the Left Party. “We are of one opinion”, Berlin SPD leader Steffen Krach told the ZDF 

heute

television network. “We do not want to work with antisemites, and we will not work with antisemites.” Berlin Green parliamentary leader Werner Graf told the media they “will not be dependent on people with antisemitic attitudes”.

In November, coalition negotiations in Berlin broke down when the SPD and Greens walked out, demanding Emde’s expulsion before talks resumed. On 6 November, the Left Party’s Berlin state co-chairs, Kerstin Wolter and Maximilian Schirmer, demanded Emde surrender her parliamentary seat. She refused. She has now been expelled in order to restart negotiations.

This is a disgraceful turn of events. It is obvious why the pro-Israel German media, the Greens and the SPD would slander Emde. Uncritical support for Israel is sacrosanct in the German political establishment, where hostility to Palestinian solidarity is fiercer than in any other Western country. The SPD is even more cravenly pro-Israel than Australia’s Albanese government, while the German Greens define Germany’s responsibility for Israel’s security as “non-negotiable” and denounce other European Green parties as antisemitic.

Why, though, would a left-wing socialist party expel Emde?

The Left Party leadership cares far more about forming government than advancing the struggle of the oppressed and exploited. They are willing to do whatever it takes to enter the halls of power, even if it means facing down a backlash from their own membership.

This is not a new problem. Formed from a fusion between a left-wing split from the SPD and former East German Stalinist politicians, the Left Party has always attracted grassroots activists while remaining firmly controlled by career bureaucrats committed to moderate progressive politics.

From 2002 to 2011, the Left Party—and its predecessor, the PDS—served as junior partners in an SPD-led Berlin government. That administration sold off 100,000 state-owned apartments, laying the groundwork for the city’s current housing crisis. Left Party ministers also signed off on wage freezes, public-sector job cuts, higher public transit fares and cuts to social and cultural programs, alienating unions and working-class voters. The party’s vote fell from 22.6 percent in 2001 to 11.7 percent in 2011.

The Left Party also led the Thuringia state government from 2014 to 2024. During that decade, Left Party Minister-President Bodo Ramelow oversaw budget cuts and deportations of refugees. When his coalition ended in 2024, the party’s vote plummeted from 31 percent in 2019 to 13.1 percent, creating space for a dramatic surge by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

More recently, the Left Party experienced a revival, drawing in tens of thousands of new left-wing members as it campaigned against the far-right.

September’s Berlin state election was a historic victory. Finishing first with 25.7 percent of the vote, the Left Party more than doubled its previous Berlin result. This followed a broader resurgence in early 2025, when membership doubled to 123,000 and national polling …

author: Lindsay McCabe
title: Changes to coronial legislation to broaden next-of-kin determinations
content:
Readers please be advised that this article mentions First Nations people who have passed away, including children.


On Tuesday 22nd September 2026, the Minns Labor Government announced changes to the

Coroners Act 2009

 NSW, specifically, the section of the legislation that instructs coroners to determine and appoint a Senior Next-of-Kin. This followed a statutory review of the Act, and is in response to one of the many recommendations made by the review. 


When a person’s death is reported to the coroner, a Senior Next-of-Kin is appointed. The Senior Next-of-Kin has the exclusive authority to make decisions regarding the person who has died while they are in the care of the coroner. For example, the Senior Next-of-Kin can object to a post-mortem examination being conducted. Being appointed Senior Next-of-Kin also means that the coroner has an obligation to provide mandatory notifications about the progress of a coronial investigation to the Senior Next-of-Kin. When, where and how a person is laid to rest is also under the authority of the Senior Next-of-Kin. 


Who is appointed as Senior Next-of-Kin is decided by a strict legal framework. The

Coroners Act 2009

 (NSW) s 6A states that the Senior Next-of-Kin must be the deceased person’s spouse or de facto partner; if they have no spouse or de facto partner, then any of the adult children of the deceased person can be appointed. If the person has no adult children, then the person’s parent/s may be appointed. 


This appointment-flow hierarchy has been problematic for Mob for many years, across many jurisdictions. It does not take into account our kinship systems, laws, or spiritual beliefs. One of the earliest challenges of the Senior Next-of-Kin hierarchy involved

two Aboriginal parents

 who could not agree on where to bury their deceased adult child. The mother wanted to hold a Catholic ceremony and burial in Darwin; the father however wanted to have a burial on their homelands, Bardi Country, and provided the Court with supporting information outlining the cultural obligations to do so. The Court ruled in favour of the mother. 


In

2016

, the NSW Supreme Court was asked to rule on a matter where the Senior Next-of-Kin appointment had been challenged. In this matter, the coroner had appointed a deceased man’s de facto partner as the Senior Next-of-Kin, as per the legislation. This allowed the partner, a Gumbaynggirr woman, to make arrangements for the deceased man’s burial to take place in Bowraville. The man’s sister however, wanted the man to be taken home to Weilwan Country and to be buried alongside his ancestors. The Court ruled in favour of the man’s de facto partner, citing common law precedent. Further, because the de facto partner of the deceased man established her de facto status to the Court, she held ‘administrative priority’; in other words, she had the highest right as per the legislation. 


More recently, in 2024, the Supreme Court of NSW decided on a dispute between a deceased man’s de facto partner and mother who could not agree on where to bury him. The de facto partner of the man insisted he wanted to be buried in La Parouse; his mother wanted to take him home to his father in Cherbourg, Wakka Wakka Country, where he could be buried on Country. The Court held in favour of the man’s de facto partner, accepting that she was the deceased man’s de facto partner at the time of his death. 


So, who is appointed Senior Next-of-Kin when a person dies has significant ramifications for where, when, and how a person is returned to Country. 


There have however been instances where the appointment of Senior Next-of-Kin has affirmed cultural responsibilities and laws, albeit outside of NSW. In

1999

, the non-Aboriginal spouse of a deceased Aboriginal man sought to bury them in Port Augusta. The deceased man’s father wished to bury him in Oodnadatta, where other members of the family had been buried, and on Yankintatjara Country. Several affidavits were presented to the Court, highlighting that, according to cultural responsibilities and practices, the head of the family should be empowered to make these decisions, not the spouse. The deceased’s spouse, on the other hand, argued that the children of the deceased would not be able to visit their father’s grave if it were located 700kms away in Oodnadatta. Significantly, the Court ruled in favour of the father of the deceased man, allowing him to take his son home, and to be buried according to …

author: Kerry Smith
title: NT Environment Centre demands full federal assessment of gas pipeline
content:
The Environment Centre Northern Territory (ECNT) is calling on Murray Watt, the federal Environment and Water Minister, to undertake a full environmental impact statement of the APA Group’s fracked gas export pipeline.

The Queensland portion of the pipeline, 899 kilometres, was referred to Watt on November 26.

Rather than submit the full plan, the APA Group is referring small sections of its pipeline at a time in a bid to avoid environmental scrutiny.

The Environment Centre NT’s Acting CEO Bree Ahrens described this as “approval by stealth”.

The 1561-kilometre North to East Australia Pipeline (NEAP) to Gladstone’s export port in Queensland is one piece of a bigger network being built to move fracked gas from the Northern Territory to the east coast.

APA has even split the Bulloo Interlink Pipeline Project into two federal referrals — one for Queensland and one for NSW.

ECNT estimates the pipeline would enable major expansion of fracking in the NT, having the capacity to transport gas fracked from 1000 yet-to-be-approved gas wells.

Environment Centre NT CEO Bree Ahrens said the reason APA is splitting this approval process up is an attempt to “downplay the impact of this fracked gas export pipeline, and try and push through approvals without appropriate environmental scrutiny”.

Ahrens said the NT fracking project has ever been assessed federally.

“This will be a major test of how willing the federal government is to stand up to frackers and ensure proper environmental scrutiny of the Beetaloo export pipeline.”

She said the pipeline “ploughs through habitat for dozens of threatened species on the NT side alone”, including greater bilbies, night parrots, plains wanderers. The it also runs through fragile Channel Country in south-west Queensland and the floodplains of the Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre Basin which is one of the world’s last free-flowing desert river systems.

“The fracked gas project in the NT is destructive at every stage of development. It risks groundwater in the NT, threatened species in Queensland and drives dangerous climate change when it’s burned. This is why Minister Watt must assess the whole Beetaloo-to-export chain as one project, not as convenient fragments.”

While it is being being split in two for assessment, at a state and Territory level, “the truth is that this is a single, massive fracked gas export pipeline” which the gas industry needs for its thousands of fracking wells across the NT.

[To find out more visit the Environment Centre NT.]

author: Jeremy Brecher, Alexandria Shaner
title: United States: ‘Now the real work begins’
content:
Voters have just delivered an overwhelming rejection of United States President Donald Trump, opening a real opportunity to limit his drive to lock the country further into oil, gas and coal.

Labour historian and organiser, Jeremy Brecher, argues that this is only a starting point. Even if the worst of Trump’s fossil fuel agenda is blocked, the US is still on course to become a “fossil fuel island”, paying more for energy and falling behind economically while much of the world shifts to cheap solar, wind and batteries.

In his new report, The Greentech Revolution, Brecher makes the case that avoiding that fate means embracing a just transition to a fossil free economy.

Brecher stresses that cheaper technology won’t get us there on its own. What decides the outcome is who owns and controls the energy system, what it’s for, and whether ordinary people get a say. That fight is already underway in city halls, statehouses, and neighbourhoods organising against data centres.

With the midterms behind us, the real work begins now. I asked Brecher what that work looks like, from policy fights to organising well beyond the ballot box.

The midterms are over, and you say limiting Trump won’t be enough. What’s the gap between blocking the worst and actually building the alternative? Who has to close it, and where, outside of Congress?

We are already experiencing climate catastrophe and if we stay on our current trajectory it will only get worse and worse. We are already experiencing historic inequality, and if we stay on our current trajectory it will only get worse and worse. The same is true for our health, education, housing and all the other necessities of life.

Even if we block new Trump depredations, we will face an American era similar to Russia’s “Yeltsin Era” following the fall of the Soviet Union, when the legal, educational, healthcare, manufacturing and other basic systems went into unending decline — marked, for example, by a six-year drop in male life expectancy.

To change that will take the kind of transformative reconstruction that was envisioned by the Green New Deal. But because conditions have changed and deteriorated so much, we need to update that to what I call a “Green New Deal 2.0”.

From the beginning, the Green New Deal was a convergence of progressives inside the political system and social movements based in civil society.

The defeat of Trumpism in the 2026 midterm elections was similarly a convergence of outside-the-system forces like the No Kings coalition and inside-the-system Democrats who cared about Gaza, war, climate, the Constitution and the wellbeing of ordinary people. Plus, the decision by ordinary people that they had to step forward, whether it was by protecting their immigrant neighbours against ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] or in voting en masse against Republicans. Those same forces need to take the lead in developing the alternative — the “Green New Deal 2.0”.

The report argues the technology is already cheaper and winning. So why isn’t the US just switching? Who is holding it back, and what does the “fossil fuel island” cost ordinary people?

While the rest of the world is racing to switch to fossil-free greentech energy production and consumption, the US is going in the opposite direction. This is due to two main factors.

The first is the power of the fossil fuel industry.

Even under Joe Biden’s “Build Back Better” program, supposedly “green” policies like carbon capture and hydrogen were coined into profits for fossil fuel developers while the US underwent its largest ever expansion of natural gas.

The second is a nationalist drive to use energy policy for geopolitical power.

The Biden administration put high tariffs on cheap Chinese solar and EV imports that could have revolutionised American energy use. The Trump administration put both of these dynamics on steroids. It has tried to destroy Greentech energy initiatives not only in the US but worldwide. And it has provided vast subsidies for fossil fuel expansion.

But this is a fool’s strategy. You can see the actual results for ordinary Americans in the price of gasoline, heating oil, diesel fuel and electricity. And you can see the long-term effects of fossil fuel domination in the devastating heat waves, floods, wildfires and other products of climate change.

Your report says technology never dictates the form or speed of social change. Why does that matter right now? The “free lunch” idea is easy to …

author: Owen Marsden-Readford
title: The irrationality of the AI bubble is the irrationality of the market
content:
The AI investment boom is one of the largest bets in the history of capitalism. Money is pouring into the tech industry. Global AI spending is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion this year and $10 trillion cumulatively by 2032. The priorities of the system are obscene. Ending world hunger, according to the United Nations World Food Programme, would cost $40 billion per year. Amazon is spending over four times this on AI infrastructure this year.

In Australia alone, $150 billion is committed to building AI infrastructure over the next five years. That money could be life-changing for workers if it was used for almost anything else. Diverting the money from the data centre buildout could fund Australia’s health and Medicare budget for one year. Imagine the improvements we could make to an over-stretched and under-funded hospital system. With $150 billion, we could house the 200,000 households on the public housing waiting list at an average cost of just under half a million dollars and still have $50 billion left over. 

The $150 billion committed to data centres could also be used to pay for the Labor government’s aged care expansion package 38 times over. Or we could fund a significant chunk of the green transition needed to limit runaway climate change. The Australian Energy Market Operator places the cost of decarbonising the National Electricity Market by 2050 at $122 billion.

​Alas, the ever-rational invisible hand of the market has decided that we need more data centres to power Elon Musk’s Grok AI and its

 epic, vulgar roasts

.

​That the AI boom is socially destructive is irrelevant to investors. Data centres guzzle fossil fuels and water and are a significant source of noise pollution, emitting a constant low, droning hum. Most of the data centre buildout is happening in working-class and poorer communities in Western Sydney, not in Mosman or Toorak.

In recent weeks, the AI stock market boom has faced a sharp downturn. This is not because the world’s capitalists have taken notice of the socially and environmentally destructive nature of the industry, but because they are concerned that future windfall profits may not materialise.

​AI is now integrated into the militaries across the world, the result of an AI arms race. The results are terrifying. Take Russia’s

 

ZALA Lancet drone

, which uses AI to spot and dive bomb targets free from human oversight.

​Bosses are using AI as an excuse to sack workers. In the past few weeks alone, Qantas, NAB and Canva have announced over 4,000 redundancies cumulatively. Moreover, the data centre buildout is pushing inflation upwards, which the Reserve Bank is using as an excuse to raise interest rates, pushing unemployment higher. It is yet another way the AI boom is coming at the expense of the working class.

​The insanities of the AI boom are the insanities of the market. It is only in a capitalist society driven by profit and competition that it makes sense for trillions of dollars to be ploughed into AI while working-class needs are neglected. For anything that would benefit the working class, governments and capitalists across the world cry poor. Yet when there’s a share market boom, trillions find their way into it with no thought for what society actually needs. 

It’s not like people are crying out for data centres. In the US midterm elections, when data centres were on the ballot, voters rejected data centre expansion or approved local restrictions in 40 out of 41 ballot measures. AI data centres are unpopular yet continue to be imposed on ordinary people. Genuine democracy and the capitalist market are incompatible.

Under capitalism, production occurs to enrich the capitalist class, not to meet human needs. Karl Marx wrote in Capital: “Accumulate, accumulate! That is Moses and the prophets!” In a market economy, maximising shareholder value counts for more than the cries of hungry children or the plight of the homeless. 

​The AI boom is making many capitalists astronomically rich. Tech billionaires gained a combined $845 billion through the first nine months of this year. The stock market has reached record highs multiple times in 2026. The benefits of the AI bubble concentrate at the top, in the hands of corporate executives, financiers and the rich more generally. Workers, on the other hand, receive almost nothing. There is no boom in wages. Huge speculative wealth sits alongside stagnant or falling living standards.

​No boom, however, can last forever …

author: @ndy
title: The struggle is real with Jillian Segal.
content:
See also : Jillian Segal and husband funding far-right group “Advance”, Anthony Klan, The Klaxon, July 12, 2025.

Jillian Segal — the South African–born Australian lawyer, business executive, and Australia’s Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism — recently dropped another Report, ASECA Priorities. According to the Special Envoy, a newly-hatched “modern progressive antisemitism” … is taking “the hostility of Islamic extremism and far-left antisemitism, together with traditional antisemitic tropes”.

My first reaction on reading this passage was to recall the unforgettable 2014 framing by the Australian Defence League of the alleged “evil anarcho-pinko-anarchist-islamic cabal of dirt”; the wicked coalition then allegedly intent on turning Penrith into a no-go zone for patriots.

In any case, inre the Report, Jeffrey Loewenstein doesn’t hold back in It’s time to sack Jillian Segal (Deepcut News, November 2, 2026), the Jewish Council of Australia (October 30, 2026) has slammed it, and Jeff Sparrow has characterised it, not unfairly, as a Trumpian plan to curtail free speech (Crikey, November 2, 2026). The Report is also subject to critical scrutiny by Robert Manne, who examines it in On the Rise of Antisemitism in Australia (November 8, 2026), along with the thoughts of Lord Andrew Roberts and Sir Simon Schama on the subject of ‘antisemitism’. Manne concludes that:

Schama believes he can help combat the rise of antisemitism in the Diaspora by defending the indefensible, the war crimes of the IDF under Benjamin Netanyahu. I believe a more likely remedy would be for leading Diaspora thinkers, like Schama, and influential publishers, like Morry Schwartz, and the leaders in Australia of the principal Israel and Jewish lobbies, like Jillian Segal, to speak the truth about what, under Netanyahu and the two Kahanist-fascist members of his Government, Israel has become, and the moral revolution that has to happen in Israel if Jews in the Diaspora are to be spared from the dreadful rise of antisemitism that is spreading around the Western world.

FWIW, for over 20 years I’ve been attempting, inter alia, to monitor and document organised, public expressions of antisemitism and other racisms in Australia — the better to disrupt it. I’m also an anarchist, and one of many people to hold the view that the Israeli state has engaged in a genocidal assault upon Palestine in the three years since October 7 (the latest chapter in a much longer history of deadly state violence). On that basis, I assume that Segal et. al. would categorise myself as an exponent of ‘far-left antisemitism’, the meaning of which is elaborated upon in this passage:

Far-left antisemitism or issue-motivated antisemitism

Far-left ideology and associated activism feature a worldview that casts the world in terms of ‘oppressors’ and ‘oppressed’. Within this binary framework, Israel is portrayed as a colonial project that is inherently racist and Jews who support Israel’s existence are portrayed as representatives of ‘whiteness’ (regardless of their ethnicity), privilege (regardless of their means), imperialism (notwithstanding the absence of an empire), greedy capitalism and the projection of Western power.

This framing allows longstanding antisemitic motifs to be repackaged in the academic language of anti-racism, decolonisation, human rights, social justice and intersectionality, often in service of a traditional Marxist revolutionary agenda.

When a cause is believed – with ideological fervour – to be absolutely just, its ends can come to justify any means and its adherents can feel free to vilify, harass and seek to destroy those who associate with what is framed as evil.

Over time, the language of human rights and its greatest crimes – apartheid, ethnic cleansing, genocide, etc. – has increasingly been appropriated to portray Israel (and, relevantly, members of the Jewish community who support it) as morally evil, often to the point of being equated to Nazis.

In contemporary Australia, elements of Australia’s historically fringe radical left have sought to appeal to well-meaning mainstream progressive Australians who may perceive the Palestinian cause as a matter of social justice. This ‘gateway’ issue, of sorts, has been used by far-left activists to magnify their appeal and prominence and to attempt to introduce traditionally moderate Australians to radical and anti-Jewish propaganda that would previously have been of little interest.

The strange – but …

author: Peter Boyle
title: Capitalism hijacks another climate summit
content:
Given the heatwaves in Europe, the catastrophic floods in Nepal and wildfire crisis in Indonesia, you would hope that the recent COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkiye, would have reached agreement on stronger action to deal with the global climate emergency.

But COP31 totally failed to take the urgently-needed action. According to some assessments, it might have even set back the snail’s pace progress towards the non-binding targets set under the 2015 Paris Agreement, which had its goal to limit global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.

“Governments had a chance to show that international cooperation can still deliver for people," said Climate Action Network International (CAN) in a press release on November 22. "Instead, the world’s wealthiest countries spent two weeks dismantling the very commitments that offered some hope of protection.”

With the exception of 2009 (in Copenhagen), every COP summit since 2003 has led to a loose and non-binding formal agreement.

Turkiye’s co-host Australia, one of the world’s largest fossil fuel exporters, led the negotiations for the draft Antalya Accords.

The draft conceded a failure to keep the global temperature from rising 1.5˚C above the pre-industrial revolution level, but the root cause of this — fossil fuels — was not even mentioned in the agreement.

The European Union, Panama and many vulnerable island nations refused to agree to any text that did not explicitly address them.

This disagreement ultimately prevented the summit from reaching consensus, said the team of climate experts from University College London (UCL) attending COP31.

“This has been the modus operandi of these summits — they start with a more ambitious draft text that gets weakened as it comes closer to adoption … But removing fossil fuels from a climate text is like removing mention of cigarettes in an anti-smoking campaign — it was simply too much for many countries to accept.”

While the UCL team labelled this outcome a “victory for fossil fuel producing nations”, CAN pointed out that the European Union exploited the legitimate outrage by the most vulnerable states from the Global South to advance its own agenda.

“Much of the attention on COP31 has focused on the disappearance of fossil fuel language from the cover decision. But that story has helped hide the obstruction taking place across the negotiations. With the United States absent, the EU has stepped into the role of chief obstructor, while presenting itself as a champion of climate ambition — even going so far as to position itself as the first to reject the cover decision in the closing plenary.

“The EU and other developed countries spent two weeks blocking progress even on existing commitments. The EU refused to engage on a baseline for tripling adaptation finance and obstructed efforts to clarify developed countries’ obligations to provide public finance under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement.

“Developed countries demanded that developing countries move faster away from fossil fuels while denying them the resources to do it. Some developed countries dressed up existing policies as ambitious fossil fuel transition road maps, even as they continued to expand fossil fuel production at home. Having blocked the means to achieve a Just Transition, they then tried to pin the failure of COP31 on developing countries.”

While the major fossil fuel exporting states, like Australia and Saudi Arabia, are culpable, ultimately it was capitalism and the world’s richest states that hijacked COP31 and previous COP meetings.

They turned this climate summit into a trade fare for fossil fuel companies, carbon dioxide removal promoters and the AI industry, which descended on Antalya in large numbers to justify the ongoing use of fossil fuels.

“COPs have become greenwashed circuses. That is the reality,” activist Greta Thunberg said at COP31. “Of course it is absolutely crucial that we still do everything we possibly can because this is an opportunity to mobilise people … The climate disasters that we have seen recently [are] something that scientists and people living on the front lines have been warning about for decades.

“And we also need to acknowledge that the COPs are not sufficient to prevent a climate catastrophe.”

Future COP summits will also fail if we don’t succeed in building the strong people-power movements that are needed for real change, which as Green Left has argued since it formed in 1991, requires system change …

author: Simon Upitis
title: Protesters Shut Down Bisalloy Steels - Again
content:
Hundreds of protesters shut down Bisalloy Steels on Sunday 15 November, preventing it from operating for 48 hours. This was the eleventh time Wollongong Friends of Palestine (WFOP) had organised a picket of the company.

Bisalloy Steels produces armour plating used by the IDF and by West Bank settlers to oppress Palestinians. Steel plate produced by Bisalloy is used to retrofit civilian vehicles with armour plating, making them bulletproof and allowing them to be fitted with roof-mounted machine guns. Bisalloy is also set to benefit from Australia’s increased military spending via the AUKUS agreement. In July, Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy announced a $2 million contract would be awarded to Bisalloy to produce steel for US Virginia-class nuclear submarines. 

The picket had a lively atmosphere. A makeshift stage was set up at one entrance with DJs, live music and poetry readings. Free food and first aid were provided by volunteers. Dozens of activists camped overnight, ensuring that the company couldn't sneak workers through the picket in the early hours of the morning. Attendees came from far and wide, with many travelling down from Sydney. Palestine Action Bega Valley attended as a group. Other groups with an official presence included the NSW Socialists and the Illawarra Greens.

At the other entrance, political discussions were held in gazebos set up on the street, often involving dozens of attendees. One member of WFOP recently returned from the West Bank recounted their experiences defending Palestinian farms from settler violence. Nurses spoke against their regulatory agency’s adoption of a Zionist definition of antisemitism. There was debate about the type of movement required to free Palestine and the tactics and strategies needed to push the struggle forwards. NSW Socialists held a forum with the candidate for Wollongong in the state election, Ryan Chapman. The success of the various workshops and discussions prove the pickets can be a place for left-wing people to gather and discuss live political questions. 

This picket experienced much less police harassment and intimidation than the previous one. In June, the company planned to break through the picket line and bring a busload of workers into the site. We stopped them, but the police maintained a heavy presence on that occasion. One attendee was arrested. Another was violently thrown to the ground, and everyone else was subjected to their petty demands and often thuggish behaviour. Riot squad cops also came down from Sydney. 

This time, we heard on Sunday night that Bisalloy wouldn’t try to bring in workers until we left. Throughout the picket, there was a very minor police presence, normally a single cop car. This was a significant victory. It shows the company wasn’t confident enough to directly confront our community campaign.

Of course, we can’t be complacent. At some point, the company will get fed up with the disruptions and take a more combative and confrontational approach. In the meantime, the campaign remains committed to stopping Bisalloy profiting from genocide.

title: El futuro del manejo del fuego se debatió en la Patagonia
content:
Foto: Gentileza UTT


Este fin de semana la Comarca Andina del Paralelo 42° fue escenario del Primer Congreso Nacional de Combate, Prevención, Políticas Públicas y Restauración Forestal, un encuentro nacional que fue el escenario para compartir experiencias, fortalecer capacidades y debatir cómo enfrentar los incendios forestales y sus impactos en los territorios.

Por Violeta Moraga (Equipo de Comunicación Popular Colectivo Al Margen).


Organizado por ATE y la Unión de Trabajadores de la Tierra Patagonia (UTT PATAGONIA), el Congreso reunió a brigadistas nacionales y provinciales y comunitarios, bomberos voluntarios, trabajadores forestales y de conservación, especialistas, técnicos, investigadores, productores, organizaciones y comunidades.


“A la hora de la tragedia, frente a un Estado que se va podando, achicando, desfinanciando, la comunidad se organiza e irrumpe. Las brigadas comunitarias son un claro ejemplo de eso”, dice Juan Pablo Acosta, coordinador general de la UTT Patagonia en diálogo con Al Margen y señala que, en la emergencia, también las organizaciones desarrollan sus propuestas, como es el curso de restaurador y restauradora forestal de la UTT.


“Frente a esa irrupción se generan instancias de coordinación con brigadistas institucionales. Para nosotros no hay una dicotomía: brigadas comunitarias sí, brigadas comunitarias no. Las brigadas comunitarias existen y van a seguir estando, sobre todo con un Estado que se retira de los territorios”, continúa Acosta.


Es en este marco es que se tomó la iniciativa de pensar este espacio: un momento donde encontrarse y construir articulaciones para que, al momento de la emergencia, haya algunos puntos que estén previamente discutidos. “El congreso tuvo esa impronta, tanto con la cuestión del combate del fuego como en la prevención y la restauración”.


“Los trabajadores enfrentamos un tiempo complejo y necesitamos respuestas urgentes. Los combatientes demandan un suplemento salarial de emergencia que se incorpore con carácter permanente al sueldo, pase a planta permanente y estabilidad, incorporación de más personal y que se impulse una ley que establezca un régimen jubilatorio diferencial por tareas de alto riesgo, como así también un régimen integral para los combatientes de incendios forestales”, expresó por su parte Rodolfo Aguiar, secretario general de ATE Nacional presente en el congreso.


“Si algo quedó claro es que no nos van a regalar nada, que vamos a tener que pelear. Aquellos que piensan que van a sobrevivir haciéndoles concesiones al Gobierno están perdidos. Sobreviven los que resisten, sobreviven los que luchan y nosotros vamos a luchar. Avanzaremos en una medida de fuerza de carácter nacional. Fueron dos días a puro debate que consolidan nuestro crecimiento y unidad. Las instituciones son los hombres y mujeres que la representan, y son ellos los que hacen la historia todos los días”, volcó el dirigente en sus redes.


“Avanzaremos en una medida de fuerza de carácter nacional. Fueron dos días a puro debate que consolidan nuestro crecimiento y unidad”, dijo Aguiar. Foto: ATE


“El congreso superó las expectativas, hubo una participación muy amplia de distintos sectores de la sociedad, de brigadas comunitarias, de brigadistas de Parques Nacionales, algunos provinciales, gente del Servicio Nacional de Manejo del Fuego y representantes de 13 provincias que estuvieron pasando por el congreso en distintas mesas propuestas”, dijo a Al Margen Marcelo “Chelo” Rojas, delegado de ATE en Parques Nacionales.


“Se pudieron abordar muy bien diversas cuestiones, algunas más relacionadas con el combate de incendios, con la prevención, con la necesaria articulación entre las instituciones y los vecinos, las brigadas, abordando este paradigma relativamente nuevo: las brigadas comunitarias y cómo pueden articular y colaborar con el laburo de las instituciones, cómo darles un marco en específico con respecto a la legislación, enfrentando también la problemática de las instituciones con sus prioridades y las de la comunidad organizada en sí misma, enfrentando este tipo de desastres que hoy en día se nos acercan a las ciudades con la noción de interfase”, continuó.


“Hubo un panel mucho más político el sábado, en el cual intervinieron diputados, senadores, legisladores provinciales. Estuvo Adriana Serquis, Ana Marks, José Glinski, Magdalena Odarda, Leandro García, vino Matías Oberlin del Observatorio de Tierras también para dar una mirada con respecto a lo que …

author: CNT Villaverde Alto - Comarcal Sur de Madrid
title: Ante las elecciones del 29N: tu candidato, el sindicato
content:
Ante la convocatoria de elecciones generales del próximo 29 de noviembre, desde CNT Comarcal Sur interpelamos al conjunto de nuestra clase, las trabajadoras, las desposeídas, las perseguidas y represaliadas a posicionarse activamente en un solo sentido:

la organización activa desde el sindicalismo

.


Consideramos que

no nos encontramos en el momento de llamar a la participación de nuestra clase en un sentido u otro del juego electoral

, ya sea ejerciendo la abstención masiva o concediendo el apoyo a quien pueda sernos de mayor interés práctico, pues creemos que la coyuntura actual no permite grandes movilizaciones organizadas, al tiempo que, hoy por hoy, pueden existir intereses contrapuestos entre distintos sectores de nuestra clase que empujen a optar por distintas vías de participación o no participación en el baile de collares que llevará el perro del capital.


No obstante, creemos indispensable posicionarnos y animar a toda nuestra clase a hacerlo en el mismo sentido. Apostamos, como no podía ser de otro modo, por el Sindicato. A nuestro juicio, la independencia de clase debe construirse desde una organización al margen de los vaivenes electorales, una organización que no aspire a la gestión del Estado ni a servir a los intereses del capital ya sea desde su ala izquierda o derecha: una organización, en definitiva,

independiente en todos sus aspectos como lo es CNT

. Abogamos, como siempre hemos hecho, por una CNT

sin subvenciones

 de ningún tipo, así como

sin liberados

; una CNT compuesta de principio a fin por compañeras de clase,

militantes que construyen día a día el Sindicato

 y lo impulsan en la dirección que consideran más juiciosa desde

la toma colectiva de acuerdos en una estructura que se despliega desde abajo hacia arriba

, donde no pueda haber dirigentes que secuestren el poder de decisión, sino una afiliación militante que, de forma verdaderamente democrática, impone la línea política para su organización.


Esta es, en suma, la independencia de clase a la que aspiramos a través de la organización activa. La organización mediante un Sindicato que despliega a la par el trabajo político necesario para alcanzar sus objetivos revolucionarios mientras, en el día a día, desarrolla el necesario trabajo de base en los centros de trabajo para

defender los intereses de nuestra clase

 y, sobre todo,

organizar a las trabajadoras en una forma alternativa de sindicalismo

 que nos oriente hacia la consecución de objetivos mucho más grandes.


Ante la pantomima electoral, nosotras decimos: Sindicato

. Si ocho años de legislatura progresista nos han demostrado algo es que, sin duda, no puede confiarse en absoluto en la palabra del ala izquierda. No debe olvidarse jamás que quien ha reprimido a las compañeras docentes y estudiantes de la Comunidad de Madrid a lo largo de las siete semanas de Huelga Indefinida ha sido

el cuerpo policial directamente dependiente del gobierno del Estado

. Mismo cuerpo que ha agredido tanto por la fuerza como por el uso de gases lacrimógenos y pimienta a las compañeras en los piquetes informativos del pasado 11N en la jornada de Huelga General,

llegando a producirse detenciones y encarcelamientos a lo largo del país

.


Si el ala progresista del parlamento pretende agitar el espantajo de la derecha para cosechar votos, no podemos olvidar por un momento que el monstruo no está a las puertas,

se encuentra ya entre nosotras

. Encarnado en un gobierno que

nunca derogó la ley mordaza

 durante ocho años en el poder, un gobierno que

ha enviado tanquetas contra trabajadoras

 en huelga, que

ha infiltrado agentes

 de policía en colectivos de distintos signo, que

jamás se molestó en atajar de raíz el problema de la vivienda

, limitándose a posicionarse tímidamente cuando pudo comprobar que la movilización en la calle había alcanzado tal punto que podía servir a sus intereses particulares. Tanto con este caso como con el de la Huelga General del 11N, jamás permitiremos que este gobierno pretenda ponerse a la cabeza de su éxito: fueron las organizaciones políticas de base en la calle la que impulsaron sendas oleadas consecutivas, organizadas de forma unitaria y ajenas por completo a los intereses partidarios, teniendo claros sus objetivos

gobernase quien gobernase

.


Sabemos igualmente bien cuál es la alternativa que se esboza al actual gobierno saliente. Lo sabemos, precisamente, porque

la llevamos sufriendo y combatiendo en la Comunidad de Madrid

 los últimos …

title: Şavşat Belediyesi'nden zorunlu emekli edilen 10 işçi için işe iade kararı
content:
Artvin – Şavşat Belediyesi'ndeki sözleşmeleri yenilenmeyerek zorunlu emekliliğe sevk edilen 10 işçi, işe iade talebiyle açtığı davayı kazandı. Belediye-İş Sendikası Rize Şube Başkanı Yaşar Kaspar, “Mahkeme, Şavşat Belediyesi’nin haksız ve hukuksuz uygulamasına dur demiştir. İşçilerimizin bir an önce görevlerine başlatılmasını talep ediyoruz” dedi.

Son yerel seçimlerinin ardından CHP’den AKP’ye geçen Şavşat Belediyesi’nde, sözleşmeleri yenilenmeyen ve zorunlu emekliliğe sevk edilen 10 işçi, işe iade talebiyle açtığı davaları kazandı.

Kararın ardından işçiler ve Belediye-İş Sendikası temsilcileri basın açıklaması yaparak belediye yönetimine mahkeme kararının uygulanması ve işçilerin görevlerine başlatılması çağrısında bulundu.

Belediye-İş Sendikası Rize Şube Başkanı Yaşar Kaspar, 10 işçinin işe iade davasının işçilerin lehine sonuçlandığını belirterek, “Mahkeme, Şavşat Belediyesi’nin haksız ve hukuksuz uygulamasına dur demiştir. Belediye başkanından ve yönetiminden arkadaşlarımızın işe başlatılması için gerekli işlemleri bir an önce yapmalarını talep ediyoruz. Burada ödenecek tazminatlar ve paralar Şavşat halkının parasıdır. Belediye başkanının cebinden ödeyeceği paralar değildir. Mahkeme, diğer duruşmamızda olduğu gibi haksızlığa bir kez daha dur demiştir” ifadelerini kullandı.

Belediye-İş Sendikası Rize-Artvin Şubesi yöneticisi ve Şavşat Belediyesi işyeri temsilcisi Vural Şimşek ise sürecin yalnızca hukuki değil, vicdani ve ahlaki boyutlarının da bulunduğunu ifade etti.

Şimşek, belediye çalışanlarının yıllarca Şavşat halkına hizmet ettiğini belirterek, “Biz büyük bir aileyiz. Biz bu ailenin dağılmasının ve parçalanmasının vicdani, ahlaki ve hukuki boyutlarıyla ilgili Şavşat kamuoyunun ve Türkiye kamuoyunun aydınlanmasını istiyorduk. Bu ailede herhangi bir hukuksuzluk yoktu, yüz kızartıcı bir suç işlenmemişti. Herkes yıllarca Şavşat halkına hizmet etmişti. Yargının vermiş olduğu karara gerçekten teşekkür ediyor ve saygı duyuyoruz. Arkadaşlarımızın bir an önce işe iade edilmesi için Sayın Belediye Başkanımızın ve yönetiminin harekete geçmesini istiyoruz. Kırgınlık ve dargınlıkların daha da büyümesine izin verilmeden, bu meselenin çözüme kavuşturulmasından yanayız” dedi.

İşe iade kararı verilen işçilerden Aşkın Kamacı da, “Şavşat Belediyesi’nden haksız yere işimizden edildik. Sokağa koyulduk diyebilirim. 20 aylık hukuk mücadelemiz sonucunu verdi. Bir ay içerisinde işe başlamamız gerekiyor. Belediye başkanından işimizi istiyoruz. Aynı belediyede çalışmak istiyoruz. Bizler mağdur edildik, mağduriyetimizin giderilmesini istiyoruz. Hukuka saygımız sonsuzdur. Belediye başkanının da hukuka saygılı olmasını temenni ediyorum” ifadelerini kullandı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Amir Khafagy
title: Airport Drivers Enter Third Year of Longest Ongoing Strike in US
content:
SkyHop Global workers have alleged backlash from management, which has so far refused to recognize the union since 2024.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

It’s 6 a.m. on a chilly October day, and outside the Hyatt Regency Hotel in Times Square, a few dozen workers already stand with picket signs in hand.

Gathered under the shadow of a giant inflatable rat known as Scabby, the workers are all striking drivers for SkyHop Global, an airport transportation company. With signs in hand, they wait to picket SkyHop vans driven by replacement workers who, throughout the day, pick up and drop off airline staff.

It’s a scene that has played out countless times since the workers first went out on strike right before Thanksgiving two years ago, on Nov. 24, 2024. Although a majority of the 60 workers, mostly immigrants, voted to join Teamsters Local 210 on May 10, 2024, they have fought an uphill battle to get management to the negotiating table.

Since they went on strike, workers have alleged retaliation, intimidation, and surveillance from management, which has so far refused to recognize the workers’ union. Many, struggling to pay their bills, have been forced to take second jobs like driving for Uber, while others have not found any jobs at all.

As the workers prepare to spend yet another Thanksgiving on the picket line — in what is now the nation’s longest ongoing strike — they hope their struggle is not forgotten.

“No, I won’t cross the picket line because this is for our benefit,” said Ana Solorzano, a 26-year-old SkyHop driver originally from Ecuador.

Edison Bonifas, a 57-year-old immigrant from Ecuador, says he has struggled to support his wife and four kids since he first walked off the job. Initially, he thought the strike would last only a few weeks. But as the strike enters its third year, making ends meet has become increasingly difficult. Although he’s tried getting another job, he hasn’t had any luck.

“The thing is, we’re waiting and waiting,” he told Documented at the rally on Oct. 21. “It’s basically hard right now because there are no jobs.”

What keeps him from crossing the picket line is his desire to secure health insurance, one of the key demands of the union. With a sick wife, it’s a demand that hits close to home.

“You know, you cannot live in New York City if you don’t have a medical,” he said.

SkyHop Global provides ground transportation for airline crew members between airports and hotels. Since the strike, several airlines have terminated contracts with SkyHop in the New York market; it currently only transports crew for Delta Air Lines.

Since its founding in 2014, the company has grown its operations to 33 airports across the country, including LaGuardia and JFK Airports. It now operates 200 passenger transport vans and employs 300 drivers, and is estimated to have generated over $70 million in revenue, according to court documents.

Instead of negotiating with the union to get drivers like Bonifas back to work, SkyHop has chosen to bust any efforts to unionize. On Aug. 31, the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) General Counsel published an investigation that found SkyHop had violated the National Labor Relations Act when it “unlawfully tried to stop its employees from unionizing” and “violated the Act with complete disregard for its employees and their rights.”

According to the report, SkyHop management discharged at least 14 employees between 2024 and 2025 who were suspected of supporting the union effort. SkyHop also allegedly engaged in a widespread campaign of interrogations, surveillance, and retaliation.

The General Counsel report noted that one of the ways SkyHop surveilled workers was through the use of a fleet management technology called Samsara. Through cameras installed in each SkyHop van, Samsara generates safety scores for each driver on a 100-point scale. When there is a driver infraction, such as using a phone while driving or not wearing a seat belt, Samsara would alert management, which would then adjust a driver’s safety score and create a record for potential discipline. The General Counsel’s report found that SkyHop adjusted Samsara during the height of the 2024 union drive to target employees suspected of supporting the union, with certain minor infractions weighted more or less heavily to target specific workers.

author: David Swanson
title: European Youth Strike: A Million Students Mobilise Against War and Austerity
content:
By

Ana Vračar,

Savage Minds

, November 25, 2026


More than 50 student organisations in 27 European countries launched an

international strike

 against war and militarisation on Friday, 20 November, drawing a million young people onto the streets.


Students issued joint demands, including an end to rearmament and all forms of conscription, investment in education and social services, and solidarity with oppressed peoples around the world. They also declared resistance to growing authoritarian trends in the region.


“We are protesting to claim our right to a better future, and we are aware that if we stand united, no one will be able to stop us from taking it,” said

Alessandro Di Miceli

 from the Italian organisation Rete della Conoscenza.


Actions took place in Norway, Sweden, Finland, Poland, Romania, Turkey, Greece, Croatia, Hungary, Slovakia, Austria, the Czech Republic, Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands, Belgium, Ireland, Italy, Britain, France, Switzerland, Spain, Portugal, Malta, and Slovenia, among others.


“From the right to education to the right to housing, from the struggle against the rising costs of living and the climate crisis to the fight against militarisation and rearmament, specific demands may differ from country to country but are all deeply connected to each other,” Di Miceli said.


Attacks on education funding


One concern shared by student groups across the region is the precarious state of public education. For almost two months, high school and university students in

France

 have led massive protests and occupations against austerity measures imposed during Emmanuel Macron’s presidency.


Similar policies took root elsewhere too. In Britain, Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s administration recently announced

cuts to student welfare

 and support while planning to invest billions in the military.


“While the government says it doesn’t have the money to invest in education or opportunities for young people without cutting welfare and potentially pushing hundreds of thousands of young people into poverty, it is right now spending an extra £15 billion a year on the military,” Stop the War’s

Shabbir Lakha

 wrote.


Teachers and parents protested side by side with youth organisations in many cities, supporting their concerns. Still in England, the

National Education Union

 (NEU) published a statement on planned school funding cuts on the day of the international youth strike. The union found that mainstream school funding in England will be slashed by £1.2 billion (USD 1.57 billion) in cash in 2027-28.


The cuts will affect approximately 11,000 schools in England, the NEU pointed out—many of them in the poorest parts of the country, including Hackney, Southwark and Tower Hamlets in London.


“Hackney and Tower Hamlets have the highest child poverty rates in the UK: half of their children live in poverty once housing costs are paid,” NEU general secretary Daniel Kebede warned.


Students refuse the return of conscription.


Another concern widely voiced among student groups is the return of military conscription. In

Germany

, more than 50,000 pupils and students organised their fifth school strike in a year. The German government plans to build Europe’s “strongest conventional army” in a matter of years while slashing welfare and social security, with the youth insisting they will not be part of this scenario. Similarly, in

Belgium

—including in Ghent, Brussels, Leuven, Liège, and Antwerp—young people tore up letters issued by the Ministry of Defence regarding military service.


In

Slovenia

, the

Rosa Collective

 described how thousands of students attended a recent arms fair as part of their “active citizenship” curriculum while structural needs remain unaddressed. “The military is targeting rural vocational and technical high schools,” the group wrote. “They aim to recruit young people from socially disadvantaged backgrounds, offering them money and adventure.”


Noting that Israeli arms companies Rafael and Israel Aerospace Industries appeared basically next door to the location visited by students, Rosa Collective warned that “young people are being recruited in secondary and primary (!) schools while some faculties and institutes are becoming incubators for the development of technologies for military use.”
