author: David Njagi
title: The tensions playing out in Kenya’s marine conservation
content:
Mombasa, Kenya:

 Khadija Dossa charmed a group of visitors at her village in Wasini Island in Kenya’s coastal region with tales of how conserving coral reefs was improving livelihoods in her community. When she finally delivered her message however, it was clear there were gaps that needed mending.


Dossa belongs to the Mkwiro Beach Management Unit (BMU), and along conserving coral reefs, her group also farms octopus and seaweed while restoring mangroves. The investment has created jobs for hundreds of youth in the island struggling with unemployment after completing school.


It has come with the price of having to abandon the community’s long-held tradition of fishing freely whenever they liked and whenever it pleased them. During the free reigning days, Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) that restrict unauthorized access by communities did not exist.


“The ocean has provided us with food and a source of income from fish sales for generations and has a cultural connection to our people,” said Dossa, referring to the Swahili people who settled on the country’s coastal region.


In recent years, the world has united around creation of MPAs not just to protect coral reefs, but also to battle unsustainable fishing, water pollution and climate change, threats that were pitched to Dossa’s community by the government to convince locals to join the ocean conservation wave.


During the pitching sessions, she also heard that there would be money coming in from the government and the development community to support communities’ efforts. On this front,

Bloomberg Philanthropies

committed over $635 million to ocean conservation since 2014.


Recently, the

Agha Khan Foundation

 launched a $500 million 10-year initiative to restore 15,000 hectares of mangroves and coastal ecosystems across six Indian Ocean countries through the ReGeneration project.


During the

Our Oceans Conference

 in Mombasa, Kenya, in June, the global community raised about $6.4 billion to support ocean conservation, sustainable fisheries, climate resilience and the blue economy.


The promised financial support pleased Dossa, especially after getting convinced that the risks her colleagues are exposed to when diving into the ocean floor to plant corals would be softened. The support too would plug the financial gap that opened after the community accepted restricted ocean access.


According to Jesse Kosgei, a marine research scientist at the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS) working with coral reefs and fisheries in Kenya, the funding from Bloomberg Philanthropies to Dossa’s community is mainly budgeted towards campaigning for conservation of unprotected coral reefs through public engagement.


In addition, the funds aim to co-manage and conserve the reefs within identified areas through a partnership between WCS, communities and the government, he added.


“We create co-management areas with communities. If it is within the MPAs, fishing practices are banned completely. There are patrols to ensure these places are not being exploited or destructive fishing gears are not being used,” said Kosgei.


But where donor money flows, politics will hitch a ride and corruption will follow. Salim Mohamed, a local from Malindi-Ungwana bay in the north-eastern side of the coastal town, Mombasa

,

 knows this better more from experience than from propaganda.


About two years ago, a donor funded a conservation project by local fishers in his community. The money was distributed through the regional government devolved system. But it never reached the fishers. Much of it was raided by county public officers themselves, said Salim.


“The money benefited politicians and county government ministry of fisheries officials. They came up with their own registered companies and took tenders which were paid for with the funds. We got nothing,” he said.


Dossa’s community is aware of the accountability gaps associated with ocean conservation but does not know how to navigate them. Her fellow Swahili at Kipini village where Kenya’s biggest river, the Tana, meets the Indian ocean, do.


In the past few years, the community has protested questionable activities that have been going on contrary to the values of conservation. According to Twaha Mohamed Yusuf, his village has embraced MPAs not just to conserve corals, but also endangered species like the Turtle and Dungong’.


But trawling, which is operated by foreign companies, has been going on over the years despite …

author: James Crump
title: Israel Has Turned Gaza Into a ‘Toxic Wasteland’, Report Finds
content:
Israel’s destruction of Gaza has poisoned the water, soil and air, turning the enclave into a “toxic wasteland” which threatens the population’s survival,

a new report has found

. 


According to Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory, heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings and raw sewage have potentially contaminated more than 99% of the territory.


Oxfam International’s executive director, Amitabh Behar, said: “Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come.”


“Raw sewage is pouring into the sea and leaking into the ground, while the destruction of Gaza’s sanitation systems leaves people with little protection from the contamination around them,” he said, adding that pregnant women and children are among those facing the highest risks.


“In an area as small, oppressed and densely populated as Gaza, continuous exposure is inevitable, with people surrounded by waste and sewage, spreading pests and the risk of disease growing.”


Oxfam’s report, which was compiled using satellite imagery and other open-source data, 

gives the most comprehensive overview of environmental damage in Gaza to date. 


The UN Environment Programme estimates that Israel’s genocide has generated 61 million tonnes of debris from pulverised infrastructure, or 29 tonnes for every person in Gaza. Much of that material includes hazardous substances, according to Oxfam. 


Gaza’s displaced population is currently facing catastrophic winter conditions, with heavy rain affecting more than 106,000 people and recently causing tents and makeshift shelters to flood and latrines to overflow.

author: anred
title: Recuerdos mapuche que duelen
content:
Foto: Carolina Blumenkranc


Joana Coluan Nahuel resultó herida en el mismo operativo de la Prefectura que asesinó a su primo Rafael en medio de la montaña. A nueve años de un crimen impune, su testimonio entrelaza la cosmovisión indígena, la violencia estatal y los sueños de quienes viven en los márgenes.

Por Melisa Cabrapan Duarte, para Revista Cítrica / Fotos: Carolina Blumenkranc.


Joana dice que hoy está bien, que está mejor, que el propio camino mapuche la fortaleció. Pasaron 9 años desde aquel día tan terrible, para el Pueblo Mapuche, para la sociedad que se solidariza con su lucha, y para ella, porque Rafa era su primo, su amigo, su

lamgen

 (hermano mapuche), y Joana fue una de las personas que lo acompañó en sus últimos respiros. Ese 25 de noviembre de 2017, el Grupo Albatros de Prefectura Naval le disparó a Rafael Nahuel por la espalda, y ella también resultó herida.


A él le quitaron la vida. A ella le dispararon en el brazo. Ambos hechos quedaron impunes: la violencia hacia ella ni siquiera se juzgó; y los oficiales condenados en 2023 por asesinar a Rafa, tres años más tarde recibieron una reducción de la pena y prisión en suspenso. Los días, meses y años que siguieron fueron difíciles:


–La tristeza y la impotencia es como que te aprieta el pecho y la bronca también, de que las cosas hayan pasado así. De pensar cómo ellos nos matan, así, como si nada. Y ahí acabaron con la vida del lamgen. Y para nosotros no hay justicia. Yo lo extraño. Extraño una charla, un abrazo. Él era una buena persona, querido por quienes lo rodeaban. Y nunca te iba a decir algo malo, siempre te iba a dar un buen consejo.


Joana Coluan Nahuel tiene 30 años, y nació y se crió en Bariloche, en Virgen Misionera, un barrio popular a la altura del km 7 de la Avenida Los Pioneros, poblado históricamente por familias de origen mapuche. Cuando iba a la escuela primaria en el barrio, todos eran vecinos y se conocían bien, pero no todos reconocían ese origen. La “india” era Joana, porque tanto ella como su familia, desde aquel entonces insistían en la institución por el reconocimiento de la

wenufoye

, con poder izarla y prometer esta bandera. Los dichos discriminatorios podían estar acompañados de golpes de sus compañeros, por lo que su padre y hermanos le decían que tenía que defenderse, no dejarse maltratar, aunque en ese entonces ella era muy tímida y callada.


En el mismo barrio continuó la secundaria, y en el mismo barrio empezaron las persecuciones y la violencia estatal contra su familia. En su

ruka

 (casa) sufrieron allanamientos y represión policial mucho tiempo antes de ser parte de la recuperación territorial del Lof Lafken Winkul Mapu. Por esto, ese día que decidieron volver al campo, al Mascardi, y llevarles abrigo y comida a los

lamgen

 que estaban escondidos en la montaña tras haberse realizado el desalojo el 23 de noviembre, Joana sabía que corrían peligro:


–Todos sabíamos que a lo que íbamos corríamos un riesgo. Rafa también lo sabía. A él le dijeron también que se quede. No se quiso quedar y yo dije “bueno, si él va, yo también voy a ir”. Pero nosotros sabíamos muy bien todos los riesgos que se corren, y él como un pibe en un barrio sabe cómo es la Policía.


Foto: Carolina Blumenkranc


Rafa vivía en el barrio Nahuel Hue, en el alto de la ciudad, en el Bariloche de las dos caras, en la ciudad que se cuenta como la “suiza argentina” cuando la mayoría de su población, por su reubicación, marginación y racialización da cuenta de un genocidio indígena que inició en el siglo XIX.


Rafa era bien campero, recuerda Joana. A pesar de vivir en una zona periurbana, su familia tenía caballos, y pese a la pobreza que atravesaban cuidaban mucho a sus animales, y expresaban mucho respeto hacia ellos, algo que había sido transmitido por el abuelo que tenían en común: “siempre ellos la sacaban a pasear a la yegua en diferentes momentos y Rafa, igual, como que veía caballos y él enseguida unas caricias y pa, se subía, era como que se entendían”. Joana recuerda ir con su primo a caballo hasta el Mascardi, aunque ella prefería caminar a la par de él.


Cuando Joana terminó la secundaria en el 2013, empezó a trabajar haciendo limpieza de casas y cuidando a una mujer mayor, durante un par de años. Siguió buscando trabajos más estables y mejor pagos, y mandando su curriculum a todos lados, pero no conseguía nada. Y fue ahí cuando una amiga de la escuela le contó que se iba a anotar en el Ejército, y la alentó a que lo hiciera …

author: Administrador
title: Rezo y Baile para un Buen Viaje
content:
Rezo y Baile para un Buen Viaje

En los Puyes (caracoles) zapatistas y en las comunidades -incluso en las partidistas-, los Tuneles y catequistas convocaron a un rezo para pedir por la delegación que va a encontrarse con las familias buscadoras en la Ciudad de México. Se rezó por su bienestar y el de las familias que tienen ese dolor y esa pena de no saber de un ser querido; para que les dé fuerza en su corazón para no desmayar hasta encontrarle.

Después siguió el baile, ahora ya tirando a la onda sonidera. Y ya de madrugada, salieron los vehículos de los 12 caracoles rumbo al CIDECI de San Cristóbal de las Casas. Algunos con hasta 8 horas de viaje, rebotando en las redilas y con una lluvia ligera limpiándoles el camino y el sueño, llegaron en horas del mediodía de este 25 de noviembre del 2026.

Mañana, 26 de noviembre, miles de manos estarán bordando para tratar de completar los regalos para las madres buscadoras. Todo por su culpa del capitán que primero dijo que 100, luego que 200, luego subió a 400, y ahora dice que más de 700 nacional de familiares que buscan. Así que va en su cuenta del capitán si no se completan.

Y miles de oídos se estarán preparando para escuchar y abrazar.

Desde las montañas del Sureste Mexicano.

Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés. Coordinador General. Noviembre del 2026.

P.D.- Aquí les mando un video de un rezo en un Puy, baile, la llegada a Cideci, y ya toda la delegación junta en el auditorio. Los que desentonan en el grito son Comando Palomitas, sólo se coordinan para los dulces y los chocolates.

Tuneles y catequistas, tecladistas, choferólogos zapatistas, delegación en pleno. Música: «Somos la fuerza», Mexikan Sound System Imágenes, edición y producción: Terci@s Compas Zapatistas

author: Rizomatica
title: Seis en huelga en la cárcel, en sus casas un gran nudo en las gargantas
content:
Revisando hoy las redes sociales me entero de que seis de los dieciocho condenados por el caso Molino Grollmus iniciaron una huelga de hambre seca en la cárcel de Biobío. Uno de ellos es José Melgarejo Calbullanca, a quien represento. La noticia me golpea, porque de todo lo que he visto de la cárcel aplicada a los mapuche, lo más duro, sin duda, es la huelga. Duro para el preso y duro para su familia, porque no solo deja de alimentarse el huelguista: les aseguro que la garganta de sus mujeres y de sus madres difícilmente traga, de solo saber que allá adentro los suyos están dispuestos a morir por justicia.


Por:

Daniela Sierra

, Abogada.


Una huelga no es una medida de presión, ni una puesta en escena. Sin agua, el cuerpo empieza a apagarse en días, no en semanas. A eso no se llega por cálculo; se llega cuando ya no quedan puertas que golpear.


¿Qué piden? Lo primero, que se anule un juicio en que se condenó con testigos que nadie vio. Así de simple. En el caso de José, dos de los testigos con identidad reservada nunca pisaron la sala: la Fiscalía renunció a ellos, y lo que supuestamente dijeron lo contaron unos policías, de oídas. Los jueces no les vieron la cara, la defensa no pudo hacerles una sola pregunta, y con eso a José le dieron más de ochenta años de cárcel.


La Convención Americana garantiza a todo acusado el derecho a interrogar a quien lo acusa (art. 8.2 f), y el Código Procesal Penal obliga a condenar solo con la prueba rendida en el juicio (art. 340). La Corte Interamericana ya se lo dijo a Chile en 2014, y en un caso mapuche, Norín Catrimán: no se puede condenar únicamente o en grado decisivo con testigos de identidad reservada. Y eso era con testigos que al menos declararon. Aquí, ni eso.


Tampoco se pide impunidad, como tanto les gusta repetir. Si la Corte Suprema anula, la ley ordena un juicio nuevo (art. 386 del Código Procesal Penal), esta vez con las reglas del juego, y si la prueba no alcanza, la absolución. Eso se resuelve el jueves en la Corte Suprema, que es donde se tiene que resolver; no en La Moneda ni en ninguna reunión con ministros.


Lo segundo que piden huele, para algunos, a privilegio: un módulo para presos mapuche en Biobío, que puedan entrar la machi y el logko, comer su comida, vestir su ropa, hablar chedungun, tener trabajo y talleres. Privilegio, dicen, como si rezar, comer lo propio y hablar la lengua de la abuela fueran lujos de hotel.


Pero el Convenio 169 de la OIT, vigente en Chile desde 2009, obliga a proteger las prácticas espirituales de los pueblos indígenas (art. 5), a considerar su cultura cuando se les impone una pena (art. 10) y a darles una salud que respete su propia medicina (art. 25). Las Reglas Mandela de Naciones Unidas exigen respetar las creencias de cada preso, ofrecerle educación y trabajo, y permitirle practicar su fe con alguien de su propia tradición (reglas 2, 4, 65 y 66). Y el Reglamento de Establecimientos Penitenciarios dice algo que debería bastar: fuera de los derechos que la condena le quita, el preso conserva la misma condición jurídica que cualquier ciudadano libre (art. 2).


Lo más curioso es que nada de esto es nuevo. Gendarmería informó a la Corte de Apelaciones de Temuco que su módulo de comuneros tiene encomiendas con alimentación culturalmente pertinente, acceso a lawen, medicina tradicional y machi, y talleres de trabajo. Es decir, lo que se pide en Biobío ya existe en Temuco. Entonces la pregunta no es por qué regalarles un privilegio, sino por qué un mapuche pierde derechos según la cárcel a la que lo manden.


El Estado tiene a estos seis hombres bajo su custodia y responde por su vida. Pero la salida no está en sentarse a mirar cuánto aguanta el cuerpo. Está en que la Corte Suprema aplique el estándar que ya se le impuso a Chile.


Lo que piden es juicio justo, no impunidad. Lo mínimo, eso que la humanidad ya pagó con demasiada sangre. Y que, mientras tanto, allá afuera, sus mujeres, sus madres, puedan volver a respirar a la espera del futuro abrazo de los suyos.


*Enviado a la radio


Esta información se publicó en

Radio Kurruf

.

author: La Zarzamora
title: Comunicado público de José Melgarejo Calbullanca, PPM del caso Grollmus en Huelga de Hambre
content:
Pu Machi, pu Lonko, pu Wuenen, pu Werken, pu Weichave, pu Kona.

Rekuluwaiñ ka yavuluwaiñ ni ta tuvachi weichan.

Inche José Melgarejo Calbullanca, tañi lov Lleu-lleu mapu, comunidad Nicolás Calbullanca, territorio lavkenche, Lago Lleu-lleu.

Doy a conocer mi situación como preso político mapuche, recluído en la cárcel CP Biobío, llevando ya 2 años y medio, de una condena de 7 años y medio y de otra por el llamado Caso del Molino Grollmus, por el cual fui juzgado por el Tribunal de Cañete y condenado a 86 años de prisión, juicio al que actualmente estamos apelando en la Corte Suprema, exigiendo su anulación y del cual me declaro, como lo he hecho anteriormente, inocente de los hechos que se me imputaron y por los que fuí condenado a esta altísima condena.

Por este motivo es que junto a otros ppm, hemos decidido iniciar una Huelga de Hambre de carácter indefinido, exigiendo 3 puntos principales:

Kiñe: Nulidad del juicio viciado y racista que nos condenó.

Epu: La creación de un módulo comuneros mapuche en el Cp Biobío.

Por esto hago un llamado a las comunidades, territorios, organizaciones, Hogares Mapuche, Estudiantes y a los demás prisioneros políticos, a que nos apoyen en este proceso. Estaremos eternamente agradecidos de su apoyo fraterno.

También aprovecho de agradecer a todas las personas que me han apoyado, a mi como a los demás ppm, todo este tiempo.

Desde acá me siento con alto newen para seguir luchando por nuestros justos derechos como pueblo nación Mapuche.

author: Brooke Siem
title: The Episode: A True Story of Loss, Madness and Healing – A Conversation With Mary Ann Kenny
content:
W

elcome to the Mad in America podcast. My name is Brooke Siem, and I am the author of the award-winning memoir on antidepressant withdrawal,

May Cause Side Effects

.


Today I am with Mary Ann Kenny. Mary Ann is an academic, and she lives in Dublin with her children. She is the author of the book,

The Episode: A True Story of Loss, Madness and Healing

.


In her book, Mary Ann details her descent into psychosis, her hopitalization, and her journey back to health and happiness. Drawing on her detailed medical files and on her own recollections, she has created a day-by-day account of what it is like to lose touch with reality while dealing with grief and living in the dreadful knowledge that everything you care about in life is under threat.


The transcript below has been edited for length and clarity. Listen to the audio of the interview here.


Brooke Siem: Mary Ann, welcome. I read your book in about two days; I just blew through the whole thing and thought it was fantastic. I think it is one of the best accounts of the complex nature of psychosis. Please tell us a little bit about your experience and

The Episode

.


Mary Ann Kenny:

 Thank you, Brooke, for agreeing to interview me. I’m delighted to be here. Yes, I am the author of

The Episode

, and the subtitle is

A True Story of Loss, Madness and Healing

.

The Episode

 was published in the UK and Ireland last year. So far it hasn’t been published in the United States, but let’s hope that this is the first step to bring it and my story to an American audience.


I absolutely do think that what I experienced was a very clear episode of psychosis. Obviously, one of the purposes of our interview today is for me to describe that and to try to explain what I think caused it.


Siem: I think what was so interesting is that it just made me so angry to read how people were treating you. I feel like maybe I’m getting a little ahead of myself here, so let’s bring it back. Please tell me, where did this all start?


Kenny:

 My story began with a bereavement. A sudden and unexpected loss: my husband and partner of 15 years went out for a jog and died from undiagnosed heart disease in 2015; that’s when it all happened. We had two small children at the time, aged eight and six. It was completely unexpected and sudden. The three of us were left as exactly as you would expect, devastated and reeling from the shock.


To begin with, what I experienced was normal grief, I would say, looking back. It was devastating, it was debilitating, and it was deeply distressing. I was particularly heartbroken for my children’s sake. Most of my focus in the early months was on them and trying to keep the show on the road. The big change in my story happened when I took an SSRI for the first time.


Siem: Sertraline (Zoloft), right?


Kenny:

 Yes, 50 milligrams of sertraline.


Siem: Another reason why your story really brought up a lot of emotion in me was because my father also dropped dead very suddenly. One day he was there; one day he wasn’t. I was the child in this situation, so I watched my mother and distinctly remember the feeling of the subtraction. You went from four to three, we went from three to two, and how odd that period can be because life still keeps going. That’s how I got medicated: I got put on psych drugs.


I think I feel a kinship with you, specifically from that standpoint of being in that situation. What stood out to me is that we meet John, he dies fairly quickly, and we immediately go to the same situation that I experienced, which was, maybe you should see someone and not much time had passed. Can we talk about that a little bit?


Kenny:

 It was approximately two months after the bereavement, when people close to me started suggesting that I needed professional help. To begin with, it was therapy that they were suggesting. I did start to see a therapist. I had never been to therapy before in my life. I’d also never experienced anything that could be categorized as depression or anxiety. I felt at the time that it was working quite well.


He was an elderly gentleman who was providing support to me, practical support, helping me to get through, I suppose, day-to-day. I was seeing him once a week, and I used to feel better while I was with him. Then I suppose the sadness would return pretty quickly afterwards.


The advice I was receiving then from other people around me was, that’s clearly not working because I wasn’t showing any signs of …

author: Unknown
title: Tekstilden markete, depodan hastaneye: İşçiler 29 Kasım’da Kartal'a aynı dertle gidiyor
content:
DİSK'e bağlı 14 sendikanın çağrısıyla 29 Kasım Pazar günü Kartal Meydanı'nda yapılacak "Adalet, ekmek, özgürlük mitingi"ne dört gün kaldı. Tekstilden gıdaya, marketten depoya, okuldan hastaneye farklı işkollarındaki işçiler aynı meydanda buluşmaya hazırlanıyor. Mitinge giden sendikaların temsilcilerine Kartal'a hangi taleplerle gideceklerini sorduk.

Herkes kendi işkolunda yaşadığı sorunlarla alanda olacağını söylüyor ama sorunlarda ortaklaşıyor: Sendikalaşmanın önündeki engeller, geç ödenen ya da hiç ödenmeyen ücretler, fon vurgununda sermayeye akan paralar ve faturası işçiye, emekçiye kesilen bir bütçe. Konuştuğumuz sendikacılar 14 sendikanın taleplerinde birleştiklerini söylüyor. Kendi işkollarının sorunlarını da bu taleplerin yanına koyarak Kartal'a gidecekler. Hepsinin beklentisi, 29 Kasım'ın birlikte mücadelenin önünü açması.

Birleşik Tekstil Dokuma ve Deri İşçileri Sendikası (BİRTEK-SEN) İstanbul Temsilcisi Ercan Tilmaş, “Çağrıcı 14 sendikanın talepleri etrafında biz de birleşiyoruz” dedi. Tekstil hafif tehlikeli işkolu sayılıyor, ama Tilmaş'ın hatırlattığı gibi burada da iş cinayetleri yaşanıyor. Sendika Kartal'da güvenli çalışma koşulları isteyecek. Haftalık 45 saatlik çalışma süresinin 30-35 saate inmesini ve merdiven altı atölyelerde sigortasız çalıştırmanın denetlenmesini de talep edecek.

Konkordato ilan eden fabrikalarda ve birçok tekstil işyerinde ücretler ya geç ödeniyor ya hiç ödenmiyor. Tilmaş sorunu bölüşümde olduğunu söylüyor: “Para yok değil, para var; çünkü toplumsal üretim devam ediyor. Sorun bölüşümde. Bir tarafta foncular bizim hayal edemeyeceğimiz rakamları bir gecede alabiliyorken milyonlarca işçi geçinemiyor, kirasını ödeyemiyor.” İstanbul'da yeni örgütlenen sendika, ilişkili olduğu fabrikalarda toplantılar yapıyor. Tilmaş, İstanbul'dan tekstil işçileriyle Kartal'a gideceklerini söyledi.

Gıda-İş Genel Başkanı Olcay Ozak'a göre gıda işkolunda çalışanların yüzde 90'ının hiçbir sendikal örgütlülüğü yok. “Düşük ücretten güvencesiz çalışmaya kadar her sorunda herkesin kendi başının çaresine bakması sanki bir anayasal kuralmış gibi” diyen Ozak, taşeronun yaygın olduğu işkolunda sendikaya yönelen işçinin tazminatsız işten atıldığını anlattı. Ücretler de iki üç ay ödenmeyebiliyor: "Patronlar ne zaman isterse o zaman ödüyor."

Fon vurgunu için ise Ozak şunları söyledi: "Sermayenin vergi borçları siliniyor ama işçilerin kredi kartları icrada. Üretmeye devam ediyoruz ama ürettiğimizden payımızı alamıyoruz. Bu tamamen siyasi bir tercih." Sendika bildiri, afiş ve işyeri toplantılarıyla mitinge hazırlanıyor. Ozak, Kartal'ın “tıkanmış önü açması” bakımından önemli olduğunu söyledi.

Büro, mağaza, market ve eğitim işçilerini örgütleyen Sosyal-İş'in Genel Yönetim Kurulu Üyesi Gökhan Keskin, 10 numaralı işkolundaki toplu sözleşme barajını anlattı: "Toplu sözleşme yetkisi alabilmek için barajımız 45 bin. Bu, dünyada ve Türkiye'de örneği olmayan bir baraj. Barajların kaldırılması, güvenceli ve sendikalı çalışma için alanda olacağız."

Market işçileri için istedikleri haklar ise en temel haklar: "Bizler işçiyiz, köle değiliz. Su içmek, oturmak en insani haklardır. Bu hakları sağlamayan marketleri teşhir edeceğiz." Sosyal-İş mitingde aynı işkolundaki Sine-Sen ve Özel Öğretmen Sendikası'yla ortak pankart açacak. Sendikalı kadın işçiler de 25 Kasım nedeniyle ve 29 Kasım'a çağrı için A101 mağazalarının önünde açıklama yaptı.

Nakliyat-İş Genel Başkanı Ali Rıza Küçükosmanoğlu'na göre mitingin talepleri sendika üyelerinin de talepleri. Küçükosmanoğlu, motokuryelerin iş hukuku yok sayılarak "esnaf kurye" diye çalıştırıldığını, işverenlerin bunu genel bir çalışma biçimine dönüştürmek istediğini söyledi. Emeklilik sistemindeki değişiklikler ve kademeli emeklilik de üyelerin gündeminde.

Özel sektörde sendikalaşma oranı yüzde 5'ler civarında. Küçükosmanoğlu bunun nedenlerini şöyle anlattı: "Anayasa Mahkemesi kararına rağmen bir yetki davamız 4-5 yıl sürüyor. Grev yasaklarıyla grev hakkı göstermelik bir hak olarak düzenlenmiş. Bunların hepsi 12 Eylül faşizminin ürünü olan yasal düzenlemeler." Sendika, nakliyat ambarlarındaki işyeri temsilcileriyle Aksaray'dan Eminönü'ne kadar yaklaşık 2 bin bildiri dağıttı.

KESK İstanbul Şubeler Platformu Dönem Sözcüsü Şahin Tanrıverdi, 2027 bütçesinin “sermayeye ve savaşa aktarıldığını” söyledi: "Eğitime ve sağlığa ayrılan payın büyük bir kısmı yine özel hastanelere ve özel okullara gidiyor. Bu hem emekçilerin çocuklarının eğitimde fırsat eşitliğini ortadan kaldırıyor hem de halkın …

author: Daron Letts
title: Forensic psychiatrist testifies in 1st-degree murder trial
content:
A man who allegedly killed his wife was not “completely psychotic” at the time she was shot, a forensic psychiatrist told an Iqaluit courtroom Monday.


 Dr. Maryana Kravtsenyuk testified Monday during the

first-degree murder trial of Danny Paul Eyaituk, an Iqaluit man charged with first-degree murder in the death of

his wife Annie Tracy Oqaituq, 36, who was found dead in their Sanikiluaq home on April 19, 2024.


The trial began June 9 in Sanikiluaq and continued until June 25 but stopped while

Kravtsenyuk was on the stand

 due to witness, judge, counsel and courtroom availability, defence lawyer Alan Regel said in an email to Nunatsiaq News.


Canada’s Criminal Code says a person cannot be held responsible for a crime committed while suffering from a mental health disorder that makes them incapable of appreciating the nature of the act.


Regel had asked Kravtsenyuk to prepare a report to assess whether Eyaituk could be found not criminally responsible.


The report established that Eyaituk has suffered from mental illness, including paranoia, since childhood and that he was addicted to cannabis and cocaine at the time of the alleged incident.


Drug use can be a contributing factor in sudden changes in mental health, Kravtsenyuk said in the report. Eyaituk’s mental health breakdowns were exacerbated by substance use and stress from conflict in his marriage, she added.


Late Monday morning, Regel asked Kravtsenyuk about Eyaituk’s state of mind on the day Oqaituq died.


“He did not appear completely detached from reality or profoundly confused regarding the consequences of the alleged act,” she replied, quoting from her report.


Eyaituk appeared alert in court, wearing a blue sweatshirt with a crucifix around his neck. His hair was tied back in a short ponytail.


The first half of the proceeding lacked an Inuktitut interpreter, for which Justice Susan Cooper apologized.


She scheduled final submissions for Tuesday morning, as long as an interpreter could go over the morning’s proceedings with Eyaituk on Monday afternoon.

author: James Crump
title: Mamdani Launches Healthcare Scheme Directly for Taxi Drivers
content:
New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani has launched a new scheme to bring accessible and affordable health care directly to taxi drivers doing airport pickups.


The new scheme will see Driver Health Hubs set up at John F. Kennedy and LaGuardia airports, where taxis make about 34,000 pickups each day. Taxi drivers who cannot afford to take time off work will now have access to facilities at places they often frequent.


The Driver Health Hubs opened on Monday and will operate weekly to provide taxi drivers with preventative screenings, vaccinations, sexual health tests, same-day doctor appointments and insurance enrollment assistance, the mayor’s office

said in a statement

 about the scheme.


The city will also be deploying mobile services vans that will bring care directly to drivers working in high-density areas across the city.


In a statement, Mamdani said: “Today, New York City is letting its drivers know that we’re here for them too. No one should be forced to choose between earning a living and seeing a doctor. We’re bringing lifesaving health care directly to the places where drivers work, so they can easily access preventative care and stay healthy.”


Bhairavi Desai, executive director of the New York Taxi Workers Alliance, said: “Four New York City taxi drivers died on the job over the summer. All suffered from chronic health conditions but couldn’t afford to take unpaid time off for their care.” She added that onsite services are a “first step” in winning comprehensive healthcare for drivers. 


Last week, Mamdani

announced plans to disband

 the controversial New York City police unit, Strategic Response Group (SRG), known for using excessive force against protesters.


Mamdani said the SRG will be scrapped in favour of a “civilian-led approach” to policing protest that will put “communication, de-escalation” and “coordination” front and centre.


Under Mamdani’s reforms, the use of tear gas, rifles, painfully loud noises above 90 decibels and kettling – the surrounding and trapping of protesters, usually before mass arrest – will all be banned.

author: Sasha Abramsky
title: The Worst Impacts of GOP Medicaid Cuts Haven’t Hit Yet. Dems Must Take Action.
content:
In the wake of the blue wave, Democrats can restore Medicaid and move toward passing Medicare for All.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Millions of people in the U.S. are currently in danger of losing their health care as a result of Donald Trump’s so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which was passed in 2025 with Trump in the White House and Republican majorities in both the Senate and the House.

The new bill tilted the economy evermore in favor of the wealthy, rolling back hundreds of billions of dollars of taxes and clawing back a portion of the lost revenue through extreme cuts to social safety net programs.

The biggest loser in the bill was Medicaid, which was coming off of more than a decade of expansion under provisions of the Affordable Care Act that allowed states to broaden eligibility for the program. Onerous new workfare requirements — requiring able-bodied recipients to prove 80 hours a month of work or community service — paired with more frequent eligibility checks, were crafted specifically to drive down the numbers enrolled in the health care program. Estimates of the impact range widely, but there is general agreement that somewhere between just under 5 million and just over 10 million people stand to lose their health care as a result of this bill.

Add in the millions being driven off of Affordable Care Act (ACA) plans by Congress’s refusal to extend tax credits as well as by rising premium costs, and there’s a real chance that, in coming years, America will revert to pre-ACA-era numbers of uninsured.

During the 2026 enrollment period, as deductibles and premium costs soared, the number of Americans in ACA-subsidized insurance plans dropped by more than one-fifth compared to the previous year; and, for those who stayed enrolled, many opted for far less comprehensive “bronze” plans rather than the increasingly unaffordable “silver” options that had previously attracted the most enrollees.

Astoundingly, according to the Commonwealth Fund, as of late 2026 nearly half of American adults under the age of 65 either have no health insurance, have experienced health coverage gaps at some point in the previous year, or are currently significantly under-insured.

Somehow the GOP thought it could dodge the issue by crafting the cuts to health care in a way that meant the worst impacts wouldn’t be felt until after the 2026 elections. Given the pain that people in the U.S. were already feeling around health care, it was a strategy doomed to failure.

In the run-up to the midterm elections, polls suggested that the U.S. public was deeply worried about access to health care. Economic issues, including the high costs associated with health care, topped voters’ anxiety lists — with democracy and corruption issues coming in next. Kaiser Family Foundation data indicates that 6 in 10 voters were “very concerned” about the cost of health care; and by a 20-point spread those voters believed that Democrats were more likely than Republicans to address this challenge.

The Kaiser Family Foundation analysis suggests that in swing states where health care was of most concern to residents, by a two-to-one margin voters worried about health care costs voted Democrat over Republican. In states such as Maine and Michigan, where Democratic candidates won on platforms that included a promise to push for Medicare for All, large majorities of the electorate told the pollsters that they wanted the government to play a larger role in securing access to affordable medical coverage for residents. In newly blue Texas, where more than 5 million residents currently lack health coverage, Democratic lawmakers have been lining up to propose legislation to expand Medicaid access in the state — almost daring the Republican majority in the state senate to block them and to then try to justify that action to voters.

Three-quarters of people in the U.S. now live in states with Democratic governors, many of them also with both state legislative bodies blue, meaning that state-level health care reforms will likely complement congressional efforts to bring more people under health coverage umbrellas.

Come January, Democrats have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reshape the health care landscape in the United States — or, at the very least, to lay out a set of policy reforms that they would enact were they able to get …

author: Maharnav Bhuyan
title: Labor and One Nation compete to arrest their way out of a mental health crisis
content:
Labor and One Nation agree on almost nothing, with the exception being on crime, where they read from the same script.

Premier Ben Carroll wants 1500 more police. One Nation wants more police, harsher treatment of repeat offenders and a 24/7 bail court. Its campaign launch promised to make Victoria the toughest state on crime. The Coalition has simply raised the bid to 3000. Labor's Attorney-General insists “tough bail is working”.

Victoria has run this experiment before. Labor funded 3135 more police between 2016 and 2021. Over 2024-25, the number of criminal incidents hit its highest level since records began.

Ask Victoria Police what drives crime and the answer reads like a social policy brief.

In June, it named the cost of living, recidivism, organised crime and drugs. In September, it listed organised crime, recidivism, mental health and illicit drugs.

Who ends up on the inside? In the latest national survey of people entering prison, from last year, 51% had been diagnosed with a mental health condition and 73% had used illicit drugs in the past year. In the month before prison, 43% were homeless and 46% were unemployed.

These statistics show that rather than being hardened criminals, prisoners are people who have been failed by a squeezed economy, a broken health system and by communities with nowhere to turn.

When people do reach out, the door is often shut.

About 4550 Victorians were waiting for drug and alcohol treatment on any given day last year. In June 2025, 14 men sat in custody waiting for a bed at Thomas Embling, the state’s secure psychiatric hospital. Victoria’s own royal commission found the mental health system had “catastrophically failed”.

On November 6, HungryPanda rider Feng Jianming was stabbed to death near the Queen Victoria Market. He was 47, a father of two, and had spent nine years working here to support his family. A second rider was seriously injured.

Roberto Urbano, 51, has been charged with the murder. He is presumed innocent, but the court has already seen something every politician promising more police should think about. Urbano’s lawyer told the court that he experiences schizophrenia.

Appearing by video link from a police cell, in front of a magistrate, Urbano stood on a stool and exposed himself to the courtroom. Police custody, a camera and a magistrate; there is no more heavily-policed place. If the law cannot reach a person in that state, another 1500 police officers on the street certainly will not.

People in a mental health crisis need care; they need treatment before things fall apart. Was Urbano seeing a doctor? Did he have somewhere safe to live? Those are the questions this case should prompt every party running in the election to answer.

None of this means people with mental illness are dangerous; they are several times more likely than others to be assaulted.

The lesson is simple: A society where vulnerable people can ask for help and get it is a safer society.

Instead, the money flows to prison cells. Since Labor’s “toughest bail laws in Australia” began in March last year, the prison population has grown by about 19%.

This year’s state budget found $229 million for new prison beds and $43 million for programs that keep people out of them.

Each prisoner costs the public purse almost $600 a day and more than a third of those released are back inside within two years.

One Nation’s other big idea — tougher sentences — is weaker still.

The Coalition offers more of the same. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson’s 3000 extra police would include recruits from Britain, Ireland and New Zealand.

The Coalition also promises a “one-strike” bail rule for serious offences and has promised to expand Adult Time for Violent Crime from eight offences to 20. Youth diversion gets a mention after the police, bail and sentencing pledges.

The Victorian Sentencing Advisory Council found that longer prison terms do not produce a matching increase in deterrence. A longer stretch inside does not treat what it was that put the person there.

You cannot handcuff the cost of living. You cannot arrest a mental illness.

This is not a call on parties to be “soft” on crime. It is about being more serious about crime prevention. That means funding mental health and drug treatment until the queues disappear. It means building the forensic beds, called for by the royal commission. People leaving prison need secure homes to go to. Nationally, a third expect to be homeless on release …

author: Freedom Editor
title: Bullshit Burnham’s war on the disabled
content:
Andy Burnham promised an end to forty years of neoliberalism. Instead, he’s embraced the persecution of its favourite scapegoats

The news that the Milburn Review is to recommend the end of Personal Independence Payment (PIP), and the health element of Universal Credit for most young people under the age of 25, is not a surprise to those of us in the disability rights community, but it is horrific all the same.

According to Labour, it’s for their own good; no-one, intones Andy solemnly, wants to be trapped in a cycle of dependency, do they? Of course, this is all bullshit. Intentions matter, and neither the Milburn Review into the number of young people not in education, employment or training (NEET) or the Timms Review into PIP itself, were commissioned for the benefit of the young or the disabled, but for the benefit of the government’s bank balance.

Put simply—and no-one is questioning this—the number of claimants has increased significantly since the pandemic. One million young people are not in work or education. And the government doesn’t want to spend money on the problem.

But the clue is in the chronology. Though COVID has been memory-holed by many, not least government, which has worked assiduously to prevent Long COVID being recognised as a disability, the UK as elsewhere went through a once-in-a-century pandemic a handful of years ago. Apart from the death toll, which the COVID Inquiry acknowledges was worsened by government policy, many were left disabled and chronically ill.

That’s not the whole story, but it’s a big part of it, and as with COVID more generally it’s one government simply pretends doesn’t exist. The Burnham/Milburn rhetoric on disability is one of sympathy, that this is a ‘moral’ choice by government, that these ‘changes’ are an opportunity for a generational reset for young people who have, by Burnham’s own admission, been failed by politicians.

On that last we can agree, but Burnham’s no break with that catalogue of failure. Like his predecessors Starmer and Reeves, Burnham’s characterised PIP as an out-of-work benefit, when it is isn’t – it’s paid to ensure folks can be independent (the clue is in the name) and meet the additional costs which are incurred by being disabled in an ableist society. This is a wilful play into right-wing ‘scrounger’ rhetoric.

Burnham’s not wrong to mention that austerity had an enormous impact on the young in the coalition years, but lest we forget this is a man who lost a previous chance at the Labour leadership primarily because he refused to vote against coalition welfare cuts in 2015, a decision which fuelled a grassroots revolt in the Labour Party and the ultimate election of Jeremy Corbyn.

Indeed, what’s proposed here is a massive real-terms saving to government dressed up as empowerment for its victims—which is the classic Labour play. But anyone with any critical faculty can read Burnham’s words and know they are bullshit.

His constant references to parity of esteem in the education sector could have been written by any government, Labour or Tory, for the last sixty years. As with everything with him, it is surface-level, hoping to play on common-sensical shibboleths that will encourage folks to look past (or not at all at) the actual policy.

The same weekend his op-ed was published, a TikTok found its way online from the Labour account with Andy saying “we used to have a laugh…talk about pub snacks” before the Union Jack came prominently into play. The more things change, the more they stay the same, as the Burnham revolution boils down to idiotic chat about pork scratchings and pints whilst the young have what precious little support they get taken from them.

Labour’s messaging this week is to say that what they propose is more humane than what the Tories want to do, that they are offering a jobs guarantee and hope. But like all Burnham’s promises it’s a mirage. Milburn has proposed a reduction in employer national insurance for young people, but not yet; young people will still be paid less for the same work too.

Young people still won’t be able to access the mental health care they need. They will supposedly be able to apply to ‘local funds’ for support, funds which don’t exist and if they ever did based on prior experience would be unlikely to be responsive. But this rhetoric is just to salve the consciences of those not directly affected.

Disabled people, and disabled young people in particular, are neoliberal capitalism’s …

author: Jordyn Tovey
title: What Would Marsha Linehan Do?
content:
Over the past few weeks, the world has shown up to mourn and honor the impact of Marsha Linehan. And I among them.

I had the formative experience of interning at a DBT clinic in Michigan on my way to becoming a licensed clinical social worker and psychotherapist. I spent over a year learning, teaching, and practicing the “gold standard” treatment.

Now, years later, I find that the tenets, theoretical formulation, skills, and dare I say, spirit of DBT have remained with me. As have the questions which ultimately led me away from practicing in a full-fidelity setting.

I struggled at the time to put words to my Catholic upbringing (and subsequent rebellion) rearing its head. Now, in her death, I am reminded of the peculiarities of what it was like to hear Marsha Linehan’s name invoked in clinical spaces.

For example, in required consultation, there would be callbacks to things Marsha had said and done in demonstrations to guide the therapist, rather than grounding in the individual, totally separate relationship of therapist and client. Dialectical behavior therapists practicing true to the texts are encouraged to borrow directly from Marsha’s style. Her cadence. Her turns of phrase. Her irreverence. Her intensity. Ask themselves the question: what would Marsha do?

The idea being that cutting through bullshit and speaking directly to a client’s pain with confidence and care was an active ingredient in the therapy. What I observed frequently, but far from always, however, was clients (and therapists) experiencing these words as arrogance or flagrant invalidation. The skills and behaviorism could read as instructional or cold despite what I would consider a near-identical delivery to the videos and writing of Marsha.

I’m reminded of her style in a popular and circulating audio clip of her guaranteeing to a client that they will get out of hell, they will not always hurt so bad…but on the condition that they don’t kill themselves.

I find the clip moving. Nearly hypnotic. Maybe it’s in my head that I feel it in my heart. She’s speaking with something adjacent to but not quite the same as authority. It’s a knowing.

Marsha Linehan empowered the field with a novel approach to outpatient care, fierce and disruptive calls for accountability where treatment can cause harm, and unrelenting empathy for an otherwise dismissed population. She related to and championed those deemed prognostically poor. Clinician-scholar and pioneer, certainly.

All things considered, as I, alongside many right now, reflect on her life, death, and legacy, I continue to go back to the open secret that Marsha relied on more than a mythical ideal of pure theory and empirical evidence.

Linehan’s obituary discusses her reluctance to speak to her own story, waiting until the scientific legitimacy of her work was sufficiently established (to whose standards, I still wonder) before discussing her own psychiatric history and how it intersected with dialectical behavior therapy.

As I’ve continued to grow and develop as a therapist, patient, critic, and maybe even hypocrite working proudly in a department of psychiatry despite misgivings about historical and current practices… I find myself experiencing never-ending conflict with the concept of evidence-based therapies. DBT as my ground zero.

I question, dialectically, how the evidence base is holding up an undeniably personal therapeutic approach. And where the lines become blurry about what is working and why.

I wonder what we lose in efforts toward replicability. Individual style, genuine moments, real connection.

Marsha Linehan’s famous irreverence was hard-earned. The passion she had was personal. The path she pointed to was forged through her now famously known story of choosing life despite being labeled a hopeless case. There are limits to repeating her words, her story, her approach.

I believe those limits are felt.

Rest in Peace, Marsha. Pray for Us.

Mad in America hosts blogs by a diverse group of writers. These posts are designed to serve as a public forum for a discussion—broadly speaking—of psychiatry and its treatments. The opinions expressed are the writers’ own.

title: AKP ilçe başkanıyla görüşmeyen ilçe sağlık müdürüne "istifa" baskısı iddiası
content:
Rize – Pazar İlçe Sağlık Müdürlüğü görevinden alınan İ.Ö'nün, AKP Pazar İlçe Başkanı Furkan Namlı’nın ziyaret talebini kabul etmediği gerekçesiyle geçen günlerde istifaya zorlandığı iddia edildi. Yeni Parti Rize İl Başkanı Saltuk Deniz, İ.Ö'nün görevine iadesini isteyerek, AKP yetkililerine “Kurum amirleri sizin hizmetkârınız değildir” dedi.

Edinilen bilgilere göre, 4 Ağustos 2026 tarihinde AKP Pazar İlçe Başkanı olan Furkan Namlı ve beraberindeki yönetim kurulu üyeleri, kurum ziyaretleri kapsamında Pazar İlçe Sağlık Müdürlüğü’nden telefonla randevu talep etti. İlçe Sağlık Müdürü Dr. İ.Ö’nün ilk talebin ardından müsait olmadığını belirttiği, ikinci telefon görüşmesinde ise 657 sayılı Devlet Memurları Kanunu’na tabi bir kamu görevlisi olduğunu ifade ederek siyasi parti ilçe başkanlarıyla makamında görüşmeyeceğini bildirdiği ileri sürüldü.

Rize'deki AKP yetkililerince bunun İl Sağlık Müdürü Prof. Dr. Gökhan Demiral’a ileterek Dr. İ.Ö’nün görevden alınmasını ya da istifa etmesinin istendiği, bunun ardından Dr. İ.Ö’ye istifa etmesi yönünde telkinde bulunulduğu ancak ilçe sağlık müdürünün bunu kabul etmediği savunuldu.

Dr. İ.Ö. bir süre sonra ise İlçe Sağlık Müdürlüğü'nden alındı.

Pazar İlçe Sağlık Müdürlüğü çalışanları da Dr. İ.Ö’ye istifa etmesi yönünde baskı yapıldığını ifade etti.

Yeni Parti Rize İl Başkanı Saltuk Deniz, Dr. İ.Ö’nün Pazar İlçe Sağlık Müdürlüğü'nden alınmasına tepki gösterdi. Kamu kurumlarında görev yapan yöneticilerin siyasi parti temsilcilerinin hizmetinde olmadığını vurgulayan Deniz, şu açıklamayı yaptı:

“Devlet kurumlarında çalışan görevlilerimiz siyasi parti temsilcilerinin hizmetkârı değillerdir. Kurum amirleri, hiçbir siyasi parti temsilcisi ile görevleri dışında görüşmek zorunda değildir. Daha önce de benzeri olaylar ilimizde yaşanmıştı. Rize İl Milli Eğitim Müdürü Halil İbrahim Akmeşe de İl Milli Eğitim Müdürlüğü görevine atanır atanmaz, daha koltuğuna oturmadan soluğu AKP İl Başkanlığı’nda aldı. Bunlar doğru şeyler değildir. Kurum amirleri sizlerin hizmetkârı değildir. Rahat bırakın çalışanları. Kurumlarda iş barışını bozmanın, amirleri ve memurları siyasal gücünüzü kullanarak görevlerinden almak ya da uzaklaştırmakla diğer kurum çalışanlarına gözdağı vermenin siyasi ahlakla da bağdaşmadığını düşünüyoruz. AKP sözcülerini ve İl Sağlık Müdürlüğü’nü bu konuyla ilgili açıklama yapmalarını, görevinden alınan doktorumuzun yeniden görevine iade edilmesini kamuoyu adına talep ediyoruz.”

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Petala Ironcloud
title: Native Youth Programs Are Building a Different Model of Mental Health Care
content:
These models are employing youth and grounding well-being in culture, relationships, and community.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Growing up in Eureka, a small city in Northern California, provided Roger “Chapreges” Jones an anchor in his Yurok culture. He took public K-12 Yurok language classes and Indian Ed covered school supplies. But when his parents divorced and he moved to Redding at 13, those resources vanished — and so did his appetite.

Chapreges got his first job at a Native American mental health clinic while grappling with an eating disorder hidden in plain sight. His new role at Two Feathers Native American Family Services became a kind of Trojan horse: He walked through the door looking for employment and found therapy waiting inside.

Founded in 1998 by a tribal consortium to strengthen Native family units in Humboldt County, Two Feathers has grown significantly since 2018, when its current executive director, Virgil Moorehead, joined. It went from having four staff members to having 32, including mental health clinicians, substance abuse counselors, and cultural coordinators.

Two Feathers serves a disproportionately large Native population across Northern California, where many Tribes and their citizens are either unrecognized federally or have been disenrolled. Critically, it serves Native families regardless of enrollment status — a stance that resists the disenrollment politics that plague underfunded tribes across Indian Country.

Chapreges is one of dozens of Native youth accessing Two Feathers services in a region where waitlists are long and federal funding cuts have gutted alternatives. A 2022 study from the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health echoes mounting research on the importance of cultural connection to Native youth’s mental health.

Chapreges’s experience speaks to that truth. He had struggled to acclimate to Redding without other Native youth or regular cultural resources beyond the annual Stillwater Powwow. In his sophomore year, he and his father, overwhelmed by the isolation, returned to Eureka, where Chapreges completed high school.

The following year, he became a youth ambassador at Two Feathers, promoting their culturally tailored programming: stick games, flower dance, trips to the local powwow, and the Young Bucks and Spotted Does programs for youth ages 8 to 12.

Moorehead is also a licensed clinical psychologist and has helmed a new era for the organization, implementing circular Native philosophy by creating a continuum of school- and family-oriented treatment services for Native youth and their families. Two Feathers’ approach reflects a broader Indigenous understanding of mental health that recognizes the effects of historical trauma while at the same time accounting for the distinct experiences of different Native communities.

One such program, the Acorn Youth Wellness Program, works with youth individually to bolster their cultural identity. “But I think giving them hope, you know, sense of belonging,” said Moorehead, “Those are all things that are measured.”

Moorehead said the program tracks attendance, cultural identity, and hope for the future. “I always say that if you don’t have kids that come to the program, you don’t have a program. And so through the way we did Acorn, it engaged kids and had them show up in the sense of coming back and back and back.”

In 2020, the California State Assembly’s Select Committee on Native American Affairs conferred the honor of a plaque, letter, and on-site visit recognizing the organization’s work to improve and stabilize the lives of Native youth and families in Northern California. The program’s success has attracted interest from other Native Nations seeking to replicate the model. Moorehead said he’s in early conversations with one tribe planning to launch their own version next year, though he declined to name specific nations in preliminary stages.

Another member of the Two Feathers staff, Jayla, who asked to be identified by first name only to protect her privacy, joined the organization at age 15 after seeing an employment ad. A year into her time at Two Feathers, in 2025, President Donald Trump proposed consolidating behavioral health funding. Despite the fact that Trump’s proposal has only been partially implemented, Jayla still sees the impact of it firsthand …

RUDOLF ROCKER NATIONALISME & CULTURE


 Rudolf Rocker Dessin de son fils Fermin


Présentation


Le 28 février

, les cendres du Reichstag encore fumantes, les Rocker décident que, pour eux aussi, c’est le moment d’abandonner l’Allemagne. Ils pensent aller voir le vieux compagnon Wilhelm Werner pour essayer de résoudre avec lui les nombreux problèmes qui surgissent devant un départ précipité, et Milly sort pour faire quelques courses pendant que Rudolf rassemble les feuilles d’un livre qu’il vient de terminer quelques jours auparavant.


 Mais Milly ne fait pas ses courses. Dans la rue, un marchand ambulant ami l’informe

sotto voce

 qu’Erich Mühsam vient d’être enlevé par la police secrète.


 Mühsam habite le même quartier de Berlin que Rocker, et ils se voient presque quotidiennement dans ces temps agités où les SA, troupes de choc du NSDAP

[1]

, font régner la terreur brune.


 Tous les révolutionnaires, tous les opposants au nazisme, étaient en danger de mort, surtout Erich Mühsam, Juif, anarchiste connu, actif participant avec Gustav Landauer aux événements révolutionnaires de Munich en 1919 (République des conseils de Bavière). Werner et Rocker, deux jours avant l’incendie du Reichstag, avaient convaincu Mühsam, réticent, de sortir du pays sans tarder. Cependant, il voulait laisser les affaires en ordre et retarda son départ. Hésitation qui lui fut fatale. Zensl, sa compagne, racontera qu’il avait le billet pour Prague dans sa poche au moment de son arrestation.

[2]


 Dans la banlieue sud de Berlin, dans ce faubourg de Britz, il y avait très peu de gens dans la rue les jours de travail, et en s’assurant de sa fenêtre qu’il n’y avait pas de mouvements suspects aux alentours, Milly Witkop et Rudolf Rocker, entreprennent la fuite d’une Allemagne livrée maintenant à la furie destructrice du nazisme. Ils ne portent pas de valises pour ne pas éveiller des soupçons, et Rocker prend sous le bras le manuscrit de

Nationalisme et culture

, fruit d’un long travail commencé à l’époque de son premier exil en 1892.


 Les idées qui imprègnent les pages de ce livre se sont formées petit à petit dans l’esprit de l’auteur, au cours de son chemin militant et de l’errance, premièrement à Paris puis à Londres, et elles ont pu s’exprimer par bribes dans des articles et des conférences jusqu’à la brutale interruption imposée par la guerre de 1914 et l’internement pendant quatre ans dans des camps, l’Olympia et l’Alexandra Palace, où il a été jeté par le gouvernement britannique en tant qu’« expatrié ennemi ».


 Expulsé vers l’Allemagne en 1918 avant l’armistice, il arrive, au bout de diverses péripéties, à se réfugier en Hollande. Et, à la fin de l’année, Rocker est à nouveau dans son pays d’origine après vingt-six ans d’absence. L’agitation politique y est fébrile entre les insurrections spartakistes et la révolution de Munich, et elles sont suivies d’une répression sanglante. Ces temps-là n’étaient pas propices au travail intellectuel et d’autres tâches plus urgentes sollicitent Rocker.


 En décembre 1919, se réunissait à Berlin le douzième congrès de la FVDG (

Freie Verinigung deutscher Gewerkschaften

) où Rocker présente les principes de l’organisation révolutionnaire anarcho-syndicaliste. Ce congrès propose aux vieilles associations qui composent la FVDG, dissoute pendant la guerre, de changer de nom et d’agir dorénavant en tant que

Freie Arbeiter Union Deutschland

 (FAUD), comme il avait été décidé à la Conférence de Düsseldorf en septembre de la même année. La force numérique du mouvement se multiplia atteignant le chiffre de 150 000 membres en 1921. Rocker s’engage profondément dans la construction de l’organisation ouvrière, et il parcourt le pays en donnant des conférences, en participant à des meetings publics et à des réunions organisationnelles. « Quelle que soit – écrit-il dans ses Mémoires – la façon dont on juge la situation en Europe après la Première Guerre mondiale, il est indubitable que la conflagration avait créé une situation révolutionnaire qui justifiait des attitudes d’attente porteuses de grands espoirs. »


 À ce moment, Trotsky et Lossovsky cherchent à mettre sur pied l’Internationale syndicale rouge, et invitent à Moscou pour le 1er mai 1921, les syndicalistes et les révolutionnaires, y compris les anarchistes, de tous les pays, mais il est clair que l’ISR resterait soumise à la politique du Kominterm …

author: Indo
title: On “Sultat al-Majalis”
content:
Rather interesting text on the Arab Council Communist group “Sultat al-Majalis” formed by Lafif Lakhdar and Mustapha Khayati. Originally published in "Al-Hewar Al-Mutamadin, Issue 8699, 6th May 2026”. Can be found here.

The Arab Communist Grouping, which published the magazine Sultat al-Majalis (The Power of Workers’ Councils), was a revolutionary organization that adopted the ideas of council communism, drawing inspiration from the experiences of workers’ councils in Europe. The group was active in the early 1970s and consisted of intellectuals and workers of Maghrebi (North African) origin living in France. Its members were influenced by the events of May 1968 in France and by the left-wing critique of the existing socialist regimes of the time.

The group focused on the idea that revolution should be led by workers’ councils elected directly by the workers themselves. It rejected the traditional Leninist party model and centralized bureaucratic authority. It regarded Soviet communism, as well as its Chinese Maoist counterpart, as systems that had nothing to do with socialism. In its view, both were forms of state capitalism, owned and controlled by a new class known as the bureaucracy, which, like the bourgeoisie, was hostile to the working class and its independent movement.

The organization also launched a scathing critique of existing Arab regimes, whether self-proclaimed progressive or conservative, as well as all Palestinian organizations and the very idea of a Palestinian revolution, insofar as it remained detached from an all-encompassing Arab revolution aimed at overthrowing the existing state structures across the various Arab countries.

The first and only issue of Sultat al-Majalis was published in January 1974. Its purpose was to promote awareness of the self-organization of workers and peasants, free from the tutelage of political parties. The magazine included translations of texts by leading international theorists of council communism, articles analyzing the Arab-Israeli conflict from a class-based perspective that rejected nationalism, and studies of Arab labor movements.

Despite its limited organizational base, the group had a notable intellectual influence in independent left-wing circles and helped introduce concepts of workers’ self-management. It remains one of the distinctive experiments in the history of the Arab Left, representing an attempt to offer a third alternative outside the frameworks of Arab nationalism and official communism aligned with Moscow.

The group operated clandestinely, which meant that some of its contributors wrote under pseudonyms while others remained behind the scenes. Its initial core included young university graduates from Beirut who had been influenced by the global New Left movement but chose to work under the umbrella of the group in order to distinguish themselves from the official communist parties and the Organization of Communist Action in Lebanon.

The relationship between Lafif Lakhdar (1934–2013) and Mustapha Khayati was central to the establishment of this tendency. In his writings, Lafif Lakhdar confirmed that he and Mustapha Khayati had overseen the publication of Sultat al-Majalis.

Mustapha Khayati was a Tunisian activist and intellectual, a prominent member of the Situationist International in France, and the author of the famous pamphlet On the Poverty of Student Life. Khayati brought Situationist thought and the critique of the “Society of the Spectacle” into the Arab context, an influence that was reflected in the pages of Sultat al-Majalis.

Lafif Lakhdar was a radical left-wing Tunisian intellectual and one of the most outspoken critics of state capitalism in the Soviet Union and the Arab regimes. He argued that the genuine alternative lay in the “power of workers’ councils,” exercising self-management. This position formed the central ideological identity of the group.

The magazine served as a platform through which Khayati and Lakhdar translated unorthodox Marxist texts and analyzed Arab conflicts from an internationalist perspective.

Regarding the joint activities of three members of the group in early 1970, before its formal establishment, the Palestinian journalist Bilal al-Hassan wrote the following in an article discussing the book Nayef Hawatmeh Speaks, published in Beirut in 1997:

В маленькой редакционной комнате еженедельной пропагандистской газеты мы с наслаждением предавались дружеской беседе между товарищами, как вдруг вошёл рослый парень с ремнём за плечами.

Он весело поздоровался с присутствующими, расстегнул ремни, поставил ящик на пол и сел на него, вытирая пот.

Пока мы ждали, что он заговорит, мы молча рассматривали его. Это был высокий, широкоплечий юноша с чёрными усиками на смуглой, загорелой коже и живыми, искрящимися глазами, как пенистое вино. Одет он был в деревенскую одежду, с некоторыми городскими штрихами или отголосками города.

Наконец, с улыбкой, очень непринуждённо, гость назвал своё имя.

Администратор газеты прекрасно знал его как неутомимого активиста, который очень часто писал ему – то из одного населённого пункта, то из другого – и с дьявольской энергией распространял брошюры. Где бы он ни проходил, люди массами подписывались на газету. Если он не был коммивояжёром, то уж точно был Вечным жидом[1]… – Вечным жидом пропаганды, – сказал парень с ящиком, широко и довольно улыбаясь.

И поскольку на наших лицах откровенно разливалась жадная любопытность, он принялся в общих чертах рассказывать о своей кочевой жизни.

В городе он был механиком и уже зарабатывал хорошую зарплату. Но, будучи человеком читающим и стремящимся к знаниям, завсегдатаем собраний, жадно ловившим каждое слово из дискуссий, которые велись в помещении профсоюза, он вскоре воспламенился нашим прекрасным идеалом человеческого освобождения. И тут же его охватила ненасытная жажда обращать в свою веру, тут же его озаботила великая проблема сельской пропаганды, сеяния за пределами промышленных центров – по этим обширным невозделанным полям провинции, тревожным и полным тайны. Далеко ли может зайти любая попытка городского рабочего, одинокого и встречающего враждебность? Почему бы не последовать прекрасному примеру русских революционеров, которые идут жить и работать среди крестьян?

Молодой и крепкий, без семейных обязательств, в один прекрасный день наш парень отправился по этим землям. Он запасся полезными и дешёвыми предметами, которые продавал с минимальной прибылью. Он изучил основы различных ремёсел и был на селе услужливым умельцем на все руки. В деревенских хижинах не было мебели или утвари, которую он не сумел бы починить или даже изготовить. Он даже чинил грубую обувь, за неимением сапожника, и нередко видели, как он вносил свой изобретательный вклад в ремонт или строительство домов…

При этом он довольствовался малым. Есть и спать – как придётся: иногда лучше, иногда хуже; иногда за несколько грошей, иногда в уплату за работу. В жаркое время он не брезговал спать под открытым небом, на гумнах или под скирдами. Умирать – не умирал. В общем: жил помаленьку – и со здоровьицем…

Таким образом он быстро завоёвывал сердца и доверие людей из деревень и маленьких городков, которые внимательно слушали его беседы и публичные чтения, охотно принимали его брошюры и газеты, задумчиво следили за ясными и светлыми картинами будущего, будущего с большей свободой и большим довольством.

Мы с волнением смотрели на доброго сеятеля, запоминая его облик и черты, словно пытаясь увидеть воплощение той благороднейшей страсти и того животворящего героизма.

— Вот уже пять лет веду эту жизнь, – просто заключил он.

Мы предположили, что он имеет в виду холеру и месть властей. Нет; мы поняли неправильно: речь шла об узах любви. Случаев и соблазнов ему не хватало; и не то чтобы он хвастался, но о многих он знал, что они не сказали бы ему «нет»… Но, честно говоря, решение не казалось ему из самых лёгких, как и не находил он лёгким найти женщину, которая бы ему подошла. Ужасная проблема…

И когда доблестный парень собрался уходить, уже приготовив свой запас печатной …

author: Unknown
title: Agnes Grundel - Novemberminnen
content:
Författare

: Agnes Grundel

Titel

: Novemberminnen

Källa

: Allarm november 1916


 Ett år har förflutit sedan vår kamrat, frihetskämpen Josef Hillström slöt sina av förtryck betyngda ögon, för att aldrig mera skåda den värld som fråntog honom allt - ja till och med rätten att leva. I den värld där han strävade att frigöra människorna, var hans egen frihet osäker. I det samhälle där han agiterade med varje gnista av sin outtröttliga energi, var hans liv icke tryggat.


Varför?

 Jo: Därför att han hade hjältemod nog att trotsa, att opponera sig mot våldets blodtörstige tyranner, som alltid mördat och stympat, bränt och krossat alla dem som försökt vrida makten ur deras järnklor, samt ersätta människornas lidande med lycka.


 Alla dem som i någon mån försökt att förbättra mänsklighetens förhållanden, alla dem som vågat fråga: med vad rätt kunna dessa legaliserade ogärningsmän tvinga mig att arbeta för dem, samt bestjäla mig produkten av mitt arbete, alltid ha de fått falla offer för den s. k. rättvisan. Sådana män äro farliga för förtryckarna, enär de ha förmågan att väcka andra och få dem att göra gemensam aktion mot förtrycket, därför måste de rödjas ur vägen.


 Josef Hillström var en av de oböjlige. Ingenting förfärade honom, in i dödens käftar trotsade han dem alla. De togo hans unga kraftiga, förhoppningsfulla liv, men hans skändligt utgjutna blod ropar på hämd, från alla delar av jorden juder det som av en tordönsstämma:

hämnd

. Så länge här finnes en slav, komma hans brännande odödliga ord och eldiga entusiasm inspirera miljoner till verksamhet.


 Josef Hillström har ej levat förgäves, oaktat han dog i blomman av sitt liv. Det säges han var en drömmare, kanske så, enär hans idé ännu ej hunnit bliva förverkligad, men han drömde ej när han i sina sånger gav slavarna råd huru att bekriga sina svurna dödsfiender. Det var realisten Joe Hill vi minnas och vörda.


 Joe Hill drömde om en bättre värld där arbetaren skördar fulla produkten av sitt arbete, där nyttiga medborgare styra samhället till allas bästa, där list, lögn, våld och bedrägeri ej längre triumferar, där små barn vårdas som praktfulla blommor.


 Att han lärde slavarna att förverkliga detta, däri låg Joe Hills brott. Någon invände hånfullt att han gick i döden för en kvinnas skull. Ja alltid ha frihetshjältar förhånats av den okunniga massan. Vi minnas kanske Robert Emmet, Irlands store frihetskämpe, en Voltaire, Thomas Payne m. fl.


 Samtidigt som Joe Hill mördades i SAlt Lake hade de samhällsbevarande här i staden konferens varvid en av de viktigaste frågorna för dagen var:

hur skola vi kunna fördriva I. W. W. männen ur U. S. A.

 Detta visar att dessa herrar tycka sig redan nu se hur deras makts sista dagar börja randas. De mötas för att uppgöra planer huru att på bästa sätt tillintetgöra denna organisation. En av deras planer är väl känd och praktiseras ofta, den att mörda de aktive ledande männen. För denna metod föll vår präktige Joe Hill, för samma försöka de få de tre kamraterna i norra Minnesota: Joe Smidt, Carlo Tresca och Sam Scharlet. Allt beror på er arbetare om de även i detta fallet skola lyckas. Skola vi låta våldets bödlar döda våra bästa och aktivaste kamrater. Nej. Låt oss visa att vi äro män och kvinnor med ett för rätt och frihet klappande hjärta och med mod att handla.


 Vi kunna ej bättre vörda Joe Hills minne än att följa hans sista uppmaning till världens arbetare:

Organisera.

content:
Author:

An Anarchist FAQ


PDF File Size:

 381 KB

The Anarchist FAQ presents a compelling vision of parenting based on freedom, mutual respect and trust in children’s natural capacity for self-regulation, challenging the authoritarian assumptions embedded in conventional family structures. Its strongest contribution is connecting the personal and political, arguing that raising children without coercion, punishment or imposed moralism is itself a form of anarchist practice. It places freedom, mutual respect and autonomy at the heart of parenting. It challenges us to reject the authoritarian structures of the traditional family and recognise that raising free, confident and independent children is an essential part of building a free society.

 An Anarchist FAQ found at

https://ananarchistfaq.anarcho-copy.org/

: Anarchist Parenting


Anarchist Parenting


 An Anarchist FAQ


 


Introduction:

 What methods of child rearing do anarchists advocate?


Part 1:

 What are the main obstacles to raising free children?


Part 2:

What are some examples of libertarian child-rearing methods?


Part 3:

 If children have nothing to fear, how can they be good?


Part 4:

 But how will a free child ever learn unselfishness?


Part 5:

 Isn’t “libertarian child-rearing” just another name for spoiling the child?


Part 6:

What is the anarchist position on teenage sexual liberation?


Part 7:

 But isn’t this concern with sexual liberation just a distraction from revolution?


Introduction:

What methods of child rearing do anarchists advocate?


Anarchists have long been aware of the importance of child rearing and education. We are aware that child rearing should aim to develop

“a well-rounded individuality”

 and not

“a patient work slave, professional automaton, tax-paying citizen, or righteous moralist.”

 In this section of the FAQ [see

here

] we will discuss anarchist approaches to child rearing bearing in mind

“that it is through the channel of the child that the development of the mature man [or woman] must go, and that the present ideas of . . . educating or training . . . are such as to stifle the natural growth of the child.”

 [Emma Goldman,

Red Emma Speaks

, p. 132 and p. 131]


If one accepts the thesis that the authoritarian family is the breeding ground for both individual psychological problems and political reaction, it follows that anarchists should try to develop ways of raising children that will not psychologically cripple them but instead enable them to accept freedom and responsibility while developing natural self-regulation. We will refer to children raised in such a way as

“free children.”


Work in this field is still in its infancy (no pun intended). Wilhelm Reich was the main pioneer in this field (an excellent, short introduction to his ideas can be found in Maurice Brinton’s

The Irrational in Politics

). In

Children of the Future

, Reich made numerous suggestions, based on his research and clinical experience, for parents, psychologists, and educators striving to develop libertarian methods of child rearing (although he did not use the term “libertarian”).


In this and the following sections we will summarise Reich’s main ideas as well as those of other libertarian psychologists and educators who have been influenced by him, such as A.S. Neill and Alexander Lowen. We will examine the theoretical principles involved in raising free children and will illustrate their practical application with concrete examples. Finally, we will examine the anarchist approach to the problems of adolescence.


Such an approach to child rearing is based upon the insight that children

“do not constitute anyone’s property: they are neither the property of the parents nor even of society. They belong only to their own future freedom.”

 [Michael Bakunin,

The Political Philosophy of Bakunin

, p. 327] As such, what happens to a child when they are growing up

shapes

 the person they become and the society they live in. The key question for people interested in freedom is whether

“the child [is] to be considered as an individuality, or as an object to be moulded according to the whims and fancies of those about it?”

 [Emma Goldman,

Op. Cit.

, p. 131] Libertarian child rearing is the means by which the individuality of the child is respected and developed.


This is in stark contrast to standard capitalist claim that children are the

property

 of their parents …

content:
