author: Ariel Giagio
title: Ajuste fiscal: cortar programas sociais não resolve o problema, dizem economistas
content:
O ajuste fiscal, muito cobrado por alguns economistas e entidades empresariais, como

Fiesp

 e

CNI

, não precisa passar por cortes em programas sociais na avaliação dos economistas Lucas Marçal e Mônica De Bolle. Ambos participaram da live da

Agência Pública


Quase Terça

, cujo tema foi o ajuste fiscal, na última segunda-feira, 23 de novembro. O programa, apresentado pelos jornalistas Thiago Domenici e Natália Viana, é transmitido no

canal da

Pública

 no YouTube todas as segundas-feiras, sempre às 17h30.  


“Não tem nenhuma necessidade de tocar em programa social, muito pelo contrário. Os programas sociais no Brasil, na realidade, o peso deles no orçamento é relativamente pequeno. Não tem nem sentido falar sobre isso.

 Eu acho que o que nós temos no Brasil, sim, é uma distribuição muito ruim dos gastos. O Brasil gasta muito mal”, avaliou a pesquisadora do Patterson Institute for International Economics, Mônica de Bolle, que foi professora da Johns Hopkins University e atuou como economista no FMI.  


O “Plano Moretti”, como ficou conhecido o projeto do governo para ajustar as contas públicas e reduzir despesas em mais de R$ 50 bilhões em 2027, foi aprovado na última terça-feira, 24 de novembro, com 353 votos favoráveis e 128 contrários pela Câmara Federal, após passar pelo Senado. Encaminhado à presidência, o plano foi sancionado por Lula no mesmo dia. A maioria dos votos contrários foi da oposição (PL), mas parlamentares de esquerda, que discordam dos riscos que a proposta traz aos programas e investimentos sociais, como Sâmia Bomfim (PSOL-SP), Erika Hilton (PSOL-SP) e Lindbergh Farias (PT-RJ), se abstiveram. 


Esse é o ponto criticado pelo pesquisador do Centro de Estudos de Conjuntura e Política Econômica da Unicamp, Lucas Marçal. “Algo que vem sendo criticado e que deve receber muita atenção é essa possibilidade de contingenciar gastos que não têm respaldo constitucional. É aí que entram os programas sociais, como o Bolsa Família, o BPC [Benefício de Prestação Continuada]. É claro que o custo político para contingenciar esse tipo de gasto é gigantesco, mas só o fato de colocar isso na mesa gera um problema”, explica o economista. 


“Na prática, é um retrocesso em relação ao arcabouço fiscal”, complementa. O texto aprovado diminui de 2,5% para 2% o limite de crescimento das despesas do governo federal acima da inflação no próximo ano, caso medidas de contenção sejam adotadas frente ao risco de descumprimento da meta. 


Entre as alternativas, De Bolle chama atenção para a avaliação das desonerações tributárias, ou seja, isenções fiscais: “Muitas delas que continuam e não estão dando resultado nenhum, não estão ajudando os setores em questão, mas estão sim prejudicando os resultados do governo. É difícil você reverter depois (…), os governos tipicamente não compram essa briga porque é politicamente complicado”.


Mesmo com dificuldade política apontada por De Bolle, a proposta aprovada aborda as desonerações tributárias. O projeto prevê uma mudança: quando as isenções eram de 90% do tributo, passam a ser de

80%

.


Nesse ponto, Lucas Marçal concorda, dizendo que

“das poucas coisas interessantes [do Plano Moretti] para serem destacadas, uma delas é a questão dos benefícios tributários e o uso que as empresas fazem deles para pagar os seus impostos. Então, uma forma de aumentar a arrecadação vai ser rever esses benefícios tributários que, de fato, são um problema e são um consenso entre a esquerda e a direita.”


Só cortar não resolve e outros ajustes podem ocorrer


Os economistas também concordam que sem ações conjuntas nas políticas fiscal e monetária, o problema não se resolve e outros ajustes serão necessários nos próximos anos. 


Para Monica de Bolle, faltou discutir um plano econômico durante as eleições e o Plano Moretti apenas resolve o que já estava colocado no arcabouço fiscal. “Sim, claro que vai [ser necessário um novo ajuste fiscal], porque isso não está abordando o problema de fundo. […] o plano Moretti nada mais é do que uma rota de voo para alcançarmos a meta de superávit primário que nós nos demos muito antes das eleições. Já tínhamos um arcabouço fiscal [com] metas fiscais definidas para o ano de 2027”, explica. 


Um novo ajuste pode ocorrer ainda este ano. Após a aprovação do Plano Moretti, o governo está pressionado a fazer mais cortes, segundo apuração da

Folha de S. Paulo

. Na matéria, economistas ouvidos pelo jornal sugerem reduzir de forma permanente despesas …

author: Brett Wilkins
title: New Pentagon Strategy Embraces Potential Use of “Tactical” Nuclear Weapons
content:
Senators Edward Markey and Jeff Merkley have called on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth “to drop these plans immediately.”

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

A pair of Democratic senators on Tuesday urged US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to abandon the Pentagon’s renewed embrace of so-called “tactical” or battlefield nuclear weapons under President Donald Trump, warning that the development and potential use of lower-yield fissile armaments makes nuclear war more likely.

Sens. Edward Markey (D-Mass.) and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) sent a letter to Hegseth condemning the Trump administration’s reported push to widen options for so-called “limited” nuclear warfare, arguing that the strategy threatens to undermine decades of efforts to prevent the use of such weapons after the US unilaterally waged history’s only nuclear war over 80 years ago.

“More nuclear weapons, particularly lower-yield weapons that leaders may perceive to be more ‘usable,’ will only increase the risk of a catastrophic nuclear war,” wrote the senators, who co-chair the Nuclear Weapons and Arms Control Working Group.

“Tactical nuclear weapons are the gateway drug to nuclear destruction, and we urge you to drop these plans immediately,” they added.

The letter comes amid reports that the Pentagon is revising US nuclear guidance to emphasize tactical weapons and limited nuclear options in conflicts, possibly including the increasingly protracted Iran War.

The push aligns with Hegseth’s doctrine of “maximum lethality,” which — when paired with his embrace of autonomous warfare and stated disdain for “stupid rules of engagement” designed to minimize civilian harm — risks treating the mass slaughter of noncombatants as the unfortunate but acceptable price of battlefield success.

Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby has defended the mainstreaming of tactical nukes as necessary to provide the president with more options in any war against a nuclear-armed adversary.

“We want to be able to give the president and secretary credible, rational nuclear options,” Colby said at an August conference hosted by US Strategic Command.

While Trump’s own intelligence agencies have concluded that Iran does not have and is not trying to build nuclear weapons, in addition to the United States, China, France, India, Israel, North Korea, Pakistan, Russia, and the United Kingdom possess such arms.

Arms control advocates warn that the very idea of a limited nuclear war is dangerously misleading. A weapon’s smaller explosive yield does not guarantee that a nuclear-armed adversary will respond in a similarly restrained fashion, or that a catastrophic escalation could be avoided, as the 1983 “Proud Prophet” war game chillingly demonstrated.

Whitley Strieber and James Kunetka’s bestselling 1984 novel Warday recounts in an investigative journalistic style a “limited” nuclear exchange between the United States and the Soviet Union that lasts less than an hour, destroying just a handful of cities on each side. Yet tens of millions of people are killed in the United States alone on the day of the war and in the following years, and five years on, much of the world has been transformed almost beyond recognition.

Recalling that perilous era of hair-trigger tensions and nuclear near-misses, Markey and Merkley noted that during the Cold War, the US military maintained thousands of tactical nuclear weapons, including torpedoes, artillery shells, short-range missiles, and even portable atomic “backpack” devices designed for soldiers to carry behind enemy lines on suicide missions.

As the Cold War wound down, the US eventually abandoned much of that arsenal. In 1991, then-President George HW Bush announced plans to eliminate virtually all US tactical nuclear weapons, and the country’s stockpile of such weapons has since declined by more than 90%, according to the senators’ letter.

But the Trump administration has been moving in the opposite direction. Trump’s first term saw the deployment of the lower-yield W76-2 warhead on submarine-launched ballistic missiles, and the president is currently pursuing a new nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missile and an accelerated weapons development initiative known as the Rapid Capabilities Program.

author: Chris Walker
title: AI Data Centers Linked to Hundreds of Premature Deaths Across US, Study Finds
content:
Those who believe they’re safe because a data center isn’t near them should “think again,” the study’s lead author said.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

A new study from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) finds that the expansion of data centers for artificial intelligence (AI) has had substantial negative health and air quality impacts — not just in the areas where most of these centers are being built, but also in regions far away from them.

As a result, hundreds of people across the U.S. are dying annually, the study suggests, with researchers finding that pollution from electricity demands of data centers resulted in around 650 premature deaths in 2023 alone. Considering the rapid expansion of data centers since that time, the number could be even higher.

“States hosting the largest data center loads do not necessarily experience the highest attributable mortality rates, while some states with little data center demand bear substantial burdens,” a summary of the study states.

Researchers compared electricity that was generated from areas with data centers and those without them. They then modeled the electrical output increase due to data centers in both areas, monitoring air pollution rates in various areas of the country.

Because the U.S. grid is interconnected, data center electricity demand is more spread out than many people realize. Different types of power plants also emit different amounts of pollution. So, while more data centers are being constructed in states like Virginia and Texas, Midwestern states, including Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota, and Kansas, are seeing higher per capita rates of death as a result of pollution from data centers.

“When people think about the negative impacts of data centers, they usually focus on the neighbors,” said Noelle Selin, senior author of the study. “But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centers are very widespread across a large region.”

“Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” Selin added.

In their findings for 2023, researchers found that data centers likely accounted for 513 premature deaths from fine particulate matter, while 137 deaths were associated with increases in ozone or fog that the data centers helped to create.

A separate study published earlier this month also demonstrated the enormous output of electricity — and pollution — due to the explosive growth of data centers in the U.S.

In that Harvard-based study, it was determined that data centers across the country emitted a total of 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide per year. That number is equivalent to the output of some countries, including Bolivia and Denmark.

Much of the research amounted to “detective work,” the authors of the study said, due to lax federal requirements on public disclosure.

“Communities shouldn’t need a team of Harvard researchers to analyze satellite images to understand their environmental impact,” said Harvard scientist Gianluca Guidi, who led the research team.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: It would cost $65M to repair all of Nunavik’s roads and culverts: Assessment
content:
Repairing all of Nunavik’s roads and culverts could cost an estimated $64.8 million, according to a new report from the Kativik Regional Government’s municipal public works department.


Director James Trimble and assistant director Ahmed Kouki presented the assessment to regional councillors during this week’s Kativik Regional Government council meeting Tuesday in Kuujjuaq.


The compiled data on 531 kilometres of roads and 781 culverts using lidar, which uses laser light for remote sensing. Municipal works staff used the data collected to create a database showing road and culvert conditions across Nunavik and cost estimates for each proposed fix.


The proposals do not include the construction of new roads.


The assessment was carried out under Isurruutiit Program 5, a $153.8-million

agreement

 between the KRG and Quebec’s Municipal Affairs and Housing Ministry to fund infrastructure projects.


Trimble and Kouki presented the assessment’s findings as part of their department’s activity report, which outlined municipal infrastructure projects under the Isurruutiit Program 5.


The public works department is preparing a report on the assessment for the ministry, and the data will also be presented to northern villages in December. Feedback from the villages will help the regional government identify priority projects, said the activity report.


The report does not specify any timeline for work or where the estimated $64.8 million would come from.


Also included in the activity report are updates on several drinking water infrastructure upgrades, reservoir installations, water treatment infrastructure improvements.


In Quaqtaq, for example, upgrades to the pumping station and water treatment plant are more than 50 per cent finished, with completion expected for early December.


In Kangiqsujuaq, wastewater lagoon construction has resumed and is expected to be complete by summer 2027.

author: Chris Walker
title: Despite Environmental Worries, Army Blasts Off 68 Barrels of Lead Azide in Iowa
content:
Some scientists urged residents to collect soil from before the blast, to compare with samples after the detonation.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The United States Army has detonated 68 barrels of lead azide in southeastern Iowa, disregarding concerns of residents and environmental groups about the potential harms of such an explosion.

The blast occurred around 9 am Central Time. Video from local news outlets showed several plumes of smoke from the detonation, and journalists covering the event said they felt a shockwave afterward.

The Army gave little notice about the planned detonation to local residents, announcing earlier this month that it would occur on November 20. After outcry over the announcement, the Army said it would delay the blast. A lawsuit against the Army from environmental groups further delayed the detonation until a panel of judges on the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals decided earlier this week to allow it to proceed.

Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) administrator Lee Zeldin claimed the mitigation efforts for the detonation on Wednesday “exceeded expectations.” President Donald Trump made the same claim in a Truth Social post shortly after the explosion took place. However, environmental experts say it will take more time to determine whether the mitigation efforts were entirely successful, as well as the extent to which hazardous materials were released into the environment.

NEW: The U.S. Army has carried out a controlled detonation at an ammunition plant in Iowa to prevent an uncontrolled explosion. pic.twitter.com/u1k715srLb

New York Times reporter Quinn Glabicki said he and other journalists covering the blast “saw smoke climbing several hundred feet into the air.”

“In the distance, what appeared to be debris flew into the sky,” he added.

The 68 barrels of lead azide amounted to 9,700 pounds of the hazardous bomb-making material. The detonation occurred at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in the small town of Middletown, Iowa. Previous warnings about the planned explosion suggested the toxins could spread beyond a 100-mile radius.

Winds were moving southwest at the time of the detonation, likely pushing any material that reached the atmosphere further into Iowa or potentially into parts of Missouri.

Before the blast, the Army issued a warning, writing: “All people, but especially infants, children, pregnant women, adults, and children with chronic diseases such as heart disease, kidney disease, or dementia, should avoid outdoor activities within affected areas until further guidance is provided.”

The Army also told nearby residents that, after an “all-clear” was issued after the blast, they should “wet-wipe high-contact exterior surfaces such as patios, decks, window sills, and outdoor play equipment to safely capture and remove any settled dust.”

Lead cleanup is notoriously difficult and often requires intervention from certified professionals. There is no safe level of lead exposure.

Two hours after the detonation, the Army held an inter-agency press conference, describing the situation as a “successful operation,” with one federal official stating that the EPA determined there was a “zero-point-zero percent detection level of lead in the atmosphere.”

Beyond the federal government’s follow-ups, some scientists said they planned to do their own investigations into the aftereffects of the blast. Shannon Bartelt-Hunt, chair of the civil and environmental engineering department at the University of Nebraska, told CNN that she urged residents in the area to collect topsoil samples before the detonation took place.

“I know the Army is doing some testing, but at the same time, I don’t think the extent of the testing that probably needs to be done is something they have fully planned,” Bartelt-Hunt explained.

Trump administration officials have claimed there was no “viable alternative” for disposing of the lead azide, which was at risk of becoming highly unstable. Incoming Democratic federal lawmakers have expressed skepticism about such claims, saying they do not excuse the government’s lack of transparency.

“I remain concerned about the potential health risks resulting from the U.S. Army’s planned detonation in Middletown and the lack of clear communication and transparency from the U.S. Army,” said Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D-Iowa), adding in a social media post before the detonation:

author: David Swanson
title: Song #3: Ya Rayeh Sub Bladi, Performed by Bara’em Ghirass
content:
By Musicians Without Borders, November 25, 2026

“Ya rayeh sub bladi” translates roughly as “Oh, Traveller Heading Towards My Homeland”, and is a piece of music written by Ahmad Qaboor about his longing for his homeland and the pain of exile. He himself is Lebanese, but the song has been adopted among displaced communities within the Arabic world, including Palestinians.

After months of rehearsals, the young musicians in our Bara’em Ghirass performed a concert on the 23rd October 2026 at the Ghirass Cultural Centre in Bethlehem. They played a number of songs including “Ya rayeh sub bladi”, which you can hear below:

Sadly, even though this concert was full of enthusiasm, dedication, and community, it did not have the finale it deserved.

During the concert, a complete lockdown was imposed on the surrounding area, making it difficult for participants and staff members to get home safely. Some did not reach their homes until the following day.

Lockdowns and imposed checkpoints like this are unfortunately a common occurrence for Palestinians living in the West Bank. This makes life unpredictable and unstable, and can make journeys of just a few kilometers last for hours.

Children deserve to take to the stage, share their culture, and be heard. They also deserve to get home safely.

These young musicians put so much into this performance, and we’re proud to share it with you, and to recognise the dedication of the teachers and team behind it. Because of their dedication, today we’re also giving you two bonus songs from the same performance , just to showcase even more of the incredible talent that comes out of our Bara’em Ghirass program:

author: Harriet Williamson
title: Cuba Life Expectancy Falls for First Time in 75 Years Under Illegal US Blockade
content:
Life expectancy in Cuba has fallen for the first time since 1950 as the island nation’s healthcare system buckles under a US-imposed economic and fuel blockade.


World Health Organisation (WHO) head Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus

called for the blockade to be lifted

 on Tuesday and warned US sanctions are endangering the lives of Cuban children.


Tedros said life expectancy in Cuba had fallen from 78.8 years in 2020 to 74.4 years in 2025 – the first decline since records began in 1950.


US president Donald Trump began escalating a decades-long economic embargo on Cuba during his first term, and this year sparked an acute humanitarian crisis by imposing a fuel blockade. 


This has led to medics struggling with daily power outages amid critical shortages of food, medicines and specialised baby formula. 


Cuban officials say

only a single tanker of oil

has reached the island since January, crippling the country’s electrical grid. 


On a three-day visit to Havana, Tedros outlined how Cuba’s infant mortality rate more than doubled between 2020 and 2025, and maternal mortality increased from 37.4 per 1,000 live births in 2019 to 44.1 last year.


“The intensification ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠of fuel restrictions and sanctions is causing direct harm to the Cuban people, especially the most vulnerable,” Tedros told reporters. 


Former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn said the blockade is “illegal, inhumane and barbaric”.


Corbyn told Novara Media: “What is Cuba’s crime? Developing public services, building universal healthcare and raising life expectancy. Somehow, this means the people of Cuba are deserving of being put under the most intense, severe and cruel sanctions imaginable. 


“Let’s be clear what this blockade is: a crime against humanity. The US’s criminal blockade is literally killing people – and our own government is standing idly by. Enough. Lift the blockade now. Viva Cuba.”


The UN has repeatedly warned of the humanitarian consequences of the blockade, calling it a violation of international law and the human rights of Cuba’s population. 


The UN General Assembly has passed a non-binding resolution calling for an end to the US embargo on Cuba every year since 1992.

author: Maureen Fubara
title: Who Checks the Incumbents? Decentralization and the Cost of Electoral Violence in Nigeria
content:
On 12 November 2026, supporters of an opposition party gathered in Lagos for a political meeting. Journalists were present to cover the

event

. Shortly after it began, attendees were attacked by a group of armed men who violently disrupted the meeting. A journalist was reportedly beaten with an axe, and his equipment was stolen. This attack in Lagos is hardly an isolated incident. Political convoys and

campaign gatherings

 have also been attacked in Katsina, Calabar and Delta State, where one person was killed and five others injured. The

European Union

 has already expressed concern over the growing incidents of violence and intimidation ahead of the 2027 elections.


For the ordinary Nigerian voter, the

consequences

 of election violence can be devastating. Families

lose

 loved ones, politically-orchestrated riots disrupts businesses, and the resulting environment of fear forces voters to choose between their safety and their right to vote. Voters should be free to choose their leaders without having to decide if voting is worth the risk. However, for political sponsors their calculations may be different and violence could be beneficial to achieve political goals. While the consequences of electoral violence are immediate for the voters, there are

hardly any consequences

 for the political sponsors and perpetrators. This raises an important question regarding who holds the sponsors of electoral violence in Nigeria accountable? In Nigeria’s violent electoral history and for the 2027 elections and beyond, this reoccurring question is deserving of attention.


Nigeria’s federal system makes the question of accountability particularly relevant. Its

constitutional federalism

 is based on decentralization expected to bring government closer to citizens, distribute resources and prevent excessive concentration of power. In principle, the distribution of power across levels of government should create opportunities for representation and accountability. However, distributing power does not necessarily mean

distributing effective checks

 on that power. This problem is not limited to presidential incumbents. Incumbents in decentralized systems have access to power, resources, and networks that can give them advantages over opposition candidates. Such advantages are not inherently unlawful, they only become problematic when incumbents misuse power and divert resources to intimidate opposition parties or facilitate electoral violence, more broadly. This triggers a related question to the one raised earlier about the unintended consequences of decentralization. If power is dispersed but accountability remains weak, does decentralization simply create more opportunities for political power to be abused?


When violence pays


Electoral violence is typically discussed in terms of its consequences for voters, opposition candidates and democratic institutions. For

incumbents sponsoring violence

, it could be beneficial for political purposes. Violence can be used to undermine opposition candidates and secure electoral victories, thereby protecting incumbents’ access to the financial benefits of holding office. Since the motivation for violence is linked to perks of power, the decentralization of that can lead to the replication of patterns of violence and intimidation at different levels. Thus, decentralization could create more opportunities for abuse of power, although these are largely unintended consequences.


Research

 on electoral violence in Nigeria has shown how fiscal decentralization in particular  can shape incumbents’ ability to recruit and maintain relationships with violence perpetrators. This suggests that electoral violence is usually not spontaneous or random, but strategically orchestrated by political actors as a means to eliminate competition and secure electoral victory. Although, Nigeria has

laws

 against electoral offences and institutions responsible for investigating and prosecuting them. Yet the existence of sanctions does not necessarily mean that politically powerful actors expect to face them. A severe punishment is ineffective if those responsible are shielded from investigations or protected from prosecution.


This is the crux of the accountability problem.


Who imposes the costs?


Consider the institutions responsible for electoral integrity. The Independent National Electoral Commission receives public funding through

constitutionally protected arrangements

 intended to …

author: Eden Fineday
title: May we all have a kôhkom — or a kokum
content:
Eden Fineday’s kokum, Irene.

Photo by Eden Fineday


In my 20s, I used to travel regularly from California, where I was attending university, to Saskatchewan to visit my family on the rez. 


My granny, Irene Fineday, lived in a little red house on Sweetgrass Reserve, now called

Sweetgrass First Nation

. 


Back then, in the 1990s, my cousin Etley also lived with her. Etley took care of her. Every day, she would brush her hair, cook her meals and generally do her bidding. She would drive granny into town for her appointments.


I only reconnected with my Sweetgrass family at the age of 14. Until then, I had lived with my white mother and my two white siblings in “Vancouver,” far away from my father and his side of the family. 


READ MORE:


Who gets to define a kôhkom?


I was told as a child that I was Native, so I understood it on an intellectual level, but I did not understand what it actually meant. Growing up, I was hungry for connection to my culture, but I had no one close to me who could teach me.


Once I was in touch with my Cree family, I began to visit at least once per year. 


Whenever I landed in Saskatoon, I would pick up a rental car and get on the road to the rez. It was about an hour and a half from the airport to my granny’s little red house. 


On the way, I always stopped in North Battleford and picked up some fried chicken. I would arrive on Sweetgrass with my offering, and my granny, my cousins, and whatever extended family was visiting would feast with me. 


Eden Fineday (right) with her kokum, Irene, around 2004.

Photo courtesy Eden Fineday


An understated, unreactive wisdom


Sometimes, I would take my granny and my cousin Etley out for a meal. On one such occasion, at a chain restaurant in North Battleford, a waiter came to our table to take our order. 


“What can I get you, kokum?” he asked my granny Irene.


I was taken aback. 


I had never heard someone non-Indigenous use a Cree word like that. In fact, until that moment, I’m not sure I had ever heard the word. I called her granny. I felt a wave of gratitude wash over me – both for him making an effort to respect my grandmother, and for teaching me the word.


Wow!

 I thought.

This white guy knew a Cree word.

 Not only that, but he used it to communicate something important — that my granny was indeed his kokum. 


All kokums are everybody’s kokums in public.


Granny Irene.

Photo by Eden Fineday


My granny was an understated person. She didn’t have big, instantaneous reactions. 


Once, I accidentally lit a frying pan on fire while I was cooking her some bacon. I yelled about the fire and the smoke, grabbed a cloth to wrap around the handle, ran to the front door with the frying pan, opened the door and the screen door, and threw the entire contents of the pan out into the snow off the side of the porch — while she watched me out the corner of her eye, barely looking up from her game of solitaire on the kitchen table. 


I’ve come to learn this non-reacting is part of our culture. So my granny didn’t jump for joy when this waiter addressed her the way he did. But her eyes twinkled and I could see that she was clearly tickled pink. 


The waiter also didn’t make a big deal of it. I think they both understood Cree ways of communicating. She placed her order.


That moment has always stuck with me. I think of it often, especially when I’m learning Cree. I hadn’t heard the word kokum very often growing up.


Even my Cree cousins on Sweetgrass called my grandmother “Granny” in my presence. Others, the ones she had raised, called her “Mama.” 


There were different names for her, depending on who was speaking and their relationship to her. I wonder now how much of that was simply family habit, and how much came from the pressure to speak English.


Eden Fineday’s grandmother Irene stands outside with her grandfather Alphonse in an archival photo.

Photo courtesy Eden Fineday


Kokum or kôhkom?


I’ve been reflecting on this because I was moved last month when I learned that the Oxford English Dictionary had added the word “kokum” in June.


It’s a version of the proper Cree word, kôhkom. Lots of people spell it without the diacritics or the letter H, both of which are actually instructions for how to pronounce the word phonetically. 


These widely accepted variety of spellings also serves a useful function — it shows us that, unlike kôhkom, which means “your grandmother” in Cree, kokum is an anglicization of the word, and the …

title: Podcast: Three Voices for Peace with Vanessa Vaglio and Alessandro Capuzzo
content:
By Marc Eliot Stein, November 25, 2026


Marc Eliot Stein, Vanessa Vaglio and Alessandro Capuzzo at the entrance to Prospect Park, Brooklyn, 2024


At the end of my freewheeling conversation with two peace activists for the November episode of the World BEYOND War podcast, Alessandro Capuzzo captured the meaning of our meeting with a succinct phrase: “A city that should be neutral, a country without a military, and the place where the United Nations exists”. The city that should be neutral is Trieste in Italy, whose government ignores protesting shipworkers and the law itself by using seaports to serve genocidal foreign militaries. The country without a military is Costa Rica, a shining and rare example of intelligent governance in a region and a planet that needs much more of the same. The place where the United Nations exists is New York City, where I first enjoyed meeting antiwar activists Vanessa Vaglio of Costa Rica and Alessandro Capuzzo of Trieste two years ago when they arrived with Juan Gomez of Chile for a global peace march, 3 Marcia Mondiale Per La Pace E La Nonviolenza.


Alessandro Capuzzo, Marc Eliot Stein, Juan Gomez and Vanessa Vaglio with a World March For Peace and Nonviolence banner in Prospect Park, Brooklyn, 2024


Vanessa and Alessandro are both part of

World Without Wars and Nonviolence

, a global organization since 1994, and I’ll be going to the United Nations on December 1 to be part of a continuing mission in support of nuclear non-proliferation and to call attention specifically to the use of ports on the Adriatic Sea for foreign military shipments, a growing operations despite the fact that shipworkers are protesting and that these violations of neutrality are illegal on many levels.


This is only one of many topics we touched upon in this month’s podcast interview. Vanessa talked about living amidst nature, the importance of women-led governments and the need to find new ways to welcome people into antiwar movements. Alessandro talked about Italy’s rightward turn, the growing crisis in Slovenia and the corrupt encroachment of foreign militarism via initiatives like the

India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor

 (IMEC). We chatted about the great novelist James Joyce’s years in Trieste, shared impressions of various recent global events, and managed to find a few laughs and lots of agreement. I really enjoyed this conversation with Vanessa and Alessandro, and I’ll be carrying the hopeful, joyful spirit of this interview with me when I join their organization’s delegation to the United Nations next week.


Musical excerpt for this episode: “Revisionist History Blues” by Moon Walker.

title: Rassemblement devant la prison des Baumettes dimanche 6 décembre
content:
Dimanche 6 décembre à 15h, rassemblons-nous devant la prison des Baumettes pour apporter notre soutien aux personnes enfermées !


Depuis la fin du mois de septembre, l'enthousiasme des lycéens à refuser l'état des choses est communicatif et nous a mis du baume au coeur. C'est cette joie et cette rage que l'État veut à tout prix empêcher de se répandre. Pour cela il réprime par tous les moyens : violences policières, interdictions de manifester, comparutions immédiates, couvre-feux et consignes explicites aux juges de distribuer des peines lourdes.


Des blocus aux manifestations, les mineur.es sont particulièrement visé.es. Iels subissent pressions et violences : mutilation et harcèlement par la police, traque et dénonciation par les proviseurs et chefs de services des foyers. Des conseils de discipline pleuvent et de nombreux·ses mineur.es passent devant le juge pour enfant.


De la rue à la prison, la justice donne à voir de manière criante son fonctionnement de classe et raciste. Comme le dit une proche d'un prisonnier des Baumettes “l'État se sert du mouvement social pour enfermer plus de pauvres et expulser plus d'arabes”. Pendant les comparutions immédiates, des peines de prison hyper dures ont été systématiquement assorties d'une ITF (Interdiction du Territoire Français) pour les personnes étrangères. Toujours la même politique raciste et sécuritaire : traquer, enfermer, expulser.


Suite aux nouvelles incarcérations, les galères des proches sont plus fortes que d'habitude : attente interminable pour obtenir un permis de visite, gros retards aux parloirs...La surpopulation des prisons atteint des records : des hamacs sont accrochés dans les cellules arrivants où s'entassent jusqu'à 4 personnes dans 9m². Les droits des prisonnier.es et de leurs proches, déjà peu respectés en temps normal, sont complètement bafoués.


Il y a de la résistance à l'intérieur, les prisonniers en promenade ont refusé massivement de rejoindre leurs cellules ces dernières semaines dans les prisons de Grenoble-Varces, de Toulouse-Seysses et de Lyon-Corbas.


Les élans de solidarité ont dépassé la rue avec des rassemblements devant les comicos et les tribunaux.


S'ils divisent pour mieux régner, notre solidarité dépasse les murs de leurs prisons.


Pour toutes ces raisons, il est important d'aller apporter notre soutien aux personnes incarcérées aux Baumettes :


Tous et toutes libres !

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: "Huna": Egyptian Author Abdelrahman ElGendy on Prison, National Book Award & Being Denied U.S. Visa
content:
This year’s annual National Book Award ceremony in New York City was marked by the notable absence of nonfiction winner Abdelrahman ElGendy, after the Trump administration denied the Egyptian author entry into the United States. ElGendy’s debut,

Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming

, chronicles his arrest and over six years of imprisonment, alongside his father, following arrest at a protest against the military dictatorship of Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. After his release from prison in Egypt, ElGendy obtained an

MFA

 in the United States but was forced to flee once again — this time from the U.S. to Europe — for fear of being targeted by immigration authorities over his criticism of Israel’s war on Gaza and U.S.-Egypt relations.


“It was a gutting thing to not be able to attend the ceremony. But it was also unsurprising,” ElGendy tells

Democracy Now!

 about being barred from receiving the National Book Award in person. “[I] have labored for so long my whole life to get to this point, only to again and again and again be forced to witness it all from afar and detached from the people I love.”


We speak to ElGendy about the weaponization of the visa process, in both the U.S. and Egypt, “as a form of transnational repression,” his arrest and imprisonment beginning at the age of just 17, and the Egyptian government’s ongoing repression of free speech, including its attempted closure of the independent news outlet

Mada Masr

, whose lawyers were in court today appealing its shutdown.


“

Mada

 carries so much of the archive of our revolutionary history … so to erase it is to erase an archive,” says ElGendy, whose early writings were smuggled out of prison and first published in

Mada Masr

. “The current Egyptian military dictatorship [is] a frantic project of erasure of everything that has to do with the revolution, and it’s an insistence on erasing every trace that would allow people to remember that revolution has happened, that this rupture has happened before.”

author: Daron Letts
title: Students serve spaghetti with help from sirens in Rankin Inlet
content:
Three Rankin Inlet elders and their households enjoyed catered spaghetti meals prepared by students at Maani Ulujuk Ilinniarvik High School on Friday.


Student chefs Theresa Ikkutaq-Kurok, left, and Jessie Twyee prepare 45 portions of garlic bread in the Maani Ulujuk Ilinniarvik kitchen on Friday. (Photo courtesy of Mark Ronald)


“It was all for the elders,” said 15-year old student chef Brandon Amarook in a phone interview about the project.


He and his classmates prepared family-sized servings — 15 portions each — of pasta with meat sauce and garlic bread as part of instructor Mark Ronald’s food studies class.


The sauce recipe came courtesy of RCMP Sgt. Darick Ramminger, who sat in on Thursday’s class as a culinary consultant.


The students agreed on a name for the officer’s signature sauce:

“No snitchin’ in the kitchen.”


Ronald and Ramminger first cooked up the idea while collaborating on the school’s breakfast program earlier this semester.


“It was a wonderful opportunity for students to put their awesome cooking skills to good use and share food with our elders, build relationships within our community and with RCMP,” Ronald said Monday during a phone interview.


The students gave the meals away through a radio contest, broadcast over the community’s 97.9 FM station.


Ronald said that 40 elders called in to participate, and students randomly drew three lucky names: Tommy Adams, Joan Kalaserk and Andy Aliyak.


Students delivered the meals to their front doors on Friday, chauffeured by Ramminger, Cst. Gabe Stuart and Cst. Stephen Edwards.


Ronald and school counsellor Lucy Makkigak accompanied the convoy as it drove from home to home.


“I never rode in a cop truck before,” said 15-year-old Jane Sanertanut.


Sixteen-year-old Brooke Schweder said “it felt good” to deliver the meals.


“The elders were really grateful,” she said. “They were smiling and that made me smile.”

author: daniel
title: Solidarität mit den Gefangenen für den Frieden!
content:
Zum Internationalen Tag der Gefangenen für den Frieden am 1. Dezember bittet die War Resisters‘ International, zu deren Mitgliedern auch die Graswurzelrevolution als assoziierte Zeitschrift zählt, um Solidarität mit Menschen, die weltweit wegen ihrer Kriegsdienstverweigerung oder ihres Engagements für Frieden inhaftiert sind. Ihre Namen und Gefängnisadressen werden in der Liste der Gefangenen für den Frieden veröffentlicht.

Die WRI ruft dazu auf, den Gefangenen Kartengrüße als Zeichen der Solidarität und der Ermutigung in die Haft zu schicken. Selbst wenn die Karten die Adressaten und Adressatinnen nicht erreichen sollten, machen sie deutlich, dass die Gefangenen nicht vergessen sind, was sich auf die Haftbedingungen günstig auswirken kann.

Die Liste enthält die Adressen von Gefangenen stellvertretend für viele andere, deren Adresse unbekannt ist oder die keine Publizität wünschen. Die Liste der Gefangenen für den Frieden von 2025 ent­hielt Haft­adressen in Aser­baid­schan, Belarus, Eritrea, Sin­ga­pur, Südkorea, in der Ukraine und in den USA. Besonders katastrophal ist die Menschenrechtslage in Eritrea. Dort werden Männer und Frauen zu einem zeitlich unbegrenzten Nationaldienst gezwungen, teils Militär-, teils Arbeitsdienst unter härtesten Bedingungen. Die diesjährige Liste der Gefangenen für den Frieden soll zum 1. Dezember 2026 auf www.wri-irg.org veröffentlicht werden.

Die Karten an die Gefangenen können sowohl gemeinsam und öffentlich als auch privat geschrieben werden. Die DFG-VK Mainz-Wiesbaden lädt ein zum gemeinsamen Schreiben der Karten an die Gefangenen für den Frieden mit Live-Musik von Strohfeuer Express, mit Film, Bilder-Schau, Speis und Trank: Zornheim bei Mainz, Samstag, 5. Dezember 2026, 13 Uhr, HerrBerts Kulturscheune, Untergasse 10, 55270 Zornheim. www.dfg-vk-mainz.de

author: Unknown
title: Rivolte contadine ed emigrazione forzata
content:
Un approfondimento a cura del

Collettivo Politico Addunati

 in merito alle mobilitazioni degli agricoltori odierne con uno sguardo che parte da un’analisi storica delle più importanti rivolte nel mondo agricolo della regione calabrese.


Le lotte agrarie in Calabria nel secondo dopoguerra e le radici dello spopolamento


Siamo alla fine di agosto, il mese dello stacco. Il lavoro — quel mostro multiforme che impone regole fisse e schematizza le nostre giornate — sembra concedere quasi a tutti una pausa dal giogo della produzione continua. Le temperature sono elevatissime, le giornate si scandiscono al ritmo delle alette dei condizionatori: un su e giù continuo seguito dal nostro sguardo fisso. Si potrebbe scappare, cercare un po’ di pace fuori dalle proprie case. Inutile dire che, provandoci, si resterebbe delusi. Strade, spiagge, montagne, colline e pianure: tutto è affollato. Turismo di massa, prezzi alle stelle e stress. Nulla che ricordi vagamente la possibilità di staccare la spina. Pare che il tentativo di trasformare ogni luogo abitabile in un centro commerciale itinerante stia finalmente funzionando. Ogni casa è una vetrina; ogni angolo vuoto tra i vicoli dei centri storici o lungo gli stradoni di provincia diventa buono per piazzare tavoli e sedie. Bar, ristoranti, lidi, camioncini di cibo da consumare in fretta. Il paradigma del «potremmo campare solo di turismo» si materializza davanti ai nostri occhi. L’illusione che basti sfruttare il patrimonio materiale (paesaggi, borghi arroccati, città) e immateriale (cultura culinaria, dialetti, folklore) per vivere di rendita è ormai diventata realtà. Del resto, è la stessa industria culturale e dell’intrattenimento — tra televisione, social network e piattaforme di streaming — a far passare l’idea che in Italia, nel 2026, non abbia senso investire tempo, fatica e denaro in nulla che non riguardi la ristorazione e l’accoglienza. Tra foodblogger, video-ricette e programmi come MasterChef, 4 Ristoranti o 4 Hotel, ci si convince dell’inevitabilità di un declino che appare irrecuperabile. Nel frattempo, assistiamo ogni giorno allo smantellamento del tessuto produttivo del Paese: delocalizzazione industriale, assenza di qualsiasi piano di rinnovamento, abbandono delle terre o svendita di piccoli appezzamenti divenuti insostenibili per costi di produzione e dispendio di forza-lavoro rispetto al ricavo netto.


La retorica bucolica e la realtà dei campi


Ma agosto volge al termine. Agosto finisce e tocca trovare un lavoro. Dalle nostre parti, questo è il tempo della vendemmia — o almeno lo era. Conosciamo bene le retoriche spicciole e false che accompagnano l’agricoltura. Il senso comune — quello di chi non ha mai messo piede in campagna se non per un’«aperivigna» — associa il lavoro agricolo a un’esistenza bucolica, a un idilliaco ritorno alla natura. È la solita poeticizzazione della vita campestre. La realtà è ben diversa: ore sotto il sole, raccolti altalenanti, condizioni spesso inumane e l’assenza pressoché totale di tutele statali. Basta una grandinata, un virus delle piante o un parassita sconosciuto per azzerare il lavoro di anni. A queste variabili — solo in apparenza “casuali”, perché cambiamento climatico e riscaldamento globale sono tutt’altro che fatalità, checché ne dica un noto Ministro che liquida la questione sostenendo che «d’estate fa caldo e d’inverno fa freddo» — si sommano le crisi strutturali. Dal crollo finanziario del 2008 fino all’economia di guerra permanente a cui i governi cercano di abituarci, l’aumento del costo del carburante e il crollo dei prezzi alla produzione hanno reso il lavoro della terra insostenibile per i piccoli coltivatori. La Calabria, segnata da una storica fragilità economica, subisce tutto questo con un peso doppio. Eppure, nel torpore generale, gli agricoltori calabresi hanno deciso di alzare la testa e scendere in piazza per pretendere misure reali di sostegno. Non è la prima volta che contadini e coltivatori diretti si mobilitano contro l’abbandono delle istituzioni per rivendicare dignità e riconoscimento. Ripercorrere alcune delle principali proteste avvenute nella regione tra il 1947 e il 1957 aiuta a illuminare il legame diretto tra lo smantellamento sistematico dell’agricoltura calabrese e l’emigrazione forzata.


1947-1957: un decennio di lotte e repressione 


Partiamo dal 1947. La favola della pacificazione sociale seguita alla Resistenza stava crollando e il terzo governo De Gasperi mostrava le prime crepe …

title: Os rastros de Peter Thiel na Argentina
content:
Na quinta-feira, 23 de abril de 2026, depois de fechar a sala de imprensa para os jornalistas pela primeira vez na história da democracia, o presidente da Argentina, Javier Milei, recebeu

Peter Thiel

 na Casa Rosada, sede do governo. Foi o quarto encontro presencial entre os dois, mas representou muito mais do que isso: serviu como anúncio formal de que o tecnomagnata havia se mudado para a Argentina.


Por que Thiel levou suas três filhas pequenas e seu marido para o país vizinho? O que veio fazer na América do Sul uma pessoa com uma fortuna de quase 32 bilhões de dólares e que, segundo a Revista Forbes, está entre os cem homens mais ricos do mundo?


Ao contrário do que sustenta a narrativa libertária, não foi a vitória de Milei que fez Thiel começar a olhar para a Argentina. Seu interesse era anterior.


De um lado, havia a preocupação com a energia, diante do que os especialistas no assunto chamam de “transição de fase”: o divisor de águas que levaria a IA à “

superinteligência

”, superior à capacidade cognitiva de toda a humanidade somada. Em janeiro de 2026, Elon Musk previu que esse momento chegaria entre 2030 e 2031. O primeiro grande sócio de Thiel foi direto: “O fator limitante da IA é a energia”.


Há tempos o Vale do Silício alerta para essa necessidade. Já no ano passado, Sam Altman, fundador da Open AI e outro que saiu da escola de Thiel, antecipou a criação de grandes

data centers

 fora dos Estados Unidos. Um deles, não por acaso, deveria ser instalado na Argentina. Para solucionar esse gargalo energético, os tecnomagnatas planejaram desembarcar em países em desenvolvimento que pudessem atender às suas demandas.


Mas Thiel não é proprietário de

data centers

 de IA. A Palantir, sua empresa mais relevante, é, antes de tudo, uma plataforma de coleta de dados, mas, para existir, depende necessariamente de

data centers

.


Em 6 de junho de 2022, quando Milei ainda aparecia com apenas alguns pontos nas pesquisas para as eleições presidenciais,

a Palantir Technologies foi registrada como marca no Instituto Nacional da Propriedade Industrial da Argentina (Inpi)

. A empresa de Thiel declarou ao Estado argentino que ofereceria, entre outras coisas, “software para análise, organização, marcação social e rastreamento de dados e informações geoespaciais, cartográficas e de localização; software não baixável para processamento de dados destinado à pesquisa avançada de produtos, engenharia e design no campo da segurança nacional”.


A mansão de Peter Thiel em Buenos Aires, comprada por 13 milhões de dólares


Ao final, a resolução esclarece que

“todos os serviços mencionados anteriormente são projetados e comercializados para usuários governamentais, empresariais ou outros usuários institucionais

, com exceção de consumidores individuais, e não são distribuídos por canais de varejo”. Thiel só pensa grande.


A pesquisa no registro do INPI responde a uma das hipóteses sobre a presença de Thiel na Argentina: ele veio fazer negócios.


Em 8 de setembro de 2017, o jornal argentino Perfil publicou

uma reportagem

 sobre como a Palantir queria assumir

a digitalização dos arquivos secretos do atentado contra a Associação Mutual Israelita Argentina (Amia).


Em 1994, a detonação de 400 quilos de explosivos em uma caminhonete parada em frente à sede da entidade matou 85 pessoas e feriu 300. Foi o maior atentado terrorista da história do país.


O projeto parecia estar em estágio avançado. Em 13 de abril daquele ano, um executivo norte-americano da empresa de Thiel havia viajado à Argentina para realizar, no Ministério da Modernização, uma demonstração para a unidade de investigação sobre o atentado no Ministério Público. “Os promotores demonstraram preocupação porque arquivos secretos estavam em jogo”, relatava a matéria.


Documento do MP da Argentina sobre a tentativa da Palantir de acessar os arquivos do processo sobre o atentado à Amia


A reportagem acessou um documento apresentado pela UFI-AMIA para fundamentar a contestação da organização e a sentença judicial. A Agrupacção pelo Esclarecimento do Massacre Impune da AMIA (Apemia) levou o caso à Justiça e conseguiu que o Ministério Público mantivesse o controle exclusivo sobre o levantamento, a gestão e a custódia da documentação. Assim, a tentativa de Thiel de administrar uma das bases de dados mais sensíveis da história recente acabou frustrada.


A cronologia começa a ficar mais clara: primeiro, Thiel tentou se apropriar dos segredos de um dos …

author: anred
title: Golfo San Matías: el Gobierno acelera megaproyecto exportador de GNL y organizaciones advierten sobre una nueva zona de sacrificio
content:
Imagen: No a la Mina.


Mientras el Gobierno nacional celebra como «la mayor inversión de la historia argentina» el megaproyecto de exportación de gas de Vaca Muerta, organizaciones ambientales, comunidades costeras y especialistas advierten sobre sus consecuencias para el Golfo San Matías, uno de los ecosistemas marinos más importantes de la Patagonia, ubicado en Río Negro. Argentina LNG, impulsado por YPF junto a la italiana Eni y la emiratí XRG, obtuvo el ingreso al RIGI por una inversión proyectada de US$ 50.750 millones hasta 2050. La iniciativa contempla dos buques de licuefacción, infraestructura industrial y un sistema de transporte que conectará la cuenca neuquina con la costa rionegrina. La audiencia pública realizada en Sierra Grande los días 16 y 17 de noviembre dejó expuestas las tensiones alrededor del proyecto: cuatro estudios de impacto ambiental que reúnen más de 11 mil páginas, restricciones para participar, un fuerte operativo policial y cuestionamientos por la falta de una evaluación integral de los impactos. Mientras la decisión final de inversión fue convocada para el 30 de noviembre, organizaciones ambientalistas alertan sobre los riesgos para la biodiversidad marina, la pesca artesanal y el turismo.

Por ANRed.


El Gobierno nacional aprobó el ingreso al

Régimen de Incentivo para Grandes Inversiones (RIGI)

 de

Argentina LNG

, el megaproyecto impulsado por

YPF

 junto a la italiana

Eni

 y la emiratí

XRG

 para

exportar gas de Vaca Muerta desde la costa de Río Negro

. El anuncio fue realizado el pasado viernes 20 de noviembre por el ministro de Economía,

Luis Caputo

, quien lo definió como «la mayor inversión de la historia argentina». La iniciativa contempla

desembolsos estimados en US$ 50.750 millones hasta 2050

y una capacidad de exportación de

12 millones de toneladas anuales de gas natural licuado

 (GNL).

La decisión final de inversión fue convocada para el próximo 30 de noviembre

.


NUEVO RIGI APROBADO!


Argentina LNG USD 50.750 millones


El Comité Evaluador aprobó el ingreso al RIGI del proyecto Argentina LNG, desarrollado por YPF, Eni y XRG. Se trata de la mayor inversión de la historia argentina.


El proyecto contempla una inversión de USD 25.000 millones entre 2027 y 2030, y una inversión total de USD 50.750 millones hacia 2050. Permitirá exportar 12 millones de toneladas anuales de GNL, además de líquidos del gas natural, por más de USD 9.000 millones al año.


Para alcanzar esos volúmenes, se prevé un plateau de producción de 65 millones de metros cúbicos diarios de gas, equivalente a más del 40% de la producción actual de Argentina.


El desarrollo incluye inversiones en producción de gas rico en Vaca Muerta, la construcción de un gasoducto y un poliducto de 524 km cada uno, que transportarán los hidrocarburos hasta la costa atlántica de Río Negro, donde operarán dos unidades flotantes de licuefacción.


También se construirán complejos industriales en Neuquén y Río Negro para el procesamiento del gas y sus líquidos.


Durante la etapa de construcción se generarán 20.000 puestos de trabajo, con picos de hasta 40.000, y otros 8.000 empleos directos e indirectos durante la operación.


Felicitaciones a @HoracioMarin_ok por este extraordinario proyecto y agradecimiento al Comité RIGI por su arduo trabajo!


Más inversión, más producción, más empleo y más exportaciones para la Argentina.


— totocaputo (@LuisCaputoAR)

November 20, 2026


El proyecto comprende una cadena de infraestructura que incluye

un gasoducto de aproximadamente 525 kilómetros desde Vaca Muerta, un poliducto para transportar líquidos asociados al gas, instalaciones industriales en tierra y dos unidades flotantes de licuefacción que se ubicarían a unos cinco kilómetros de la costa, en el Golfo San Matías

. Allí el gas será enfriado y transformado en líquido para su transporte en buques metaneros hacia los mercados internacionales. Según los anuncios oficiales, l

a inversión prevista entre 2027 y 2030 rondaría los US$ 25.000 millones y las exportaciones superarían los US$ 9.000 millones

 anuales una vez que el emprendimiento alcance su capacidad operativa.

author: Unknown
title: Invisible violence: Psychological violence
content:
How do people come to hate themselves, reject their own identities and feel ashamed of who they are? To get to the root of this question, I would like to address a form of violence that often remains invisible: psychological violence.


Psychological violence targets our existence, our sense of self, our differences and, above all, our connections with one another. By psychological violence, we mean violence directed against our experiences, self-esteem, emotions, thoughts, perceptions and all our internal processes. This violence does not consist of a single action or word. Rather, it is a continuous process of humiliation that takes effect through repetition. This makes it difficult to recognize and equally difficult to find the words to describe what is actually happening to us. Psychological violence can take the form of bullying and stalking, as well as isolation and control. Psychological violence is not simply perpetrated by an individual but stems from a system of violence that creates the conditions for people to be humiliated because of their identities, characteristics and personalities. People are not born with a tendency towards violence; they learn such violence from their surroundings. As long as we live within a patriarchal, state-centered system, no sphere of life is safe from psychological violence, whether family relationships, schools, workplaces, neighborhoods, cities or even interactions on social media. Within these systems, people are devalued, and their identities, cultures and characteristics are portrayed as weak, stupid and ugly. They are declared unacceptable by the system, their identities and personalities are rejected, and they are not allowed to be themselves. This reaches a point where those subjected to violence begin to ask themselves: Which of these things actually belong to me, and which have been instilled in me? Those affected begin to see themselves through the eyes of those who humiliate them. The devaluation imposed by others becomes their own internal standard. This leads to a rupture with one's own self, accompanied by a breakdown of trust in one's surroundings. This rupture lays the foundations for exploitative dynamics of dependence through hierarchical relationships or systems. People's perceptions of themselves and their surroundings are increasingly determined by others. Ultimately, this violence is internalized and leads to a loss of self-confidence.


Human beings exist through their relationships


Human beings are highly complex. Their souls, bodies, thoughts and emotions constitute a form of existence capable of producing both incredibly beautiful and meaningful actions and cruel and meaningless ones. One phenomenon that we constantly experience today, and whose consequences have an enormous impact on our existence, is the separation of our bodies from our souls. We separate ourselves from our surroundings, society and nature. The fragmentation of human existence and the world deprives us of the connections necessary to better understand ourselves and our circumstances. If we want to understand who we are today, we must recognize that thousands of years of development are also embodied within us. The experiences of our ancestors continue to shape our worldview and identity today. For example, we cannot understand what it means to be a woman or a man without examining how identity has been constructed and transformed over thousands of years. Similarly, we cannot understand illnesses without considering environmental factors such as stress, pollution and their effects on the body.


Symptoms such as coughing may be signs of an illness. However, if we merely treat the symptoms without addressing their causes, they may intensify and occur more frequently. We then find ourselves primarily occupied with combating these symptoms rather than resolving the underlying problem.


Human beings can only be healthy when they are in harmony with nature and themselves. This is because human beings constitute a unity of body and mind or soul. This means that we must understand our psychological condition in relation to our bodies and surroundings. Anxiety, fear, stress and psychological problems, for example, can lead to sleep disorders, heart palpitations and even heart attacks. The expression "broken heart" is used when people in romantic relationships experience separation or another form of rupture. Those affected describe a pain as though their hearts have been broken, as …

author: Unknown
title: Women in Southern Kurdistan face violence, impunity and social pressure
content:
Femicide, domestic violence, forced marriage, economic dependence and gender inequality continue to threaten women's lives in Southern Kurdistan (Başûr). The March 8 Network, which reported that 69 women were killed in 2025, recorded 46 femicides as of October 2026. Women journalists and activists face political repression and digital violence, while Yazidi women continue their struggle for justice, overcoming displacement and rebuilding their lives following ISIS attacks.


Women's lives in Southern Kurdistan are shaped by interconnected social, economic, political and legal inequalities. Femicide, domestic violence, child and forced marriage, female genital mutilation, discrimination in employment, economic dependence and repression in the public sphere are among the fundamental problems threatening women's right to life and freedom.


Various legal reforms have been introduced in the field of women's rights, but their failure to translate into everyday life demonstrates the seriousness of the problem. Significant shortcomings remain in protecting women from violence, enabling them to achieve economic independence, ensuring their equal participation in political and social life and allowing them to organize independently.


Statements issued by women's rights organizations and reports published by international institutions in 2026 also indicate that this situation remains unchanged. Data on femicide, digital violence and women's access to justice particularly demonstrate the need to reassess existing protection mechanisms.


Legal regulations remain only on paper


The Southern Kurdistan Region adopted Law No. 8 on Combating Domestic Violence in 2011. The law established an important legal framework for preventing domestic violence and protecting survivors.


However, the adoption of the law does not mean that women have access to safety and justice in practice. Significant shortcomings remain in the effective handling of women's complaints, the prosecution of perpetrators, the implementation of protection orders and the provision of adequate living conditions for women.


Research published by Amnesty International in 2024 pointed to serious difficulties in holding perpetrators of domestic violence accountable. A report published by the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) in November 2026 also draws attention to the inadequacy of shelters in the Southern Kurdistan Region and the legal and institutional barriers to independent accommodation services for survivors of violence.


Women forced to leave abusive households struggle to rebuild their lives due to economic and social circumstances. This demonstrates that protection mechanisms must go beyond providing temporary accommodation. Conditions must be created in which women can live safely, work, receive an education and make their own decisions.


Child and forced marriages threaten the future of girls


Child and forced marriages are among the major problems restricting women's freedom in Southern Kurdistan. These practices directly affect girls' right to education, physical and psychological development, economic independence and ability to make decisions about their future.


Data from the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) show that 27.9 percent of women aged 20 to 24 in Iraq were married before the age of 18. Although this figure applies to Iraq as a whole, it reveals the extent of child marriage in the country.


Poverty, unequal access to education, family pressure and traditional social norms are among the factors behind early marriage. Forced marriages deprive women and children of the right to make decisions about their own lives.


Female genital mutilation: A violation of bodily integrity


Female genital mutilation (FGM) is another major problem that must be addressed in Southern Kurdistan. The practice affects the bodily integrity and physical and psychological health of women and girls, constituting a violation of fundamental human rights.


UNFPA data indicated that the prevalence of female genital mutilation across Iraq stood at 7.4 percent, while the figure reached 37.5 percent in the Southern Kurdistan Region.


Economic dependence is a barrier to women's freedom


Women's limited participation in economic life constitutes a significant dimension of gender inequality in Southern Kurdistan. Unemployment, precarious employment, low wages and the disproportionate burden of unpaid care work placed on women deepen economic dependence …

title: Mehmet Uçum cannot distort the facts
content:
Mehmet Uçum has once again written an article distorting the facts. It appears that Mehmet Uçum has been assigned such a task. He reflects the views of the state side in the Peace and Democratic Society Process. He is being made to write these views. In this respect, what Mehmet Uçum writes reveals the approach of those who instruct him to write.


He criticized the language used by the movement's leadership and members of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party). He is thus attempting to prevent the movement's leadership and DEM Party members from explaining the facts to the public. One purpose of this article is also to exert pressure on the movement's leadership and DEM Party members.


The difficulties in securing broad social support for the process are entirely the responsibility of the Justice and Development Party (AKP) government. The pro-AKP media does not speak of a peace and democratic resolution process. It speaks of eliminating terrorism and disarmament. The attacks and attempts at liquidation that have continued for decades are now presented as being pursued through different means. The AKP government has not prepared its own political base for this process and is trying every possible means and method to turn opposition political circles against it. It is attempting to turn a significant portion of society against the process through provocative practices. Mehmet Uçum makes baseless accusations against the movement's leadership and DEM Party members to conceal this reality.


If there is a Peace and Democratic Society Process today, it is thanks to the approach of Kurdish People’s Leader Abdullah Öcalan and the unprecedented steps taken by the Kurdish Freedom Movement in the context of such conflicts. The process continues today because of the Kurdish side's flexible approach and its efforts to encourage the AKP government to take steps. There is a widespread public perception that the Kurdish side is taking steps while the government is doing nothing. Mehmet Uçum is also attempting to conceal this public perception and the reaction against the government.


The Kurdish Freedom Movement has taken steps to eliminate all risks of confrontation with the Turkish military. It has left no armed forces inside Turkey and has withdrawn its armed forces from areas close to the Turkish border and the Turkish army. Downplaying these steps could result in the sabotage of the process. According to Mehmet Uçum, these steps are not particularly significant. He suggests that they should be unarmed wherever they are. He is almost suggesting that they should be left at the mercy of predators. The leadership and cadres of this movement must protect themselves until they return to Turkey. Otherwise, they could be eliminated in various ways. The movement's leadership has already stated that no one should expect them to seek refuge elsewhere. However, they insist that they will return to Turkey if a legal and judicial environment conducive to democratic politics is established. Devlet Bahçeli said after the weapons-burning initiative on 11 July 2025 that he wished the necessary laws had been enacted so that they could return.


Have laws enabling democratic politics been enacted, only for the Kurdish side to say that it will not lay down its arms or return to Turkey? Would anyone in their right mind take a step that would lead to their arrest? In fact, the issue of disarmament has already been resolved. Its implementation requires facilitating returns to Turkey. It is the AKP government's responsibility to make this possible. The Anti-Terror Law remains in force. This law should have been amended so that it no longer constitutes an obstacle to democratic political struggle. We have given just one example, because there are laws under which those engaged in democratic political struggle can immediately be arrested.


All the steps taken by the Kurdish side to date have been aimed at laying down arms and returning to Turkey. No one has said that they would refuse to lay down arms. author: Unknown
title: YRK reports Iranian airstrikes in Pêncewîn region
content:
Iranian regime forces once again attacked positions of the Eastern Kurdistan Defense Units (YRK) in the border area of Pêncewîn in Southern Kurdistan on Tuesday evening. According to the YRK Press Center, four consecutive airstrikes were carried out within an hour, beginning at 9 p.m. on November 24.


“Our forces suffered neither casualties nor material damage in these attacks. All our units are safe,” the organization stated.


The YRK described the bombardment as part of a series of Iranian attacks on various areas of Kurdistan in recent days. “The attacks are an expression of the Iranian regime’s ongoing policy of war, which targets not only the YRK but also the people and nature of Kurdistan.”


In its statement, the guerrilla organization characterized the repeated attacks as a sign of weakness on the part of the Iranian regime, which it said was attempting to compensate for its limitations and military shortcomings through airstrikes. “Such attacks not only fail to change the actual situation on the ground but also reveal the regime’s fear and helplessness in the face of the peoples’ demands,” the statement concluded.

author: Unknown
title: Parliamentary Monitoring Committee to consist of 19 members
content:
In a letter signed by Numan Kurtulmuş and sent to political parties by the Parliament Speaker’s Office, the parties were asked to submit the names of their members for the Monitoring Commission, to be established pursuant to Article 7, Paragraph 5 of the “Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Cohesion,” by 5 p.m. on Monday, November 30, 2026.


The distribution of seats among political parties on the committee has also been finalized. Accordingly, the AKP will be represented by nine MPs, the YENİ Party by three, the DEM Party by two, the MHP by two, the CHP by one, the İYİ Party by one, and the YENİ YOL Party by one. The committee will thus consist of 19 members.


The seats allocated to political parties that do not participate in the committee are expected to be redistributed among the other political parties.

author: Unknown
title: De Gennaro si è suicidato. Noi a Genova c’eravamo, ricordiamo e non perdoniamo
content:
Da

Osservatorio Repressione


Mentre politica e media celebrano il “servitore dello Stato”, noi ricordiamo Carlo Giuliani, la Diaz, Bolzaneto e le migliaia di persone colpite dalla repressione. La morte dell’ex capo della Polizia non cancella le responsabilità istituzionali del G8 del 2001.


Gianni De Gennaro, 78 anni, ex capo della Polizia e dell’intelligence italiana, si è tolto la vita con un colpo di pistola nella sua casa di campagna a Montiano, in Toscana. Il suo corpo è stato ritrovato questa mattina, 21 novembre, dopo che dalla sera precedente non aveva più dato notizie di sé. La morte arriva a pochi giorni dalla notizia dell’indagine della Procura di Caltanissetta che lo vedeva accusato di depistaggio nell’ambito degli accertamenti sulla strage di via D’Amelio e sulla scomparsa dell’agenda rossa di Paolo Borsellino.


Già si moltiplicano le dichiarazioni di cordoglio, i riconoscimenti istituzionali, le celebrazioni del grande investigatore e del fedele servitore dello Stato. Una narrazione che rischia di lasciare sullo sfondo ciò che per noi non può essere dimenticato. Perché Gianni De Gennaro era il capo della Polizia durante il G8 di Genova del luglio 2001. E noi a Genova c’eravamo. Ricordiamo quello che accadde, ricordiamo chi impartiva gli ordini, chi dirigeva gli apparati, chi costruì false ricostruzioni e chi, nonostante tutto, continuò a occupare i vertici dello Stato. Non intendiamo partecipare a nessuna operazione di riabilitazione postuma.


Ricordiamo Carlo Giuliani, ucciso in piazza Alimonda. Ricordiamo le persone massacrate nella scuola Diaz, quelle trascinate nella caserma di Bolzaneto, torturate, umiliate, private dei diritti più elementari. Ricordiamo i feriti, le persone colpite dalle cariche, quelle che non denunciarono le violenze subite, chi per anni ha dovuto affrontare processi, spese legali, condanne e conseguenze personali devastanti. Ricordiamo le vite segnate per sempre da quelle giornate e la lunga battaglia per smontare menzogne, falsificazioni e depistaggi. Non era stato il sasso, non era stato l’estintore, non erano stati i manifestanti a produrre quella sospensione materiale dei diritti. Era stato lo Stato, attraverso i suoi apparati coercitivi.


De Gennaro era al vertice di quell’apparato. Fu processato per induzione alla falsa testimonianza e definitivamente assolto dalla Cassazione nel 2011. Ma l’assoluzione penale non cancella la questione della responsabilità politica e istituzionale di chi dirigeva la Polizia durante una delle più gravi operazioni repressive della storia repubblicana. E non cancella il fatto che, dopo Genova, De Gennaro abbia continuato la propria carriera ai vertici della sicurezza nazionale, del coordinamento dei servizi segreti, del governo e dell’industria strategica, sostenuto da esecutivi di diverso orientamento politico. Mentre le vittime cercavano giustizia, il capo della Polizia di Genova 2001 continuava ad accumulare incarichi e potere.


C’è poi un nome che collega due pagine particolarmente oscure della storia italiana: Arnaldo La Barbera. L’ex dirigente della Squadra mobile di Palermo, figura centrale nel depistaggio delle indagini sulla strage Borsellino, venne inviato a Genova proprio da De Gennaro dopo l’uccisione di Carlo Giuliani e partecipò alla gestione delle operazioni culminate nell’irruzione alla Diaz. La nuova inchiesta di Caltanissetta chiamava in causa De Gennaro per una distinta ipotesi di depistaggio, relativa alle presunte pressioni esercitate su Salvatore Contorno affinché non rendesse dichiarazioni ai magistrati e all’occultamento di documentazione. Accuse ancora da accertare, per le quali il giudice aveva respinto la richiesta di arresti domiciliari avanzata dalla Procura.


La sua morte lascia inevitabilmente senza una risposta giudiziaria definitiva quelle contestazioni nei suoi confronti. Ma non deve interrompere la ricerca della verità sulle stragi, sui depistaggi e sulle responsabilità degli apparati. Né può diventare il pretesto per trasformare un’indagine della magistratura in una persecuzione giudiziaria, come già suggeriscono alcune reazioni politiche.


Non sappiamo quali ragioni personali abbiano condotto De Gennaro a togliersi la vita e non intendiamo attribuirgliene. Non proviamo gioia per la sua morte e non consideriamo il suicidio una forma di giustizia. La pietà umana non è in discussione. Ma non ci si chieda di cancellare il giudizio su ciò che De Gennaro ha rappresentato, né di unirci al coro delle …
